M2: same + memset(dstbuf,0) -> 10 TFAIL compare lines followed by ‘TPASS: Test 6’ (failflag not set). M3: Test 1 io_prep_pwrite from buffer (void*)8 (event.res=-EFAULT) -> TPASS

testcases/kernel/io/ltp-aiodio/aio-stress.c (runtest: ltp-aio-stress/ADS1000-ADS1053+)

  • Category: WRONG (secondary: WEAK, FRAGILE)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: creates files and runs AIO write, then read / random write / random read stages, reporting failure on I/O errors.
  • Problem: (1) check_finished_io() only treats a short/negative res as an error for READ/RREAD; any failed AIO write (-EIO, -ENOSPC, -EINVAL for misaligned O_DIRECT) is silently ignored, so write stages can never fail. (2) Every runtest entry passes exactly one -oN; for -o1 (read) and -o3 (random read) the only stage run is a read of the freshly created, empty fileN.bin in TMPDIR, so every read returns 0 bytes and st_size > offset + res is false, so it is not counted as an error. These entries (ADS1005-1012, 1018-1025, 1031-1053, …) pass without reading any data. (3) -o0 is meant to add the write stage, but if (stages_i) skips 0, so -o0 silently falls back to “all stages”. (4) With the default -a 500 iterations and 1 GB file size, record sizes <= 256k never finish the write stage, so read/verify stages are never reached anyway. (5) -v verification mismatches are printed as TINFO and never fail. (6) Default 1 GB per file x up to 8 files with no free-space check; ENOSPC is then ignored per (1). Also: stages_i is uninitialised when -o is omitted; -m is declared without ‘:’ so it always TBROKs; SAFE_SHMGET result is not stored in shm_id.
  • Evidence: aio-stress.c:324-358 (check_finished_io), :1205-1208 (stages_i), :1283-1290 (first_stage), :1060-1063 & :1117-1118 (iterations loop / restart), :1310-1318 (fresh files); runtest/ltp-aio-stress.
  • Suggested action: count any res != buf_size on writes as an error; turn verify mismatches into failures; always run a write stage (or pre-fill files) before read-only stages and fix -o0; reduce default -s or check free space; otherwise drop the read-only runtest variants.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,READ. HPE: ADS1000/ADS1005 TPASS. On a 4 MiB tmpfs TMPDIR, ‘aio-stress -o2 -r4k -f1 -s 64m’ (random writes far past ENOSPC) -> TPASS, no ‘io err’ line: write errors ignored. ‘-o1 -s 16m -v’ reads a fresh empty file -> TPASS. ‘-o0’ prints no ‘Adding stage’ (stage 0 skipped -> all stages). ‘-m’ -> ‘TBROK: Invalid shm option’. Also -s is bytes (‘-s 64’ TBROK too small), help says MB

testcases/kernel/io/ltp-aiodio/aiodio_append.c (runtest: ltp-aiodio.part4 AD000-AD009)

  • Category: WRONG (secondary: DOCS)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: “Append zeroed data to a file using libaio [O_DIRECT] while other processes are doing buffered reads and check if the buffer reads always see zero” - i.e. a buffered reader at EOF must never see stale/uninitialised blocks while AIO DIO extends the file.
  • Problem: the reader children run common.h io_read_eof(), which does offset = SAFE_LSEEK(fd, SEEK_END, 0);. SAFE_LSEEK’s signature is (fd, offset, whence) (include/tst_safe_macros_inline.h:183), so this is lseek(fd, 2, SEEK_SET): every iteration seeks to byte 2 and reads 4096 bytes from the start of the file. The readers therefore never touch the region being appended (after the first 64K write lands, bytes 2..4098 are stable zeros forever), and the test can only PASS. The claimed race (buffered read racing an O_DIRECT append past EOF) is never exercised. The bug predates the new-API conversion: the 2004 code already had lseek(fd, SEEK_END, 0) (git show 2283d3c0559b), so this test has been a no-op for its entire history. Secondary: -n help says “default 16”, code default is 8 (line 32 vs 193).
  • Evidence: testcases/kernel/io/ltp-aiodio/common.h:122; include/tst_safe_macros_inline.h:183-184; aiodio_append.c:148.
  • Suggested action: change common.h:122 to SAFE_LSEEK(fd, 0, SEEK_END) (and consider reading a little before EOF, e.g. seek to max(0, size - bufsize), since a read exactly at EOF returns 0 bytes and checks nothing). Fix the -n help text.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION. HPE: AD000 TPASS as-is (also VIRT). Mutation: every AIO append after the initial batch writes 0x41 instead of zeros -> still ‘TPASS: All bytes read were zeroed’. Same + common.h io_read_eof seeking to EOF-4096 (SAFE_LSEEK(fd, 0, SEEK_END)) -> ‘TFAIL: Non zero bytes read’. Readers never look near EOF

testcases/kernel/io/ltp-aiodio/dio_append.c (runtest: ltp-aiodio.part4 ADI000-ADI009)

  • Category: WRONG
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: “Appends zeroed data to a file using O_DIRECT while a child processes are doing buffered reads after seeking to the end of the file and checks if the buffer reads always see zero.”
  • Problem: identical to aiodio_append: readers use io_read_eof() whose SAFE_LSEEK(fd, SEEK_END, 0) is lseek(fd, 2, SEEK_SET). The children read bytes 2..4098 of the file in a loop and never read near EOF, so the description (“after seeking to the end of the file”) is false and the test cannot detect the stale-block-at-EOF problem it was written for. The only way it could FAIL is if the first 4K of the file were non-zero.
  • Evidence: common.h:122; include/tst_safe_macros_inline.h:183; dio_append.c:69.
  • Suggested action: fix common.h:122 (SAFE_LSEEK(fd, 0, SEEK_END) / read the tail of the file); both dio_append and aiodio_append are fixed by the same one-line change.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION. HPE: ADI000 TPASS as-is. Mutation: io_append() writes 0x41 for every block after the first -> ‘dio_append -c 2000’ still TPASS ‘All bytes read were zeroed’; same + io_read_eof() seeking to EOF-4096 -> ‘TFAIL: Non zero bytes read’. Same root cause as aiodio_append (common.h:122)

testcases/kernel/mem/hugetlb/hugemmap/hugemmap02.c (runtest: hugetlb/hugemmap02)

  • Category: WRONG (secondary: WEAK, OBSOLETE)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: 32-bit processes cannot open the low hugepage region when normal mappings exist there; 64-bit processes get the hugepage mapping from the high region.
  • Problem: In the 32-bit branch (lines 196-203), any successful mmap gives addr2 > 0 and TCONF. The TPASS branch requires addr == 0, but addr is the earlier MAP_FIXED mapping at low_addr and is never 0. So 32-bit can only TFAIL or TCONF, never pass. The 64-bit branch only checks that a hugetlbfs mmap with a non-MAP_FIXED hint succeeds anywhere, which hugemmap01 already covers. The low/high region model (2-3G, 1-1.5T) describes the old ppc64 slice layout and says nothing about x86/arm64. The five 256MB /dev/zero mmaps are unchecked.
  • Evidence: hugemmap02.c:110-123, 161-165, 186-204.
  • Suggested action: Drop, or rewrite as a ppc64-hash-only slice test with a correct 32-bit expectation.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,READ. HPE: hugemmap02 ‘TPASS: huge mmap succeeded (64-bit)’: on x86_64 only the 64-bit branch is built and it accepts any successful hugetlbfs mmap with a plain hint. 32-bit branch could not be built (no -m32 glibc on hosts); by source, success gives addr2 > 0 -> TCONF and failure -> TFAIL, TPASS needs addr==0 (MAP_FIXED low_addr) -> unreachable
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): UNCHANGED via MUSL,RUN. HPE glibc: ‘TPASS: huge mmap succeeded (64-bit)’; musl: same TPASS. Finding is about test logic (unreachable 32-bit TPASS, 64-bit branch accepts any hugetlbfs mmap) and raw mmap; libc choice adds nothing

testcases/kernel/mem/hugetlb/hugemmap/hugemmap14.c (runtest: hugetlb/hugemmap14)

  • Category: WRONG
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: No off-by-one around the 4GB boundary between a hugepage mapping and normal mappings (old ppc64 bug).
  • Problem: In the third mmap failure path (lines 99-110), the “region not free -> inconclusive” branch prints TPASS. Because there is no else/goto, execution falls through to an unconditional TFAIL. The first two failure paths have an else. The impact is small, since MAP_FIXED of an anonymous page rarely fails, but the inconclusive case is reported as both pass and fail.
  • Evidence: hugemmap14.c:103-109 vs 52-57, 75-80.
  • Suggested action: Add else before the TFAIL (or goto cleanup after TPASS).
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION. HPE: hugemmap14 as-is TPASS. Mutation: pre-map a page at the 3rd address and use MAP_FIXED_NOREPLACE so that mmap fails with the region occupied -> output ‘TPASS: Successful but inconclusive’ followed by ‘TFAIL: mmap() normal 2 failed unexpected: EEXIST’, rc=1: the inconclusive path falls through to TFAIL

testcases/kernel/mem/mmapstress/mmapstress09.c (runtest: mm/mmapstress09)

  • Category: WRONG
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: “The test fails if a child sees incorrect data” in a shared anonymous mapping stressed by forking children.
  • Problem: A child that detects corrupted data calls anyfail() -> tst_brkm(TFAIL) and exits non-zero. The parent sees WEXITSTATUS != 0, prints “child exit with err” and goto cleanup with no_prob still 0, so mapokay() is skipped and execution falls through to ok_exit() -> tst_resm(TPASS) -> exit status 0. The child’s TFAIL line is printed but the test’s exit code (what runltp/kirk use) is PASS. Same for fork/sigaction/wait errors.
  • Evidence: mmapstress09.c:292-297 (goto cleanup on child error), :353-364 (no_prob==0 path still reaches ok_exit()), :410 (child anyfail), :488-492 (ok_exit TPASS).
  • Suggested action: on the error path call tst_brkm(TFAIL/TBROK) instead of ok_exit(); better, convert to the new API (as mmapstress01 was) so child TFAIL is propagated automatically.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION. HPE: mmapstress09 -p 20 -t 0.2 TPASS as-is. Mutation: child data check forced true (if (1)) -> 12x ‘TFAIL: Test failed’ from children, parent ‘child exit with err ’ then ‘TPASS: Test passed’, exit status 0 -> child failures do not reach the verdict

testcases/kernel/mem/mmapstress/mmapstress10.c (runtest: mm/mmapstress10)

  • Category: WRONG (secondary: DOCS)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: mapper children verify file data while a writer child grows the file; parent checks file at the end.
  • Problem: Identical error propagation bug to mmapstress09: child data mismatch -> anyfail() in child -> non-zero exit -> parent goto cleanup with no_prob=0 -> skips fileokay() -> ok_exit() TPASS, exit 0. Additionally anyfail() in a child is tst_brkm(TFAIL, tst_rmdir), so a failing child removes the shared tmpdir under the running siblings. The header describes a third child that “maps the file in extend mode”; no such child exists in the code.
  • Evidence: mmapstress10.c:430-435, :486-511, :643-650 (child anyfail), :935-938; description :57-60.
  • Suggested action: make the error path report TFAIL/TBROK, use plain exit(1) in children; convert to the new API; remove the extend-mode text.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION. HPE: as-is TPASS rc=0. Mutation: child data check forced true -> children print TFAIL, parent ‘child exit with err ’ then ‘TPASS: Test passed’; rc=4 only because the failing child’s tst_rmdir removed the shared tmpdir (parent TWARN ENOENT), never TFAIL -> finding holds incl. tmpdir side effect

testcases/kernel/mem/shmt/shmt05.c (runtest: mm/shmt05)

  • Category: WRONG
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: “Create two shared memory segments and attach them … The addresses DO BUMP into each other. The second attach should Fail.”
  • Problem: The second shmat() is shmat(shmid, cp + SHMSIZE/2, 0) with SHMSIZE=16, i.e. an address 8 bytes into an existing page and without SHM_RND. The kernel rejects it at the alignment check before ever checking for an overlapping mapping, so EINVAL would be returned even if the overlap check were missing. It also re-attaches the first segment (shmid); shmid1 is created and never attached (the old version used shmid1).
  • Evidence: shmt05.c:34-35; ipc/shm.c:1542-1557 (if (addr & (shmlba - 1)) ... if (addr & ~PAGE_MASK) goto out; -> -EINVAL) precedes the overlap check at ipc/shm.c:1655-1661 (find_vma_intersection(...) -> -EINVAL). shmat(2): “EINVAL … unaligned (i.e., not page-aligned and SHM_RND was not specified)” vs SHM_REMAP text “Normally, an EINVAL error would result if a mapping already exists in this address range.”
  • Suggested action: attach shmid1 at a page-aligned address inside the first attachment (e.g. cp itself, or cp + page with a multi-page first segment), or rename the test to “unaligned shmaddr -> EINVAL” (already covered by shmat02).
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION. HPE: shmt05 TPASS EINVAL as-is. Mutation: shmdt(cp) before the 2nd shmat so nothing overlaps -> still ‘TPASS: shmat(shmid, cp + 8, 0) : EINVAL’ (alignment check). Control: shmat(shmid1, cp, 0) (aligned, overlapping) -> EINVAL from the overlap check. Test never exercises overlap

testcases/kernel/mem/shmt/shmt09.c (runtest: mm/shmt09)

  • Category: WRONG
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: “Attach at an address that is less than the break value: should FAIL.”
  • Problem: The heap is moved by +16384, -4097, +512 bytes, leaving the break 511 bytes past a page boundary (kernel stores the unaligned brk value; glibc malloc keeps its own brk page-aligned). vp = sbrk(0) - 32 is therefore not page aligned, and shmat() without SHM_RND fails with EINVAL at the alignment check, not because the address lies inside the heap VMA. The heap-overlap rule is never exercised. (The later SHM_RND attach above brk + sbrk() -> ENOMEM part is valid.) Side note: sbrk(-16000) shrinks 3201 bytes below the break the test started from, i.e. into glibc’s own heap.
  • Evidence: shmt09.c:47-60, :62; ipc/shm.c:1542-1557 vs :1655-1661.
  • Suggested action: use a page-aligned address inside the heap (e.g. (void *)((unsigned long)sbrk(0) & ~(SHMLBA - 1)) - SHMLBA after growing brk by several pages) so the EINVAL comes from the overlap check.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION. HPE: instrumented vp=0xeba31df page-offset=479 (unaligned; brk ends 0x…1ff as phase 1 said). Mutation: vp=0x200000000008 (unmapped, unaligned, far from heap) -> still TPASS EINVAL. Control: vp page-aligned inside heap -> EINVAL (overlap). The heap-overlap rule is never exercised; the SHM_RND/sbrk ENOMEM part passes
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): NEW (second finding, secondary category UNDEF/high; primary kept) via MUSL,RUN,SRC. [m01: UNCHANGED] HPE glibc: TPASS shmat EINVAL + TPASS sbrk ENOMEM; musl: ‘shmt09.c:48: TFAIL: Error: sbrk failed, errno = 12’ (separate problem, see NEW line). The unaligned-vp/EINVAL mechanism is kernel-side (ipc/shm.c) and libc-independent; phase-2 mutation stands || [m01: NEW] musl src/linux/sbrk.c:9 ‘if (inc) return ENOMEM’ by design -> under musl shmt09 aborts with TFAIL at its first sbrk(16384) on a correct kernel, and the final TST_EXP_FAIL(sbrk(INCREMENT), ENOMEM) would pass vacuously. glibc misc/sbrk.c:74 moves the break. Use the raw brk syscall (tst_syscall(__NR_brk), as brk01/02) or TCONF when sbrk(n!=0) is unsupported
  • Verification conclusion: The original finding (an unaligned vp, so the EINVAL comes from the alignment check, not from overlapping the heap) is kernel-side, and the phase-2 mutation stands. Under musl the test never gets that far (next section).

testcases/kernel/sched/clisrv/pthcli.c (runtest: sched/sched_cli_serv via run_sched_cliserv.sh)

  • Category: WRONG
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: client writes each line of a data file to the TCP echo server and reads it back (scheduler/threads client-server test).
  • Problem: The echoed line is never compared with the sent line; it is just printed to stdout. writen()/readline() failures are only perror()’d and the loop continues, and main always exits 0 once connect() succeeded. If readline() returns -1, recvline[n] = 0 writes recvline[-1]. So the only thing that can make the test fail is socket()/connect()/fopen() failing; the client/server data path is unverified.
  • Evidence: pthcli.c:63-95 (no comparison, errors only perror’d, recvline[n] with n<0), 137-150.
  • Suggested action: compare recvline with sendline and exit non-zero on mismatch or I/O error; better, rewrite as a new-API test with the server as a thread/child and checkpoint synchronization.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,VIRT. HPE+VIRT: run_sched_cliserv.sh passes as-is (3/3 each). With pthserv mutated to memset the echoed line to ‘X’ before writen(), pthcli prints ‘XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX’ for every line, clientCode=0, script exit 0 on both hosts -> echoed data is never compared.

testcases/kernel/sched/hyperthreading/ht_affinity/smt_smp_affinity.sh (runtest: hyperthreading/smt_smp_affinity)

  • Category: WRONG (secondary: FRAGILE)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: wrapper running ht_affinity on SMT/SMP systems.
  • Problem: The exit status of ./ht_affinity is not captured; the script then runs tst_resm TINFO "End: ..." and a bare exit, which returns the status of that last tst_resm (0). A TFAIL from ht_affinity is therefore never reflected in the exit code. Conversely, when CPUs are offline it prints TCONF but exits 1 (TFAILCNT incremented), i.e. reports a failure on a configuration it means to skip. cpu_cores from grep "cpu cores" | ... | uniq can be several lines on hybrid/heterogeneous systems, which breaks [ $cpu_cores -ge 1 ], and the script then prints “TBD” and exits 0 without testing anything.
  • Evidence: smt_smp_affinity.sh:31-35, 39-46, 47-59, 64.
  • Suggested action: drop with ht_affinity, or propagate ./ht_affinity’s exit status and exit 32 (TCONF) for the offline-CPU case.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION. HPE: in a dir with the real ht_enabled and a fake ht_affinity that prints ‘tst_resm TFAIL’ and exits 1, smt_smp_affinity.sh prints ‘TFAIL : MUT: fake ht_affinity failure’ then ‘End: SMT/SMP Affinity’ and exits 0 (script_rc=0) -> ht_affinity’s failures never reach the exit code.

testcases/kernel/sched/sched_stress/sched_stress.sh (runtest: sched/sched_stress)

  • Category: WRONG
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: run sched_driver for ~2 minutes as the scheduler stress test.
  • Problem: The script’s exit status is that of its last command, rm -rf /tmp/tmp$$ ./sched_datafile sch.measure, which is always 0. sched_driver’s exit status is discarded (its output goes to /tmp/tmp$$ and only tail -n 5 is shown). The test can never fail, even if sched_driver or the tc programs crash. It also writes to /tmp rather than $TMPDIR, and creates sched_datafile/sch.measure in the cwd (testcases/bin under kirk).
  • Evidence: sched_stress.sh:29-35.
  • Suggested action: propagate sched_driver’s exit status (sched_driver ... ; rc=$?; ...; exit $rc) and use a temp dir, or drop together with sched_driver.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,VIRT. VIRT: with a fake sched_driver that prints and exits 1 first in PATH, sched_stress.sh exits 0 (script_rc=0). Run as-is from an empty cwd (no ./sched_tc*, so every execl of a workload fails silently) it still prints ‘successful!’ and exits 0. Output goes to /tmp/tmp$$; only tail -n 5 is shown.

testcases/kernel/sched/sched_stress/sched_tc6.c (runtest: sched/sched_stress)

  • Category: WRONG (secondary: WEAK, DOCS)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: “a real time process is waiting on a file lock owned by a user process. The scheduler should elevate the user process priority to the same level as the real time process”.
  • Problem: (1) Linux has no priority inheritance for fcntl() locks; the claim is AIX-specific and nothing in the code measures it anyway. (2) With -f, fork_realtime() builds the child command from argv[2]/argv[3] assuming a fixed positional layout (sched_tc6.c:279-292), but the driver invokes sched_tc6 -tvariable -lsch.measure -pNN -df, so the child is exec’d as sched_tc6 1 -lsch.measure -pNN 0: it is NOT “fixed”/real-time (default priority_type “variable”), i.e. the scenario the test describes never happens. (3) The child writes its own result with fopen(logfile,“w”) (sched_tc6.c:204), truncating the parent’s line, so sched_driver’s measure_test() (expects two lines for sched_tc6) gets the child’s time as line 1 and an uninitialised t2asc for line 2 (fgets fails, atof(garbage)). (4) Same time()/100.0 units bug.
  • Evidence: sched_tc6.c:26-33, :146, :199-216, :276-305; sched_driver.c:468-473.
  • Suggested action: Drop (legacy AIX port whose core claim does not apply to Linux); at minimum fix the child argv construction and append instead of truncating the results file.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): REVISED via RUN,VIRT,READ. VIRT: exec-logging shims over a full sched_stress.sh run: 1620 sched_tc6 execs, all with argv ending ‘< -d >’ or ‘< -df >’ (leading space), and 0 re-execs of the forked child (argv ‘<1>…’). getopt never sees -f because of the space, so fork_realtime() never runs. Claims (1) and (4) stand. The ‘forked child’ timing line comes from fgets() on a missing second line.
  • Verification conclusion: The finding is right, and the mechanism is worse than phase 1 described. sched_driver passes ” -d ” and ” -df ” with a leading space, so getopt treats them as operands. fork_flag stays 0 and fork_realtime() never runs, which means the “real-time process waits on a user process’s lock” scenario never happens. The “forked child” result line is computed from a second fgets() on a one-line sch.measure, so it uses an uninitialised buffer. Points (2) and (3) about the child’s argv and truncating the log are moot because no child runs. Points (1) (no PI for fcntl locks on Linux) and (4) (time()/100.0) stand. Suggested action: drop.

testcases/kernel/sched/sysctl/proc_sched_rt01.c (runtest: sched/proc_sched_rt01)

  • Category: WRONG (secondary: WEAK)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: writing 0 or -1 to /proc/sys/kernel/sched_rt_period_us fails with EINVAL (regression test for 079be8fc6309 “Disallow writing invalid values to sched_rt_period_us”).
  • Problem: TST_EXP_FAIL(write(period_fd, "0", 2), EINVAL, ...) (proc_sched_rt01.c:45) writes TWO bytes: ‘0’ and the string terminator ‘\0’. In the kernel, proc_get_long() parses “0”, then because len < *size and the next char ‘\0’ is not in proc_wspace_sep {’ ‘,’,‘’} it returns -EINVAL (kernel/sysctl.c:311-312) before proc_dointvec_minmax ever compares against extra1=SYSCTL_ONE. So the “0 -> EINVAL” subcase passes on any kernel, including one without 079be8fc6309 (where 0 would otherwise be accepted). The “-1” and “-2” writes are exactly 2 bytes and are fine; the period_us+1 write uses strlen() and is fine.
  • Evidence: proc_sched_rt01.c:45-46; /usr/src/linux/kernel/sysctl.c:276-320 (proc_get_long), :595 (proc_wspace_sep), :699-706; kernel/sched/rt.c:33-41 (extra1 = SYSCTL_ONE).
  • Suggested action: use write(period_fd, "0", 1) (or strlen) so the range check is what produces EINVAL.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,VIRT. HPE+VIRT: as-is 5/5 TPASS. Mutant replacing write(period_fd, “0”, 2) by write(period_fd, “1000000”, 8) (the current valid period plus the trailing NUL) still gives ‘TPASS: echo 0 > sched_rt_period_us : EINVAL’ on VIRT -> the NUL alone yields EINVAL (proc_get_long), so the 0 subcase cannot detect a kernel lacking 079be8fc6309.

testcases/kernel/sched/tool/trace_sched.c (runtest: sched/trace_sched01 trace_sched -c 1)

  • Category: WRONG (secondary: WEAK)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: each thread “sets its priority … reads the priority that the scheduler sets for this task and also reads from /proc the processor this task last executed on”.
  • Problem: (1) The program never compares exp_prio with act_prio; it prints a table and exit(0) (trace_sched.c:446-462), so it cannot fail. (2) get_proc_num() returns atoi(&fbuff[fsize - 2]), the last two bytes of /proc//stat (trace_sched.c:166-183). Since 2.6 the last field is exit_code (fs/proc/array.c:660); the processor is field 39 (fs/proc/array.c:641). So every task is reported on “processor 0”. (3) The threads call sched_setscheduler(getpid(), ...) / sched_getparam(getpid(), ...) (trace_sched.c:237, :253): on Linux the pid argument is a TID and getpid() is the main thread’s TID (sched_setscheduler(2) NOTES), so 100 threads race to set the MAIN thread’s policy/priority and read it back; the threads themselves stay SCHED_OTHER. The collected data therefore describes neither the threads nor their CPUs.
  • Evidence: trace_sched.c:166-183, :237-262, :446-462; /usr/src/linux/fs/proc/array.c:641,660; sched_setscheduler(2) “the thread whose ID is specified in pid”.
  • Suggested action: Drop (data is meaningless and nothing is asserted), or rewrite with gettid()/ pthread_setschedparam, parse field 39, and assert act_prio == exp_prio.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,VIRT. HPE (24 CPUs) ‘trace_sched -c 24’: exit 0; all 2400 rows under ‘processor number = 0’, 1 distinct ‘pid of task’ (main PID), and 1953/2400 rows with priority requested != assigned (e.g. requested 37, assigned 22). VIRT ‘trace_sched -c 1’: 100 rows, 1 PID, 48 mismatches, rc 0. Nothing is asserted.

testcases/kernel/security/filecaps/verify_caps_exec.c (runtest: capability/filecaps via filecapstest.sh)

  • Category: WRONG (secondary: FRAGILE)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: file capabilities: unprivileged users cannot set them; pP’/pE’/pI’ computed correctly on exec for every fP, fE and fI bit.
  • Problem: Before the inheritable loop the parent calls cap_set_proc(cap_fullpi) (verify_caps_exec.c:291-303), where cap_fullpi = cap_init() + only CAP_INHERITABLE bits. That sets the parent’s pP and pE to empty. Every following cap_set_file(TSTPATH, fcap) (lines 331, 355) therefore fails with EPERM, because writing security.capability needs CAP_SETFCAP in pE; the failure only prints TINFO “” and continues. So none of the fI/pI subcases ever run, and the test still reports “All tests passed”. The same silent continue in the first loop (lines 252-256, 274-278) turns any setxattr failure (e.g. no xattr support, or TSTPATH “print_caps” not in the cwd, since it is a relative path) into a skip. perms_test() likewise reports TPASS for any cap_set_file() failure, including ENOENT when print_caps is not in the cwd (lines 110-113).
  • Evidence: verify_caps_exec.c:291-303, 329-335, 353-358; security/commoncap.c:587 if (!capable_wrt_inode_uidgid(idmap, inode, CAP_SETFCAP)) return -EPERM; (cap_convert_nscap, called from fs/xattr.c:336).
  • Suggested action: keep pE/pP when filling pI (add CAP_PERMITTED/CAP_EFFECTIVE to cap_fullpi, or set pI in the child after fork); treat cap_set_file() failure as TBROK; use an absolute path to print_caps; require EPERM in perms_test.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,VIRT. The tool always reports TPASS “found sha1 hash”.

  • Suggested action: allocate a new ctx for the final aggregate and call EVP_DigestFinal_ex() before freeing.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/accept/accept01.c (runtest: syscalls/accept01)

  • Category: WRONG
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: accept() fails with EINVAL for an “invalid socket buffer” (addr=(struct sockaddr *)3), for an “invalid salen” (addrlen=1) and for “no queued connections”.
  • Problem: socket_fd is only bound, never listen()ed. All three cases therefore fail in inet_csk_accept() with EINVAL because sk_state != TCP_LISTEN, before the kernel looks at addr or addrlen. The address is only copied out (move_addr_to_user) after ops->accept() succeeds, so the bad-buffer and bad-length cases never run the code they name. “No queued connections” on a blocking listening socket would block, and with O_NONBLOCK it gives EAGAIN, not EINVAL. The three cases are the same test.
  • Evidence: accept01.c:47-57,70-71 (no listen); net/socket.c:2059-2071 (ops->accept before getname/move_addr_to_user); net/ipv4/inet_connection_sock.c:662-664 (EINVAL if not TCP_LISTEN). accept(2): “EINVAL Socket is not listening for connections, or addrlen is invalid (e.g., is negative).”
  • Suggested action: Keep one “not listening -> EINVAL” case. For the bad-buffer case, use a listening socket with a pending connection and an invalid addr, and expect EFAULT. For the bad-length case, use a negative addrlen on a listening socket with a pending connection (EINVAL from move_addr_to_user). Drop the “no queued connections” case or turn it into a nonblocking EAGAIN case.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,VIRT. HPE+VIRT: accept01 5/5 TPASS as-is. Mutant with the ‘invalid socket buffer’ addr (struct sockaddr *)3 replaced by &fsin1 and ‘invalid salen’ 1 replaced by sizeof(fsin1): still ‘TPASS: invalid socket buffer : EINVAL’ and ‘TPASS: invalid salen : EINVAL’ (5/5) -> EINVAL comes from the non-listening socket, not from addr/addrlen.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/acct/acct02.c (runtest: syscalls/acct02)

Separately, tmp2 = user_time/clock_ticks does integer division before the float assignment, so the bounds are coarser than intended. The elapsed bound (< 2 s for a helper that sleeps 1 s) can be exceeded on a heavily loaded system. In that case no record matches, and the test reports “end of file reached” as a FAIL.

  • Suggested action: Use ac_utime for user_time. Optionally do float division and relax the elapsed bound.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION. HPE: acct02 TPASS as-is. Mutant helper burning ~7 s of USER cpu in 6 threads (wall 1.2 s): original acct02 still ‘TPASS: acct() wrote correct file contents!’; control build with user_time = UNPACK(ac_utime) rejects the same record (‘user_time/clock_ticks > 1 (717/100: 7.00)’) and ends ‘TFAIL: end of file reached’ -> ac_utime is never checked.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/clock_adjtime/clock_adjtime01.c (runtest: syscalls/clock_adjtime01)

  • Category: WRONG
  • Confidence: high

After the SET call, ttxc therefore no longer holds the requested value val; it holds whatever the kernel now has. The final check compares that write-back against a second read (verify), so it only checks that two consecutive reads agree. If the kernel ignored the requested value, both reads would return the old value and the test would PASS. Also, the nano-resolution detection at line 214 tests saved.modes & ADJ_NANO. modes is an input field and stays 0 after a read, so the ADJ_OFFSET scaling for STA_NANO is never applied (cleanup correctly uses STA_NANO). TPASS is also printed after a TFAIL in the same iteration (line 177, missing return).

Account for unit conversion: ADJ_OFFSET is only applied with STA_PLL and is the remaining slew, so skip or relax it; freq is in scaled ppm. Detect nano mode via status & STA_NANO. Add a return after TFAIL.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,VIRT. VIRT: as-is 9/9 TPASS. Mutant setting ttxc.modes=0 right before the SET call (so the kernel applies nothing; SET becomes a pure read) still prints ‘TPASS: clock_adjtime(): success’ for all 9 modes (8001,a001,403f,1,2,4,8,20,4000) -> the final check only compares two reads.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/clock_settime/clock_settime04.c (runtest: syscalls/clock_settime04)

  • Category: WRONG (secondary: DOCS)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: setting CLOCK_REALTIME has no effect on a thread blocked in clock_nanosleep(CLOCK_REALTIME), for both relative and absolute sleeps.

The target is decades in the past, so the sleep returns at once, delta is about 0 and the test passes without testing anything. (2) The claim itself is wrong for absolute sleeps. POSIX and Linux both say an absolute CLOCK_REALTIME sleep follows clock changes: if the clock is set back 2 s, the sleeper wakes 2 s later. If the target were computed correctly, the test as written (no CHILD_SLEEP_US subtraction for ABSTIME, delta must be <= 1 s) would FAIL on a correct kernel. Only the relative case is valid.

  • Suggested action: drop the TIMER_ABSTIME subcase, or rewrite it to take a CLOCK_REALTIME target and expect the wake-up to move by the clock change. Fix the description.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,VIRT. HPE as-is 4 TPASS; ABSTIME cases report delta 51/58 us, i.e. the MONOTONIC-based absolute REALTIME target is in the past and the sleep returns at once. testcases/kernel/syscalls/copy_file_range/copy_file_range02.c (runtest: syscalls/copy_file_range02)

testcases/kernel/syscalls/creat/creat03.c (runtest: syscalls/creat03)

The claim itself is also not Linux behavior. The create path masks the mode with S_IALLUGO, which includes S_ISVTX, and only S_ISGID is ever stripped (mode_strip_sgid).   • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION. VIRT as-is: ‘TPASS: save text bit cleared’ (mode requested is decimal 444 = 0674, no S_ISVTX). HPE mutant creat(pfilname, 01444): ‘TFAIL: save text bit not cleared’ on 7.2.9/btrfs. Linux keeps the requested sticky bit, so the claim is wrong and the as-is test verifies nothing.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/dup/dup07.c (runtest: syscalls/dup07)

Both fds refer to the same inode, so st_mode (inode type + permission bits) is identical by construction, and the “read only”/“write only” labels refer to inode permissions, not the open access mode. The access mode of the open file description (fcntl(F_GETFL) & O_ACCMODE) is never checked. The test cannot fail.

HPE mutant replacing dup(oldfd) with open(testfile, O_RDONLY) (a new description with a different access mode than creat()‘s O_WRONLY): still ’Passed in read only/write only/read/write mode’, 3 TPASS. st_mode comparison of the same inode cannot fail.

Kernel requires EPERM here: fs/notify/fanotify/fanotify_user.c:1968-1970 (mark_type != FAN_MARK_INODE && !ns_capable(group->user_ns, CAP_SYS_ADMIN) -> -EPERM) and :1606-1609 for init flags.

  • Suggested action: add an expected-errno field per test case; TFAIL when fanotify_init/fanotify_mark succeeds for a case that expects EPERM (e.g. use TST_EXP_FAIL / TST_EXP_FD_OR_FAIL).
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION. HPE: as-is 9 TPASS. Mutant using seteuid(nobody) and switching back to euid 0 for the FAN_MARK_MOUNT/FILESYSTEM cases (so the mark succeeds, i.e. the regression the test should catch): those 2 cases print ‘TPASS: fanotify_init() and fanotify_mark() returned successfully, as expected’; 9 TPASS 0 TFAIL.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/fanotify/fanotify22.c (runtest: syscalls/fanotify22)

  • Category: WRONG
  • Confidence: medium (phase 1: high)

If open() fails with a wrong errno (ret == -1), the condition is false and nothing is reported; if open() unexpectedly succeeds, errno is stale (usually not EUCLEAN, so it may report, but the fd is leaked). The intended check is ret != -1 || errno != EUCLEAN. Impact is limited because a missing error event is still caught by the 5 s poll timeout, but the errno assertion is dead code.

Mutant expecting EPERM instead of EUCLEAN in both trigger helpers: still 4 TPASS, no TFAIL, so the errno assertion is dead code. Mutant with the intended ‘ret != -1 || errno != EUCLEAN’: 4 TPASS (kernel returns EUCLEAN), fix is safe. Event check still guards; lowered to medium impact.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/futex/futex_cmp_requeue03.c (runtest: syscalls/futex_cmp_requeue03)

The top-down mmap allocator hands back the address that was just freed, so unmapped_addr == prot_none_addr. The two “unmapped” cases therefore pass a mapped PROT_NONE page, and the unmapped-memory path is never tested. The four cases reduce to two distinct ones. (Checked locally: mmap/munmap/mmap(PROT_NONE) gave the same address in 3/3 runs.)

  • Suggested action: Create the PROT_NONE mapping first (or map 2 pages and munmap only one of them, or use tst_get_bad_addr()), so the unmapped address cannot be reused. Optionally assert unmapped_addr != prot_none_addr.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION. HPE: work copy printing addresses after setup(): ‘unmapped_addr=0x7f257b7a1000 prot_none_addr=0x7f257b7a1000’ -> identical; ‘uaddr unmapped’/‘uaddr2 unmapped’ cases pass a mapped PROT_NONE page, no-VMA path never hit. All 4 TPASS EFAULT.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/get_mempolicy/get_mempolicy01.c (runtest: syscalls/get_mempolicy01)

  • Category: WRONG (secondary: -)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: get_mempolicy() returns the policy/nodemask previously set by set_mempolicy()/mbind() for MPOL_DEFAULT, MPOL_BIND, MPOL_INTERLEAVE, MPOL_PREFERRED, with and without MPOL_F_ADDR.
  • Problem: setup() runs every test case’s alloc hook (set_mempolicy) back to back, before any check runs. The thread policy is a single per-thread value, so only the last call (case 10, MPOL_PREFERRED + node0) is still in effect when do_test() runs. Every case without MPOL_F_ADDR (cases 1-5) therefore reads the same MPOL_PREFERRED/node0 policy. Case 1 (“MPOL_DEFAULT, no target”) expects nodemask (node0 set). A real MPOL_DEFAULT returns an empty mask (get_policy_nodemask() clears it for default_policy), so the expectation is only met because of the overwrite. Copy printing policy: cases 1-5 all return policy 1 (MPOL_PREFERRED from case 10’s setup call), e.g. MPOL_DEFAULT case ‘returned 1, tc->policy 0’. Copy calling set_mempolicy right before get_mempolicy: case 1 (MPOL_DEFAULT) and case 4 TFAIL ‘masks are not equal’ (empty mask returned).

HPE glibc: PASS (rc 0); musl: ‘TCONF: test requires libnuma development packages with LIBNUMA_API_VERSION >= 2’ (rc 32), 2/2 runs. Artefact of the musl build env: HAVE_NUMA_V2 undef in /root/ltp-musl/include/config.h (no libnuma in /usr/x86_64-linux-musl); ci/alpine.sh installs it, so upstream musl CI builds it. Nothing learned about the finding

testcases/kernel/syscalls/getrandom/getrandom02.c (runtest: syscalls/getrandom02)

  • Category: WRONG
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: getrandom() succeeds and fills the buffer with random-looking bytes.

Both loops then run zero times and the function returns 1, so a failing getrandom() reports TPASS “getrandom returned -1”. (2) The histogram check iterates for (i = 0; i < nb; i++) table[i], so with nb=64 only byte values 0..63 are checked for over-representation. Values 64..255 are never examined. (3) Nothing checks TST_RET == bufsize.

  • Suggested action: fail when TST_RET != bufsize (or <= 0), and loop over all 256 table entries.

Mutation m2 (memset(buf,0xff,64) after call): 4x TPASS though every byte is 255 (histogram checks table[0..63] only). Loop-bound bug latent until git ea1cab5ce29b reduced bufsize to 64.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/landlock/landlock02.c (runtest: syscalls/landlock02)

  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: landlock_add_rule() fails with EINVAL for invalid flags and for a network port greater than 65535 (plus other errno cases).

The ruleset was created with handled_access_net == 0, so the kernel returns EINVAL from the “allowed_access not in handled mask” check before it reaches the port > U16_MAX check. The port range check is never exercised, and with a correctly handled net mask this call would succeed. (2) The “Invalid flags” case passes flags = 1, which on current kernels is the valid LANDLOCK_ADD_RULE_QUIET. That case still gets EINVAL only because rule_type is 0 (“invalid rule type”), so the flags check is no longer covered.
  • Evidence: landlock02.c:44-52, 105-114, 147-160; security/landlock/syscalls.c:421-431 (mask check before net_port_attr.port > U16_MAX), :485-486 (flags && flags != LANDLOCK_ADD_RULE_QUIET); include/uapi/linux/landlock.h:129 #define LANDLOCK_ADD_RULE_QUIET (1U << 0).
  • Suggested action: Use port = U16_MAX + 1 (65536) and create the ABI>=4 ruleset with handled_access_net = LANDLOCK_ACCESS_NET_BIND_TCP so that only the port check can fail. Use an undefined flag bit (e.g., 1U << 31) together with a valid rule type for the flags case.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,VIRT,READ. HPE as-is 8 TPASS. Mutant A: port case uses port 80 (valid) and ‘Invalid flags’ uses flags=0 -> still 8/8 TPASS EINVAL (mask check / rule_type 0). Mutant B: port 65536 -> still EINVAL from handled_access_net==0. 7.2 has no LANDLOCK_ADD_RULE_QUIET so flags=1 still hits the flag check there; on 7.3 (QUIET=1) it does not. Port check never reached.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/listmount/listmount02.c (runtest: syscalls/listmount02)

  • Category: WRONG

The loop ends only once count reaches LISTSIZE. If the kernel’s iterator returned 0 too early (the bug the test should catch), the loop would spin forever until the harness timeout instead of reporting TFAIL. This affects only the failure path; correct kernels pass.

Mutant simulating an early-ending iterator (ret forced to 0 once count>=60): no TFAIL; loop spins (TST_RET stays 128 so ‘TST_RET < GROUPS_SIZE’ never breaks) -> ‘Test timeouted, sending SIGKILL!’ TBROK after 30 s, plus TWARN LOOP_CLR_FD / rmdir mntpoint EBUSY. testcases/kernel/syscalls/membarrier/membarrier01.c (runtest: syscalls/membarrier01)

  • Category: WRONG (secondary: FRAGILE)

  • Claim under test: membarrier() commands return the documented results. Cases 00/01 must fail with EINVAL, and cases 03/06 must fail with EPERM when not registered.

  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,VIRT,READ. VIRT as-is 12 TPASS. Mutant: case00 exp_errno EINVAL->EPERM, case03 EPERM->EBADF -> still 12/12 TPASS (‘cmd_fail failed as expected’, ‘cmd_private_expedited_fail failed as expected’): errno never compared on enabled&&!force path. nohz_full part not reproducible (hosts have none, no reboot) but kernel/sched/membarrier.c:654-661 masks/EINVALs CMD_GLOBAL.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/migrate_pages/migrate_pages03.c (runtest: syscalls/migrate_pages03)

  • Category: WRONG
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: regression test for 4b0ece6fa016 (“mm: migrate: fix remove_migration_pte() for ksm pages”). 20 zero pages are merged by KSM and migrated back and forth between two nodes 600 times.
  • Problem: Since 53eac722fd37 the migration loop runs after SAFE_SETEUID(nobody). That drops CAP_SYS_NICE from the effective set, so kernel_migrate_pages() uses MPOL_MF_MOVE rather than MPOL_MF_MOVE_ALL. With MPOL_MF_MOVE, migrate_folio_add() skips any folio for which folio_maybe_mapped_shared() is true, which for a small folio means mapcount > 1. The KSM stable page is mapped by all 20 PTEs (mapcount 20), so it is never queued for migration. Skipped shared folios are “not counted as a failure”, so migrate_pages() returns 0 and the test passes without migrating a KSM page or reaching remove_migration_pte() for KSM. Only the process’s private pages move. The test cannot detect the bug it is tagged for.
  • Evidence: migrate_pages03.c:121-136; mm/mempolicy.c:1935-1936 (capable(CAP_SYS_NICE) ? MPOL_MF_MOVE_ALL : MPOL_MF_MOVE), :1262 (if ((flags & MPOL_MF_MOVE_ALL) || !folio_maybe_mapped_shared(folio))); include/linux/mm.h:2999-3000 (small folio: return mapcount > 1); migrate_pages(2): “pages shared with another process will be moved only if the initiating process has the CAP_SYS_NICE privilege”.
  • Suggested action: Keep the cost low (the reason for 53eac722fd37) but migrate the KSM page with privilege. As root, call mbind(test_pages range, MPOL_BIND, other node, MPOL_MF_MOVE_ALL) or move_pages(0, N_PAGES, test_pages, nodes, …, MPOL_MF_MOVE_ALL) on just the test pages instead of migrate_pages() on the whole process. Optionally check with get_mempolicy(MPOL_F_NODE|MPOL_F_ADDR) that the page moved.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via READ,GIT. Not runnable: HPE and VIRT have only node0 (test needs 2 nodes, TCONF). Re-checked: migrate_test() SAFE_SETEUID(nobody) drops effective CAP_SYS_NICE -> mm/mempolicy.c:1935 MPOL_MF_MOVE; migrate_folio_add() l.1262 skips folio_maybe_mapped_shared() (small folio: mapcount>1, mm.h:3000) and ‘is not counted as a failure’. Since 53eac722fd37 (2018, run as nobody) the 20-PTE KSM page is never migrated.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/mlock/mlock03.c (runtest: syscalls/mlock03 -i 20)

  • Category: WRONG (secondary: OBSOLETE)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: repeated mlock/munlock over every /proc/self/maps range must not shrink the [stack] mapping (RHEL5 bug 643426).
  • Problem: After the new-API conversion, first and last are locals of verify_mlock(), and both are set from the same [stack] line during one pass over /proc/self/maps (lines 197-198 and 209-210 use the same from/to). So last < first can never be true, and the test always passes. The original old-API version recorded first at lc==0 and last in the final iteration (hence -i 20 in runtest). That cross-iteration comparison was lost. The targeted bug is in RHEL5’s 2.6.18 kernel, far below the LTP minimum.
  • Evidence: mlock03.c:180-181,196-198,208-210,216; original code (git a0413366ae45) used if ((lc == 0) && strstr(b,"[stack]")) first = ....
  • Suggested action: Drop the test as obsolete. Or, if kept, re-read /proc/self/maps after the mlock/munlock pass (and over several internal loops) and compare the [stack] size before and after.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,VIRT,GIT. VIRT: ‘mlock03 -i 20’ 20/20 TPASS. HPE mutant: inside the maps loop munmap() the bottom 64KiB of [stack], then re-read maps: ‘V07: real [stack] now 68 KiB’ yet ‘TPASS: stack size is not decreased’ (first/last both taken from the same line). Cross-iteration compare (lc==0 vs last loop) was lost in new-API conversion 25925917a21e.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/mlockall/mlockall02.c (runtest: syscalls/mlockall02)

  • Category: WRONG (secondary: WEAK, DOCS)
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: mlockall() fails with ENOMEM (RLIMIT_MEMLOCK too small, unprivileged), EPERM (unprivileged, RLIMIT_MEMLOCK 0) and EINVAL (flags 0).
  • Problem: If the ENOMEM or EPERM case unexpectedly succeeds, the test reports TCONF (“did not BEHAVE as expected”) rather than TFAIL. So a kernel that ignores RLIMIT_MEMLOCK for unprivileged callers is not caught. Both errors are documented and are deterministic in mm/mlock.c (can_do_mlock() -> EPERM; total_vm > lock_limit -> ENOMEM). The three cases are the same as mlockall03’s (rlimit 7 bytes as nobody -> ENOMEM; rlimit 0 as nobody -> EPERM; invalid flags -> EINVAL). The header comment says the test checks “mount(2)”, and it says EPERM means “not super user” (EPERM requires RLIMIT_MEMLOCK == 0).
  • Evidence: mlockall02.c:140-143 (TCONF for i <= 1 on success); mlockall02.c:35-41 (mount(2) text); mlockall(2) ERRORS: “ENOMEM (Linux 2.6.9 and later) the caller had a nonzero RLIMIT_MEMLOCK soft resource limit, but tried to lock more memory than the limit permitted” and “EPERM The caller is not privileged, but needs privilege (CAP_IPC_LOCK)”.
  • Suggested action: merge mlockall02 and mlockall03 into one new-API test that uses TST_EXP_FAIL. Report unexpected success as TFAIL, and drop the other file.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via MUTATION,VIRT,READ. Mutant skips seteuid(nobody) for the ENOMEM case so mlockall() succeeds despite RLIMIT_MEMLOCK=7 (what a kernel ignoring the limit would do): ‘TCONF: mlockall02.c:142: mlockall02 did not BEHAVE as expected.’ then 2 TPASS; overall no TFAIL. Header text still says mount(2). Duplicates mlockall03 cases.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/mmap/mmap03.c (runtest: syscalls/mmap03)

  • Category: WRONG
  • Confidence: high

That check only proves read(2) works. The mapping content is never checked, and the SIGSEGV branch in the parent can never be reached by the test’s own action. This is a regression from the refactor in 5c778f6cd65d: the old code compared dummy with addr. The parent’s PASS messages (“Use of return in child…”) come from another test and do not describe this one.

  • Suggested action: compare addr against tmpdata in the child. Keep accepting SIGSEGV for exec-only mappings (x86 PKU, arm64 EPAN/PIE exec-only, mips). Fix the messages.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,VIRT,GIT. VIRT as-is: 2 TPASS. Mutant built on HPE, run on VIRT: child maps MAP_ANONYMOUS|MAP_PRIVATE (no file at all) instead of the file -> still ‘TPASS memcmp(data, tmpdata) == 0’ + ‘TPASS Use of return in child…’. Mapping content is never read; 5c778f6cd65d removed ‘memcmp(dummy, addr, page_sz)’.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/mmap/mmap20.c (runtest: syscalls/mmap20)

  • Category: WRONG
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: mmap(MAP_SHARED_VALIDATE | ) fails with EOPNOTSUPP.
  • Problem: The “invalid” flag is hard-coded as (1 << 10) = 0x400. On mips and xtensa, 0x400 is MAP_NORESERVE, which is in LEGACY_MAP_MASK, so do_mmap() accepts it and mmap() succeeds. The test then reports TFAIL on a correct kernel. (On alpha 0x400 is the legacy _MAP_INHERIT; it is unused on x86/arm64/ppc/s390.)
  • Evidence: mmap20.c:18, 42-50; arch/mips/include/uapi/asm/mman.h:41 and arch/xtensa/include/uapi/asm/mman.h:48 #define MAP_NORESERVE 0x0400; include/linux/mman.h LEGACY_MAP_MASK includes MAP_NORESERVE; mm/mmap.c do_mmap(): case MAP_SHARED_VALIDATE: if (flags & ~flags_mask) return -EOPNOTSUPP; with flags_mask = LEGACY_MAP_MASK (| MAP_SYNC).
  • Suggested action: pick a bit that is unused on every arch, or build it as a high bit outside LEGACY_MAP_MASK | MAP_SYNC (for example 1 << 24, after checking the arch headers). Another option is to compute it as a bit not in the known-flags set.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,VIRT,READ. VIRT x86 as-is: TPASS EOPNOTSUPP. Simulated mips/xtensa on x86 by setting INVALID_FLAG to MAP_NORESERVE (what 1<<10 is in arch/mips and arch/xtensa uapi mman.h:41/48): ‘TFAIL: mmap() is successful, but it should have failed’. LEGACY_MAP_MASK includes MAP_NORESERVE, so do_mmap MAP_SHARED_VALIDATE accepts it.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/mount/mount03.c (runtest: syscalls/mount03)

  • Category: WRONG
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: after mount(2) with each flag, statfs() reports the matching flag. For MS_STRICTATIME, NOATIME/RELATIME must not be reported.
  • Problem: Two statfs assertions cannot fail. (1) For the MS_REMOUNT case, flag2 is MS_REMOUNT (32). In statfs f_flags, 32 is ST_VALID, which the kernel always sets, so stfs.f_flags & MS_REMOUNT is always true. (2) For MS_STRICTATIME, the test checks f_flags & (MS_NOATIME | MS_RELATIME). MS_RELATIME is 1<<21, but statfs reports relatime as ST_RELATIME (0x1000), so the relatime part never fires and an ignored MS_STRICTATIME (left at the default relatime) would still pass. The atime check in test_strictatime() also cannot tell strictatime from relatime, because the file was just written and the directory was just created, so relatime updates atime too. Other subcases (RDONLY, NODEV, NOEXEC, NOSUID, NOATIME, NODIRATIME) are fine. The remount subcase is still checked through open().
  • Evidence: mount03.c:182, 223-235; include/linux/statfs.h:28-43 (“ST_VALID which has the same value as MS_REMOUNT”, ST_RELATIME 0x1000); fs/statfs.c:51 return ST_VALID | ...; include/uapi/linux/mount.h:35 MS_RELATIME (1<<21).
  • Suggested action: for remount, check that ST_RDONLY is cleared (it was mounted RDONLY before). For strictatime, test f_flags & (ST_NOATIME | ST_RELATIME). To tell strictatime from relatime, read a file whose atime is already newer than its mtime/ctime.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,VIRT,READ. VIRT as-is all TPASS. Mutant: MS_STRICTATIME case mounts MS_RELATIME instead, remount uses MS_REMOUNT|MS_RDONLY -> strictatime case still ‘TPASS st_atime > atime’, ‘dir_st.st_atime > dir_atime’ and ‘mount03.c:227 TPASS statfs() gets the correct mount flag’; remount: open TFAIL EROFS but ‘mount03.c:233 TPASS statfs()’ (ST_VALID==MS_REMOUNT). Both statfs checks vacuous.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/mprotect/mprotect02.c (runtest: syscalls/mprotect02)

  • Category: WRONG
  • Confidence: medium (phase 1: low)
  • Claim under test: writing to a PROT_READ mapping raises SIGSEGV; after mprotect(PROT_WRITE) it does not.
  • Problem: After waitpid() it does switch (status) on the raw wait status. A child that did not fault does exit(255), which gives status 0xff00, so case 255 (“memcpy did not generate SIGSEGV”) can never match. The kernel bug is then reported via default: as TBROK “got unexpected signal: 65280”. Both real failures (no SIGSEGV; SIGSEGV after PROT_WRITE) are reported as TBROK rather than TFAIL, so CI would count a kernel regression as a broken test. It is not a false pass.
  • Evidence: mprotect02.c:96-115, 132-137.
  • Suggested action: use WIFEXITED/WEXITSTATUS and report TFAIL. Better, convert to the new API, as mprotect05 already is.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via MUTATION,VIRT. Mutant maps PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE so the first child does not fault and exits 255 (= kernel not enforcing PROT_READ): ‘TBROK: mprotect02.c:112: got unexpected signal: 65280’ + ‘Remaining cases broken’. ‘case 255’ on raw status never matches; a real regression is reported as TBROK, not TFAIL.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/mq_notify/mq_notify01.c (runtest: syscalls/mq_notify01)

  • Category: WRONG

A kernel delivering the wrong si_code, sival_int, si_pid or si_uid passes. The -d debug output also prints the expected/received labels the wrong way round (E: is the received value).

  • Suggested action: after the wait loop, if (!cmp_ok) tst_res(TFAIL, ...) for SIGEV_SIGNAL and SIGEV_THREAD. Also bound the wait loop with a timeout or tst_remaining_runtime().

Mutant registers sigev_value.sival_int = USER_DATA+1 for both SIGEV_SIGNAL and SIGEV_THREAD (so sigfunc/tfunc compute cmp_ok=0) -> still 7/7 TPASS ‘mq_notify and mq_timedsend exited expectedly’. cmp_ok is never read.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/mq_timedsend/mq_timedsend01.c (runtest: syscalls/mq_timedsend01)

  • Category: WRONG (secondary: FRAGILE)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: mq_timedsend() success and error cases, including EAGAIN on a full O_NONBLOCK queue, EINVAL/ETIMEDOUT/EINTR on a full blocking queue.
  • Problem: (1) The EAGAIN case uses fd_nonblock with .send = 0, and nothing ever fills that queue. mq_timedsend() therefore succeeds. verify_mqt_send_receive() never checks tc->ret on success, so it receives the 16-byte message back and reports TPASS. EAGAIN is never exercised. (2) More generally, any “expected failure” case that succeeds falls through to the receive/compare path and gets TPASS (e.g. ETIMEDOUT/EINTR if the queue is not full). (3) “Full queue” is assumed to be MSG_LENGTH=10 sends, which relies on /proc/sys/fs/mqueue/msg_default being 10. The MAX_MSGSIZE / EMSGSIZE cases rely on msgsize_default being 8192 (the queue is opened with attr=NULL).
  • Evidence: mq_timedsend01.c:60-65 (EAGAIN case without .send); :170-182 (only failure path compares errno); :184-226 (success path ends in TPASS without checking tc->ret); utils/mq.h:51-53 (queues opened with NULL attr); mq_send(3): “EAGAIN The queue was full, and the O_NONBLOCK flag was set”.
  • Suggested action: set .send = 1 for the EAGAIN case (fill fd_nonblock), and add if (tc->ret < 0) { tst_res(TFAIL, "succeeded unexpectedly"); return; } after a successful send. Open the queues with an explicit mq_attr (maxmsg=10, msgsize=8192), or read msg_default, instead of relying on defaults.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,VIRT,READ. VIRT as-is: 34 TPASS; the EAGAIN tcase (fd_nonblock, len 16, no .send) shows ‘TPASS: mq_timedreceive() returned 16, priority 0’ in both variants, i.e. mq_timedsend() succeeded and the success path passed it; EAGAIN never exercised. utils/mq.h opens queues with attr=NULL (relies on msg_default=10/msgsize_default=8192).

testcases/kernel/syscalls/munmap/munmap03.c (runtest: syscalls/munmap03)

  • Category: WRONG
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: munmap() fails with EINVAL for (1) a range outside the process address space, (2) len == 0, (3) an addr that is not page aligned.
  • Problem: run() calls munmap(tc->addr, *tc->len), where tc->addr is char **, i.e. the address of the static pointer variable (in .bss), not the mapping address. Case 1 passes &map_addr_out. Case 2 passes &map_addr. Case 3 passes &map_addr + 1 (the address of the next 8-byte .bss slot), not map_addr + 1. These .bss addresses are just not page aligned, so all three get EINVAL from the offset_in_page(start) check. Neither the “outside address range” condition nor the “unaligned mapping address” condition is ever exercised. If the linker ever placed one of these variables on a page boundary, munmap() would unmap the test’s own .bss. This was introduced by the new-API conversion 0c7346cb0974.
  • Evidence: munmap03.c:31-34 ({ EINVAL, &map_addr_out, ...}, &map_addr + 1); munmap03.c:40 (munmap(tc->addr, ...) without dereference); mm/vma.c:1717-1718 (offset_in_page(start) -> -EINVAL).
  • Suggested action: store the addresses directly (e.g. an unaligned_addr = map_addr + 1 variable) and call munmap(*tc->addr, *tc->len). For the “outside address space” case, use an explicit address above TASK_SIZE, not RLIMIT_DATA’s rlim_max (which only works because RLIM_INFINITY is unaligned).
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,VIRT. Mutant (HPE build, VIRT run): map_addr_out = map_addr (a valid, aligned, mapped address) plus TINFO of the pointer passed -> ‘V07: munmap(0x438160) map_addr=0x7feb25052000’ (and 0x438168, 0x438170: .bss slots) and 3/3 TPASS EINVAL. munmap() gets &var, never the mapping; all three EINVALs are just offset_in_page() of .bss addresses.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/open/open12.c (runtest: syscalls/open12)

  • Category: WRONG (phase 1: FRAGILE)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: O_LARGEFILE lets the file be seeked/written past 4 GiB (run on all filesystems).
  • Problem: .all_filesystems=1 with no skip list, so it also runs on vfat (in the default whitelist). vfat sets s_maxbytes = 0xffffffff, so lseek(fd, 4GiB+1MiB) returns EINVAL (vfs_setpos rejects offset > maxsize) and the test reports “TFAIL lseek() past 4GB range failed” on a correct kernel. The limit is a property of the filesystem, not of O_LARGEFILE.
  • Evidence: open12.c:153-159 (lseek 4ULL*TST_GB + TST_MB, TFAIL on <0), 192-198 (.all_filesystems, no .skip_filesystems); /usr/src/linux/fs/fat/inode.c:1697 “sb->s_maxbytes = 0xffffffff;”; /usr/src/linux/fs/read_write.c:61-62 “if (offset > maxsize) return -EINVAL;”.

VIRT: LTP_SINGLE_FS_TYPE=vfat open12 -> 4 TPASS: no .mount_device, so lib only reserves a device and never mkfs/mounts it; all 10 fs iterations test the btrfs TMPDIR (and MS_STRICTATIME is never applied). Mutant with .mount_device=1: vfat ‘TFAIL lseek() past 4GB range failed: EINVAL’, exfat ‘TBROK write … ENOSPC’. Since 26a59051d940.
  • Verification conclusion: As written, the test never mounts the device. Every “=== Testing on ===” iteration exercises the same TMPDIR filesystem, and the MS_STRICTATIME mount flag is never used, so the per-filesystem coverage is vacuous. The new-API conversion 26a59051d940 (the old code mounted with MS_STRICTATIME) is where this came from. Phase 1’s vfat failure does not happen today, but it appears as soon as .mount_device = 1 is added, together with an exfat TBROK (ENOSPC, no sparse files). Corrected action: add .mount_device = 1, and at the same time skip vfat/exfat for the largefile subtest (or TCONF on EINVAL/EFBIG/ENOSPC), or seek just past 2 GiB.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/perf_event_open/perf_event_open02.c (runtest: syscalls/perf_event_open02)

  • Category: WRONG (phase 1: FRAGILE)
  • Confidence: medium (phase 1: low)
  • Claim under test: task-clock counters in groups with a HW counter stop while the group is multiplexed off the PMU, so sum(task clock in groups)/overall task clock <= number of HW counters.
  • Problem: nhw comes from count_hardware_counters(), which returns the index i at which time_enabled != time_running is first seen. If the very first counter is already multiplexed (all suitable counters held by other pinned/system-wide events) it returns 0; if multiplexing is never observed within MAX_CTRS (1000) events it also returns 0 and leaks the 999 enabled events. With nhw == 0 the check ratio > nhw + 0.0001 always fails, so the environment problem shows up as TFAIL instead of TCONF.
  • Evidence: perf_event_open02.c:118-170 (hwctrs init 0, set only on mismatch), 228-229 (ntotal = nhw + 4), 330-334 (ratio check).
  • Suggested action: tst_brk(TCONF) when nhw == 0 (cannot determine HW counter count), and close all opened fds.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): REVISED via RUN,REPEAT,MUTATION,VIRT. As-is: HPE ltprepeat 5 pass=5, VIRT 4/4 pass (nhw=5). Condition created: a helper holding 8 pinned CPU-wide INSTRUCTIONS events: ‘[0] value:0 time_enabled:569359453 time_running:0’, ‘nhw: 0’, ‘ratio: 0.000000’, ‘TPASS: test passed’ -> nhw==0 gives a vacuous PASS (groups never run, ratio 0), not the TFAIL phase 1 predicted
  • Verification conclusion: Phase 1 was right that nhw becomes 0 when other pinned or system-wide events hold the counters, but wrong about the outcome. The HW group leaders then never get scheduled, the task-clock sum is 0, ratio 0 <= nhw, and the test reports TPASS without having measured anything. Corrected finding: in that environment (e.g. a profiler running), the check is vacuous. The “never multiplexed within 1000” path is theoretical. Corrected action: tst_brk(TCONF) when nhw == 0, and also require a non-zero hw/task-clock sum (TFAIL or TCONF otherwise). Close the leaked fds.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): NEW (second finding, secondary category UNDEF/high; primary kept) via MUSL,BULK,RUN,SRC. Secondary to the existing WRONG/medium (nhw heuristic, unaffected). HPE glibc: TPASS; musl: ‘TBROK: sched_setscheduler(0, SCHED_FIFO, …) failed: ENOSYS’ 2/2. musl src/sched/sched_setscheduler.c:5-8 is ENOSYS by design; perf_event_open02.c:276,291 call libc directly although include/tst_sched.h has sys_sched_setscheduler()
  • Verification conclusion: New secondary finding: the test raises itself to SCHED_FIFO with the libc sched_setscheduler(), which musl never implements (Linux’s syscall is per-thread, POSIX’s function per-process). Action: use sys_sched_setscheduler() from tst_sched.h. The primary WRONG/medium finding stays as is.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/pipe/pipe15.c (runtest: syscalls/pipe15)

  • Category: WRONG (secondary: UNDEF)

testcases/kernel/syscalls/semop/semop05.c (runtest: syscalls/semop05)

  • Category: WRONG (secondary: FRAGILE)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: a SEM_UNDO adjustment made by one thread is not undone when that thread exits, only when the last thread (process) exits.
  • Problem: The semaphore is initialised to 1 (SETVAL val=1). The poster thread does V (value 2, semadj -1) and exits; the waiter later does P (-1). If the kernel wrongly applied the undo at thread exit the value would be 1 and P would still succeed immediately, so the test cannot detect the bug it describes. The pass condition is also racy: after sleep(20) main does IPC_RMID and immediately reads err_ret; if the waiter was blocked, RMID wakes it with EIDRM, the semop() return is unchecked, and the waiter sets err_ret = 0 (a plain int shared without synchronisation), which can produce a false TPASS. Synchronisation is pure sleep(10)/sleep(20) and the test takes 20 s. TCID is “sem02”, not semop05.
  • Evidence: semop05.c:88-89 (initial value 1), :132-134 (unchecked semop then err_ret=0), :107-113 (sleep then RMID then check); semop(2): “semadj … adjustments are performed when the process terminates”; clone(2) CLONE_SYSVSEM: threads share the undo list.
  • Suggested action: initialise to 0, check semop() return in the waiter, synchronise with pthread_join instead of sleeps (use IPC_NOWAIT or semtimedop for the P after the poster has been joined); or rewrite in the new API.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,VIRT. VIRT as-is ‘sem02 1 TPASS: passed’ (20 s). Mutant where the poster immediately undoes its V (semop -1, as if the undo ran at thread exit): ‘MUT: poster undid its V, semval=1’ and still ‘TPASS: passed’ -> initial value 1 hides the bug the test targets

testcases/kernel/syscalls/sendmsg/sendmsg01.c (runtest: syscalls/sendmsg01)

  • Category: WRONG (secondary: UNDOC, FRAGILE)
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: sendmsg() returns the proper errno for various failure cases.
  • Problem:
    1. “invalid cmsg length” (tdat[13]) originally set cmsg_len = sizeof(cmsghdr) - 4 (still visible commented out); now setup6() sets controllen = cmsg_len = 0, which the kernel treats as “no control data”, and the entry expects retval 0. The subcase no longer tests an invalid cmsg length at all, but still prints “invalid cmsg length successful”.
    2. “connected TCP” (tdat[3]) is meant to send to a different address (sin2) on a connected TCP socket, but main() only sets msg_name for non-SOCK_STREAM sockets, so sin2 is never passed; the case is a plain send on a connected socket.

Two datagrams per iteration succeed (tdat[11], tdat[13]); once the queue exceeds net.unix.max_dgram_qlen (default 10) the blocking sendmsg() waits forever, so sendmsg01 -i 6 hangs.
    4. “not connected TCP” expects EPIPE. That is what Linux returns (sk_stream_wait_connect() returns -EPIPE for a socket not in SYN_SENT/SYN_RECV), but send(2) documents ENOTCONN for an unconnected socket and EPIPE only for “local end has been shut down”.

  • Suggested action: restore a really invalid cmsg_len (expect EINVAL) or drop/rename the subcase; set msg_name for the connected-TCP case (expect success or EISCONN); have the server read the UNIX dgram socket; accept EPIPE or ENOTCONN for the unconnected TCP case. Overlaps heavily with send01/sendto01; converting to the new API would fix most of this.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,REPEAT,READ,VIRT. VIRT as-is 15 TPASS (‘invalid cmsg length successful’ with cmsg_len=0, retval 0). Hang confirmed: ‘sendmsg01 -i 300’ (Fedora net.unix.max_dgram_qlen=512) hangs after 3853 TPASS (iter 257), rc=124; with qlen=10 (kernel default, restored to 512) ‘sendmsg01 -i 6’ hangs after 88 TPASS in case 14, rc=124. Items 1/2/4 re-read: setup6 sets cmsg_len=0; msg_name only set for non-stream
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): NEW (second finding, secondary category UNDEF/high; primary kept) via MUSL,BULK,RUN,SRC. Secondary to WRONG/high (unaffected). HPE glibc: 15 TPASS; musl: 14 TPASS then ‘TBROK: unexpected signal SIGSEGV’ 2/2 at ‘invalid cmsg pointer’ (msg_control=(void*)-1, sendmsg01.c:663-667). musl src/network/sendmsg.c:19-25 memcpy()s the control buffer into a local copy before the syscall; EFAULT via the libc wrapper is not guaranteed
  • Verification conclusion: New secondary finding: the invalid-cmsg-pointer subcase expects the kernel’s EFAULT through libc sendmsg(); musl (64-bit) copies msghdr and control data in userspace to clear padding, so the bad pointer faults in libc. Action: use tst_syscall(__NR_sendmsg) for the bad-pointer subcases or run them in a child and accept SIGSEGV. Primary WRONG/high stays.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/sendmsg/sendmsg02.c (runtest: syscalls/sendmsg02)

  • Category: WRONG (secondary: OBSOLETE)
  • Confidence: medium (phase 1: low)
  • Claim under test: reproducer for a NULL deref in selinux_socket_unix_may_send caused by a unix_release() race (fixed in 3.9, ded34e0fe8fe). Client/server pairs are meant to run in lock-step via a pipe.
  • Problem: In reproduce(), the parent closes both pipe ends right after forking the server (i even), before forking the client (i odd). The client inherits closed fds, so its write(pipefd[1], ...) fails with EBADF, and the server’s read(pipefd[0], ...) returns EOF at once (no writers left). The intended handshake never happens; the two processes just loop independently. The race may still be hit, but not in the way the test was designed. Also mh.msg_control is set and then wiped by the following memset (dead code), and read(pipefd[0], &fd, 1) would overwrite one byte of the server’s fd if it ever read anything. The bug was fixed in 3.9, well before the LTP minimum kernel (4.4); the only pass criterion is “did not crash”, after a fixed 15 s sleep.
  • Evidence: sendmsg02.c:138-166 (close at :162-165 happens before the client fork), :80-84, :92, :115-116.
  • Suggested action: move the parent’s pipe close to after the client fork (i odd), or drop the test as a reproducer for a pre-4.4 bug.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,VIRT. VIRT as-is ‘TPASS: finished after 15 seconds’. Instrumented copy (report first failing pipe op per child): every client ‘write(pipefd[1]) failed: EBADF’ and every server ‘read(pipefd[0]) returned 0’ (4 pairs on 1 CPU), still TPASS -> the parent closes the pipe before forking the client, so the lock-step handshake never happens

testcases/kernel/syscalls/set_mempolicy/set_mempolicy05.c (runtest: numa/set_mempolicy05, cve/cve-2017-7616)

  • Category: WRONG (secondary: OBSOLETE, UNDEF)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: CVE-2017-7616, the 32-bit compat set_mempolicy leaking kernel stack into the user stack. EFAULT means “compat assumed” (TPASS) and EINVAL means “non compat assumed” (TCONF).
  • Problem: The EFAULT/EINVAL heuristic only matched the old COMPAT_SYSCALL_DEFINE3(set_mempolicy), which copied the bitmap before validating it. That entry point and compat_alloc_user_space() are gone: the compat numa syscalls were unified into kernel_set_mempolicy() in 5.15. Now sanitize_mpol_flags() runs first, then get_nodes() rejects maxnode=UINT_MAX with EINVAL. So on every current kernel the test ends in TCONF, even when it really ran the compat syscall and the stack-pattern check passed. Also, on i386, const int mode; (line 53) is never initialized, so a garbage mode is passed in ebx (EINVAL from sanitize_mpol_flags, or anything else).

  • Suggested action: Initialize mode to 0. Accept EINVAL as a valid outcome on new kernels and report TPASS when the stack pattern is intact, rather than TCONF. Or restrict the test to kernels < 5.15 (the vulnerable code no longer exists).

Probe issuing the i386 set_mempolicy (276) via int 0x80 from x86_64 (real compat entry, same args as the test): returns -22 (EINVAL) for mode 0 and for a garbage mode -> on 7.2 the i386 test would always end in TCONF ‘non compat assumed’; syscall_32.tbl maps 276 to sys_set_mempolicy

For CORE, reset SIGSEGV to SIG_DFL in the child and check WCOREDUMP plus file size, with core_pattern controlled. Separate setrlimit tests may already cover these.

Instrumented: ‘MUT: 20 of 20 forks succeeded with RLIMIT_NPROC=10’ then ‘TPASS: RLIMIT_NPROC functionality is correct’; ‘MUT: SIGSEGV child status 0x0 signaled=0 exited=1’ then ‘TPASS: RLIMIT_CORE functionality is correct’ -> NPROC not enforced for root and the SIGSEGV child _exit(0)s via the inherited handler

testcases/kernel/syscalls/setsid/setsid01.c (runtest: syscalls/setsid01)

Main therefore always sees status 0 and reports TPASS “all misc tests passed”, so the exit code is 0 even after a failure. B also orders itself after A’s setpgid(0,0) only with sleep(1): if A has not created its process group yet, B’s setpgid(0, getppid()) fails with EPERM and a TFAIL is printed, though still not propagated. The setsid check also tests errno == EPERM without checking that the return value is -1.

  • Suggested action: Rewrite with the new API: shared-memory results, a checkpoint instead of sleep(1), and TST_EXP_FAIL(setsid(), EPERM).
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,VIRT. VIRT as-is TPASS. Mutant expecting EINVAL instead of EPERM: ‘TFAIL: setsid failed, expected -1, return 1’ and ‘TFAIL: Test {53996} exited status 0x300’ are printed, then ‘TPASS: all misc tests passed’, exit code 0 -> descendant failures not propagated

  • Category: WRONG (secondary: UNDOC, DOCS)

Not run (tool access lost). linux fs/namespace.c: SYSCALL statmount rejects only flags & ~STATMOUNT_BY_FD (BY_FD=1); flags=1 then hits copy_mnt_id_req ‘if (kreq->mnt_id || kreq->mnt_ns_id) return -EINVAL’; prepare_kstatmount returns EOVERFLOW for any STATMOUNT_STRING_REQ bit when bufsize==sizeof(sm), unknown mask bits ignored

testcases/kernel/syscalls/statvfs/statvfs01.c (runtest: syscalls/statvfs01)

  • Category: WRONG
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: For every filesystem, statvfs() succeeds and f_namemax is correct: a name of f_namemax chars can be created and one of f_namemax+1 fails with ENAMETOOLONG.
  • Problem: f_namemax is read from mntpoint/testfile (the device fs), but creat(valid_fname) and creat(toolong_fname) use bare relative names, so both files are created in the test’s cwd (the tmpdir, usually tmpfs/ext4), not in mntpoint/. The name-length check therefore always runs against the tmpdir fs. It only passes because most filesystems have a 255-byte limit (and vfat’s is divided by 6 to get 255). A wrong f_namemax on the device fs would not be caught.
  • Evidence: statvfs01.c:28-46 (TEST_PATH is MNT_POINT”/testfile”, creat() uses valid_fname/toolong_fname without the MNT_POINT prefix)
  • Suggested action: Build the filenames as MNT_POINT "/" + name (PATH_MAX buffers suffice) so that creat() runs on the filesystem under test.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION. HPE: as-is TPASS on 10 fs. Instrumented copy after the creat() checks: ‘INSTR: access(cwd/valid)=0 access(mntpoint/valid)=-1’ on all 10 fs, so both name-length creat() calls run in the tmpdir (btrfs here), never on the device fs whose f_namemax was read

testcases/kernel/sysfs/devices/system/cpu/sys_cpu_cache01.c (runtest: sysfs/sys_cpu_cache01)

  • Category: WRONG
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: ways_of_associativity is greater than zero for every cache index.
  • Problem: The generic cacheinfo code deliberately exposes ways_of_associativity whenever the cache size is known, including a value of 0, which means fully associative. In the DT path, cache_associativity() only computes ways when nr_sets != 1 and all of sets/size/line_size are non-zero. A fully associative cache (cache-sets = 1), or a DT cache node without a cache-sets property (common for L2/L3 nodes on arm64/riscv), therefore reports ways_of_associativity = 0, and the test TFAILs on a correct kernel.
  • Evidence: test lines 54-56; /usr/src/linux/drivers/base/cacheinfo.c cache_default_attrs_is_visible() “if ((attr == &dev_attr_ways_of_associativity.attr) && this_leaf->size) /* allow 0 = full associativity */“; drivers/base/cacheinfo.c:186-198 cache_associativity().
  • Suggested action: assert ways_of_associativity >= 0 (RANGELL(0, LONG_MAX)), optionally TINFO “fully associative” for 0.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,VIRT,READ. HPE+VIRT (x86, CPUID cacheinfo) TPASS, ways 8/16/20; failure needs DT/fully-associative cache, not available. Re-read /usr/src/linux drivers/base/cacheinfo.c:820-821 ’this_leaf->size) /* allow 0 = full associativity */’ and cache_associativity() leaving ways=0 for nr_sets==1 or missing cache-sets -> test’s RANGELL(1, …) wrong

testcases/kernel/sysfs/devices/system/cpu/sys_cpu_smt01.c (runtest: sysfs/sys_cpu_smt01)

  • Category: WRONG
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: when control is “notsupported” or “notimplemented”, active reads back as 0.
  • Problem: That holds for “notsupported” (SMT not supported by the CPU). For “notimplemented” it does not: control is CPU_SMT_NOT_IMPLEMENTED whenever CONFIG_HOTPLUG_SMT is off, while active is sched_smt_active(), driven by sched_smt_present_inc() whenever a core has two online siblings (CONFIG_SCHED_SMT). On sparc64 (ARCH_SUPPORTS_SCHED_SMT, no HOTPLUG_SMT) with an SMT CPU, or arm64/loongarch built without HOTPLUG_CPU on SMT hardware, control is “notimplemented” and active is 1, and the test TFAILs.
  • Evidence: test lines 190-199; Documentation/ABI/testing/sysfs-devices-system-cpu:631-643 (“notimplemented” SMT runtime toggling is not implemented for the architecture); include/linux/cpu_smt.h:13-23; kernel/cpu.c active_show() -> sched_smt_active(); kernel/sched/core.c sched_smt_present_inc(); arch/sparc/Kconfig:114.
  • Suggested action: restrict the active==0 assertion to “notsupported” only.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,VIRT,READ. HPE (control=on, active=1) and VIRT (notsupported, active=0) TPASS; ‘notimplemented’ needs !CONFIG_HOTPLUG_SMT. Source re-check: include/linux/cpu_smt.h defines cpu_smt_control as CPU_SMT_NOT_IMPLEMENTED without HOTPLUG_SMT, kernel/cpu.c active_show() returns sched_smt_active() regardless, sparc selects ARCH_SUPPORTS_SCHED_SMT but not HOTPLUG_SMT

testcases/kernel/sysfs/devices/system/cpu/sys_cpu_topology02.c (runtest: sysfs/sys_cpu_topology02)

  • Category: WRONG
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: core_id is in [0, highest possible CPU id] (“there can be at most as many cores as possible CPUs”), and physical_package_id is in [-1, highest possible CPU id] on bare metal.
  • Problem: core_id and physical_package_id are hardware or firmware identifiers, not dense indexes, so counting cores says nothing about their numeric values. On x86, core_id is the package-relative APIC ID shifted by the SMT width, and APIC IDs are routinely sparse (fused-off cores, hybrid parts with differently spaced P/E-core APIC IDs, nr_cpus=/maxcpus= limiting possible CPUs). On arm64/ACPI, a threaded CPU’s core_id and the package id are generated by find_acpi_cpu_topology(), which returns the PPTT node’s byte offset in the table (or the firmware UID) and can easily exceed the CPU count. The test therefore TFAILs on correct kernels. The comment’s NUMA-node argument only covers the arch_topology cpu_to_node() fallback.
  • Evidence: test lines 127-151, 185-190, 223-226; Documentation/ABI/stable/sysfs-devices-system-cpu:33-37 (“Typically it is the hardware platform’s identifier (rather than the kernel’s). The actual value is architecture and platform dependent.”); arch/x86/kernel/cpu/topology_common.c:198-200; drivers/base/arch_topology.c:870-913 parse_acpi_topology(); drivers/acpi/pptt.c:548-551 (“return ACPI_PTR_DIFF(cpu_node, table)”).
  • Suggested action: assert only core_id >= 0 and physical_package_id >= -1. If a consistency check is wanted, check that CPUs with equal (package_id, core_id) are exactly core_cpus_list.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,VIRT,READ. HPE TPASS (144 checks): core_id values are sparse, 0-5 and 8-13 for 24 possible CPUs; with possible CPUs <= 13 (nr_cpus=12, SMT off in firmware) core_id 13 would exceed the bound. x86 core_id = (apicid & pkg mask) >> smt shift (topology_common.c:198-200); pptt.c returns ACPI_PTR_DIFF offsets. VIRT TPASS (1 CPU)

testcases/kernel/tracing/ftrace_test/ftrace_stress/ftrace_trace.sh (runtest: worker of tracing/ftrace-stress-test)
