testcases/open_posix_testsuite/functional/semaphores/sem_lock.c (openposix: functional/semaphores/sem_lock)

  • Category: WRONG (secondary: FRAGILE)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: a semaphore protects a critical section between several processes.
  • Problem: The sem_t is allocated with malloc() and sem_init(…, pshared=1, 1); after fork() every process has its own private copy of the semaphore, so there is no cross-process exclusion at all. POSIX: a pshared semaphore is usable by any process “that can access the semaphore”, which requires it to live in shared memory. Nothing is verified (output is only printed), so the test always passes. The fork loop lets children continue the loop, creating 2^(num-1) processes (16 by default), each parent sleeping 2 s per fork; children are never reaped and their status is ignored. SEM_NAME is unused.
  • Evidence: sem_lock.c: sem_lock = malloc(sizeof(sem_t)); sem_init(sem_lock, shared, value); for (i = 1; i < num; i++) switch (fork()) { case 0: break; default: sleep(2); }; sem_init(3): “If pshared is nonzero, then the semaphore is shared between processes, and should be located in a region of shared memory”.
  • Suggested action: allocate the semaphore with mmap(MAP_SHARED|MAP_ANONYMOUS), have children increment a shared counter non-atomically inside the critical section and check the total, fork in a flat loop and wait for every child; or drop.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION. HPE as-is PASS, 160 lines from 16 distinct pids (2^(5-1) processes). Mutation deleting sem_post() still PASS with all 16 processes entering the ‘critical section’ (160 lines): each has a private copy-on-write malloc’d sem_t, so there is no cross-process exclusion and nothing is checked.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/functional/timers/clocks/twopsetclock.c (openposix: functional/timers/clocks/twopsetclock)

  • Category: WRONG (secondary: FRAGILE)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: two processes setting CLOCK_REALTIME concurrently both succeed and the later setting takes effect (clock ends near TESTTIME +/- DELTA).
  • Problem: The pass condition is `(delta <= ACCEPTABLEDELTA - DELTA) || (delta <= ACCEPTABLEDELTA
    • DELTA), i.e. justdelta <= 6`: there is no lower bound, so any clock value before TESTTIME+9s passes, and the “later one wins” claim is not tested. clock_settime() failures (EPERM without CAP_SYS_TIME) are only printed as “Note”, after which the clock is far past TESTTIME and the test reports FAIL instead of UNRESOLVED. The child returns PTS_UNRESOLVED from test_main and is never waited for. The final reset uses the time captured before the 3 s sleep, setting the system clock back ~3 s.
  • Evidence: twopsetclock.c pass condition; if (clock_settime(...) != 0) printf("Note: ..."); clock_settime(2): EPERM “does not have permission to set the clock indicated”.
  • Suggested action: return UNRESOLVED when clock_settime fails, check abs(delta - DELTA) <= 1 || abs(delta + DELTA) <= 1, wait for the child, restore saved time + elapsed (CLOCK_MONOTONIC).
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION. Not run as root (it steps the shared hosts’ clock to 2002). Mutation with clock_settime no-op’d and tpget forced 1000 s before both settings -> ‘Test PASSED’ (no lower bound). Unmodified binary as nobody (setpriv, no CAP_SYS_TIME): ‘Note: clock_settime() failed’ x2, ‘Need to manually reset time’, ‘Test FAILED’ rc=1 instead of UNRESOLVED.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/functional/timers/timers/twoptimers.c (openposix: functional/timers/timers/twoptimers)

  • Category: WRONG
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: timers in two processes set to the same absolute time both expire.
  • Problem: The child returns CHILDPASS (1) on success, PTS_FAIL (1) on wrong signal and PTS_UNRESOLVED (2) on setup errors; the parent passes on WEXITSTATUS(i) != 0. So every child outcome except exit(0) is a PASS, and the child’s FAIL is indistinguishable from success. The claim “expire at the same time” is not measured.
  • Evidence: twoptimers.c #define CHILDPASS 1; child return PTS_FAIL; / return PTS_UNRESOLVED;; parent if (WEXITSTATUS(i)) { printf("Test PASSED\n"); ....
  • Suggested action: child exits PTS_PASS (0) on success; parent requires WIFEXITED && WEXITSTATUS == PTS_PASS.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION. HPE as-is PASS. Mutation making the child’s timer_create fail (invalid clock): child prints ‘timer_create() did not return success: Invalid argument’ and returns PTS_UNRESOLVED, parent prints ‘Test PASSED’ rc=0, because any non-zero child status is treated as pass (CHILDPASS==PTS_FAIL==1).

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/stress/threads/sem_init/s-c1.c (openposix: stress/threads/sem_init/s-c1)

  • Category: WRONG (secondary: OBSOLETE, FRAGILE)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: sem_init duration does not grow with the number of semaphores; the test fails if the latency trend is non-constant or the final failure is unexpected.
  • Problem: The block-filling loop is mis-bracketed (s-c1.c:178-262). The “link block into list + append measure” code sits inside for (i...), so after every successful sem_init the same block is relinked. From i=1 on, sems_tmp->prev = sems_cur makes the block point to itself. nsem++ sits inside the if (ret != 0) error branch, so it never increments on success. Cleanup then loops while (sems_cur != &sems) on the self-linked block, re-destroying it. Meanwhile m_cur = m_cur->prev runs past the sentinel, and the write through a NULL m_cur crashes. Built by hand with gcc and run, it dies with SIGSEGV within seconds. PASSED is also inside while (1). The scalability verdict uses r1 > 1.1*r2 (constant vs. least-squares linear fit). The linear fit never has a larger residual than the constant model, so ordinary timing noise or trend can trigger FAILED. Not built in LTP anyway (no stress/threads/Makefile).
  • Evidence: s-c1.c:155 while (1), :178-262 (for-loop body), :280-320 (cleanup), :360 status check, :730-732 (thresholds); local run: “Segmentation fault … exit=139”.
  • Suggested action: Drop (the broken code has never run in LTP). A rewrite would need correct bracing and a non-statistical pass criterion.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,BUILD. Never built: stress/threads has no Makefile so stress/Makefile’s */Makefile loop skips it; HPE logfile.stress-all has 0 stress/threads entries, no binary in /opt/ltp. Built manually on HPE (gcc … -lcommon -lrt -pthread -lm) and run: ‘timeout: the monitored command dumped core’, rc=139 (SIGSEGV) within seconds.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/stress/threads/sem_open/s-c1.c (openposix: stress/threads/sem_open/s-c1)

If it is killed (t0 timeout; its own message says cleanup “can take up to 10 minutes”), tens of thousands of /dev/shm/sem.sem_open_scal_s* files are left behind, because unlinking happens only after the loop. Same r1 > 1.1*r2 heuristic issue as sem_init. Never built (no stress/threads/Makefile).

Code: loop exits only via error break, then FAILED (heuristic) or UNRESOLVED(status); PASS unreachable.

testcases/realtime/func/async_handler/async_handler_jk.c (realtime profile: func/async_handler async_handler_jk -c 100)

  • Category: WRONG (secondary: FRAGILE, WEAK)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: An async event server thread (FIFO 83) woken by a user thread (FIFO 43) runs its handler within 100us.
  • Problem: (1) main() computes delta = end - start right after join_thread(user_id). Nothing waits for the server to have run handler1(): the server is pthread_detach()ed and join_threads() cannot join it. On SMP the server wakes on another CPU and end may still be 0, giving a negative delta and “Result: PASS”. (2) user_thread clears THREAD_FLAG_SUSPENDED and broadcasts without holding server->mutex. The server tests the flag under the mutex and then calls pthread_cond_wait, so the wakeup can be lost. The flag can also be cleared before the server’s own thread->flags |= THREAD_FLAG_SUSPENDED runs: the usleep(1000) in main runs after both threads are created and orders nothing. Either way the handler never runs, end stays 0, and the result is “PASS”.
    1. Only one sample is taken, and main returns 0 even when it prints FAIL.
    2. join_threads() calls pthread_join on a detached thread, which POSIX makes undefined.
  • Evidence: async_handler_jk.c:86-104 (server), :107-123 (user, no mutex), :139-160 (no wait for handler, delta printed); lib/librttest.c:395-405 (join_threads joins every listed thread).
  • Suggested action: Clear the flag and broadcast under server->mutex. Have main wait for an “handled” flag or condition (with timeout -> FAIL) before reading end. Take many samples. Or drop the test: async_handler.c already covers cond-signal wakeup latency.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION. HPE as-is 3/3 ‘delta = 29..48 us Result: PASS’. Mutation removing the pthread_cond_broadcast (server never woken, handler1 never runs): 3/3 ‘delta = -3874644071 us’, ‘Result: PASS’, exit 0. main never waits for the handler; end==0 gives a negative delta that passes.

testcases/realtime/func/pi-tests/testpi-5.c (runtest: realtime profiles/default func/pi-tests testpi-5)

  • Category: WRONG (secondary: UNDEF, WEAK)
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: “verifies if a thread can lock the priority inheritance mutex multiple times”.
  • Problem: The child locks a default-type PI mutex twice; PASS is printed only when the 20s alarm in test-skeleton.c kills the hung child. Relocking a PTHREAD_MUTEX_DEFAULT mutex is undefined per POSIX; the kernel returns -EDEADLK for FUTEX_LOCK_PI by the owner and glibc chooses to block forever. If the implementation instead returned an error, the second lock “fails” and the child exits: no Result line and exit 0, i.e. no FAIL is ever reported. The description says the opposite of what is checked (it expects a deadlock, not multiple locking).
  • Evidence: testpi-5.c:46-63 (double lock), :94 (#include “test-skeleton.c”); test-skeleton.c:72-122; kernel/futex/pi.c:606-609 (return -EDEADLK); POSIX pthread_mutex_lock: “If the mutex type is PTHREAD_MUTEX_DEFAULT, attempting to recursively lock the mutex results in undefined behavior.”
  • Suggested action: Use PTHREAD_MUTEX_ERRORCHECK and expect EDEADLK (or RECURSIVE and expect success), or drop.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,READ. VIRT as-is: child hangs on 2nd lock, after 20s ‘Result:PASS’, rc=1. HPE work copy with PTHREAD_MUTEX_ERRORCHECK: 2nd lock returns 35 (EDEADLK, kernel futex_lock_pi owner check), child exits, no Result line, rc=0 -> PASS means ‘glibc deadlocks on UB relock’, any other behavior yields no FAIL; description says the opposite
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUSL,SRC. HPE glibc: child hangs, 20s alarm, ‘Result:PASS’ rc=1; musl: same ‘Result:PASS’ rc=1. Both libcs block forever on owner relock of a NORMAL PI mutex: glibc nptl/pthread_mutex_lock.c:419-431 (‘Delay the thread indefinitely’), musl src/thread/pthread_mutex_timedlock.c:48-52 (EDEADLK returned only for ERRORCHECK, else wait forever). PASS = ‘libc deadlocks on UB’

testcases/realtime/func/sched_football/sched_football.c (runtest: sched/sched_football)

The earlier threads are also never joined.   • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,VIRT,GIT. VIRT work copy with offense prio 60 (above fans): -i 2 -> iter1 ‘Final ball position: 390027758’ TFAIL, iter2 ‘Final ball position: 0’ TPASS (game_over never reset, since e523ba88dd9b). Extra: offense at 45 (above defense, below fans) still ball 0 on HPE and VIRT: 2N fans at prio 50 saturate all CPUs, so defense never matters

testcases/realtime/func/thread_clock/tc-2.c (runtest: realtime profiles/default func/thread_clock “tc-2 -c 0.5”)

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/functional/mqueues/send_rev_2.c, stress/mqueues/multi_send_rev_1.c, stress/mqueues/multi_send_rev_2.c (openposix: functional/mqueues/send_rev_2, stress/mqueues/multi_send_rev_1, multi_send_rev_2)

  • Category: WRONG (secondary: FRAGILE / UNDEF)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: threads send/receive on message queues concurrently; “set different priority to the messages … to see whether the highest priority is received first”.
  • Problem: (1) All threads report failure via pthread_exit((void *)1) but main joins with pthread_join(t, NULL) and unconditionally returns PTS_PASS, so the tests cannot fail.
    1. The priority-ordering claim is never checked (received messages are only printed).
    2. Queues are opened O_NONBLOCK and receivers start concurrently with senders, so mq_receive can legitimately return EAGAIN on an empty queue; if failures were propagated this would be a false FAIL. (4) multi_send_rev_1/2 call mq_send(q, s_msg_ptr[i], MSG_SIZE /128/, …) with 9-11 byte string literals, reading past the end of the literal (C UB).
  • Evidence: send_rev_2.c test_main pthread_join(send1, NULL) ... return PTS_PASS;; multi_send_rev_1.c msend(): mq_send(send_info.mqID, s_msg_ptr[i], MSG_SIZE, i); mreceive() even calls pthread_exit(NULL) on error. Stress variants are run with arg “1” (*.args).
  • Suggested action: open without O_NONBLOCK (or send before starting receivers), collect thread return values, verify that messages come out in priority order, send strlen()+1 bytes. Otherwise drop as duplicates of conformance/interfaces/mq_send|mq_receive.

UNDOC: Relies on undocumented or implementation-specific behavior

The test demands behavior that no man page, kernel document or standard promises: errno precedence when several error conditions apply, internal limits, ordering, exact strings. The kernel could change legitimately and the test would fail without any kernel bug. Action: relax the check to the documented contract, or document the dependency with a kernel reference, or drop the subcase.

24 testcases. Sorted by path; confidence shown in each entry.

testcases/kernel/mem/tunable/max_map_count.c (runtest: mm/max_map_count)

  • Category: UNDOC
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: a process can have at most /proc/sys/vm/max_map_count memory map areas.
  • Problem: the test TPASSes only if the number of lines in /proc/pid/maps is exactly max_maps + 1 and TFAILs on max_maps. That depends on the kernel’s off-by-one check mm->map_count > sysctl_max_map_count (it should be >=). The test’s own comment (l.173-177) says this is “the mm failure point at the time of writing this COMMENT!”. The documented limit is “the maximum number of memory map areas a process may have”. If the kernel changed the check to >=, which matches the docs (nommu.c and split paths in vma.c:640 already use >=), the test would FAIL. It also depends on every /proc/pid/maps line matching one counted VMA, apart from a hand-kept per-arch filter for vsyscall/vdso.
  • Evidence: max_map_count.c:178; /usr/src/linux/mm/mmap.c:381 and mm/vma.c:3031 (if (mm->map_count > get_sysctl_max_map_count()) return -ENOMEM;), compare mm/vma.c:640 and mm/nommu.c:1039 (>=); Documentation/admin-guide/sysctl/vm.rst:464 “This file contains the maximum number of memory map areas a process may have.”
  • Suggested action: accept map_count in {max_maps, max_maps + 1} (and possibly a small arch slack), or cite the kernel check in a comment and accept both outcomes.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/chown/chown04.c (runtest: syscalls/chown04)

  • Category: UNDOC
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: chown() fails with EROFS when the named file is on a read-only filesystem.
  • Problem: setup() leaves euid=nobody for every case. The EROFS case runs chown(“mntpoint”, nobody_uid, 0) as nobody on the root-owned mount root of the read-only fs. That also changes the owner of a file the caller does not own, so EPERM applies as well. The kernel returns EROFS only because do_fchownat() calls mnt_want_write() before chown_common()/notify_change(). Neither chown(2) nor POSIX orders the two errors.
  • Evidence: chown04.c:48,64,88-95; fs/open.c:849-853 (mnt_want_write before chown_common). chown(2) lists both “EPERM The calling process did not have the required permissions” and “EROFS The named file resides on a read-only filesystem” without precedence.
  • Suggested action: Run the EROFS case with euid 0 (as chmod06 does), or chown to (-1, -1) so that only EROFS applies.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,VIRT,READ,GIT. VIRT: chown04 8/8 TPASS. Same creds (euid nobody, egid 0) give EPERM on root-owned tfile_1 (case 1), so for the root-owned ro mount root both EPERM and EROFS apply; EROFS wins only because do_fchownat() calls mnt_want_write() before chown_common() (fs/open.c:849-853). Unchanged since the old-API version (euid nobody for all cases).

testcases/kernel/syscalls/dup3/dup3_02.c (runtest: syscalls/dup3_02)

  • Category: UNDOC
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: dup3() returns EINVAL for oldfd == newfd (with and without O_CLOEXEC) and for invalid flags.
  • Problem: The test uses hard-coded old_fd = 3 without opening it. The LTP library closes its IPC fd after mmap (lib/tst_test.c:149), so fd 3 is normally not open, and every subcase also meets the EBADF condition (“oldfd isn’t an open file descriptor”). The test passes only because ksys_dup3() checks flags and oldfd==newfd before looking up oldfd. dup(2) lists EBADF and both EINVAL conditions without ordering them.
  • Evidence: dup3_02.c:22, :29-33; fs/file.c:1429-1442 (EINVAL checks before fd lookup); dup(2) ERRORS lists EBADF/EINVAL with no precedence.
  • Suggested action: open a real file in setup and use its fd as oldfd (and a known-valid newfd for the invalid-flags case).
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,VIRT. VIRT probe mutant with fd 3 closed (exec 3<&-, as under a normal harness): ‘fcntl(3, F_GETFD) = -1 errno=EBADF’ yet all 3 cases TPASS with EINVAL, so EBADF also applies and the pass relies on ksys_dup3() checking flags/oldfd==newfd first. Under ltprun fd 3 is the inherited flock fd (/run/lock/ltp-verify.lock): result then depends on the harness’s leaked fds.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/fchmod/fchmod06.c (runtest: syscalls/fchmod06)

  • Category: UNDOC (secondary: DOCS)
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: fchmod() fails with EPERM (not owner), EBADF (closed fd), EROFS (read-only fs).
  • Problem: setup() switches to euid nobody before all cases run. mntpoint/file on the needs_rofs mount is created by root (lib/tst_test.c:1204-1206), so in the EROFS case both EROFS and EPERM apply. The test only passes because chmod_common() calls mnt_want_write() (EROFS) before notify_change()/setattr_prepare() (EPERM); chmod(2) lists both errors without ordering them. Also, the docparse line “EROFS – file descriptor opened as a read-only” is wrong: EROFS comes from the read-only mount, not from the O_RDONLY fd.

Probe before the EROFS case: ‘euid=65534 file st_uid=0 mode=100777’, so the EPERM condition (not owner, unprivileged) also holds; EROFS wins only because chmod_common() calls mnt_want_write() before notify_change() (fs/open.c). Docparse ‘EROFS – file descriptor opened as a read-only’ is wrong too.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/fchown/fchown04.c (runtest: syscalls/fchown04, fchown04_16)

  • Category: UNDOC
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: fchown() fails with EPERM (not owner), EBADF (invalid fd), EROFS (file on read-only fs).

testcases/kernel/syscalls/fcntl/fcntl11.c (runtest: syscalls/fcntl11)

  • Category: UNDOC
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: Region locking: a write lock split/converted by a read lock is reported correctly by F_GETLK from another process.
  • Problem: Most probes query a range that overlaps several of the parent’s locks (e.g. the whole file do_test(F_WRLCK,0,0,0) in blocks 1-8 overlaps both the read and the write lock) and require F_GETLK to return the lowest-offset one. fcntl(2) only promises “details about one of those locks”; POSIX says “Get any lock which blocks”. Linux returns the first conflicting entry of inode->flc_posix, which happens to be sorted by start for a single owner because posix_lock_inode() inserts locks in order. That is an implementation detail. The kernel has kept this for decades, so a real failure is unlikely.
  • Evidence: fcntl11.c:280-281, 432-433, 477-478, 518-519, 560-561, 598-599; fs/locks.c:1027-1041 (posix_test_lock returns first list match); fcntl(2) “returns details about one of those locks”; POSIX fcntl F_GETLK “Get any lock which blocks …”.
  • Suggested action: query ranges that overlap exactly one lock (e.g. probe [0,5) then [10,15)), or document that the test relies on Linux’s per-owner sorted lock list.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,READ. HPE: runs clean (blocks 1-9, rc=0; old API reports no TPASS lines). Kernel fs/locks.c posix_test_lock() returns the first conflicting entry of flc_posix, ordered by start only within one owner. Block 1 probe [0,EOF) overlaps RD 1-5 and WR 10-14 and requires 1-5. Reliance on undocumented order confirmed; real failure unlikely.

Test is glibc-specific || [m09: UNCHANGED] HPE glibc: PASS; musl: ‘TFAIL: len is smaller than the actual size succeeded’ (rc 1). Same as m01 record (CONFIRMED UNDOC high: musl src/unistd/gethostname.c:9-12 truncates, POSIX-allowed); nothing new

Work copy adds probes: io_cancel(ctx=0, valid iocb ptr) -> EINVAL; io_cancel(valid io_setup ctx, NULL, NULL) -> EFAULT. Both errors apply to the original call; EFAULT wins only because fs/aio.c:2238 get_user(iocb->aio_key) precedes lookup_ioctx(). Valid ctx makes EFAULT unambiguous.

Commit 4b8e26706d10 and test header admit it is the auth-token fallback; man page only says view permission is needed. Accept EACCES too.

In ‘unshare -nm’ with sysfs remounted: ‘ip link add v09d0 type dummy; ip link set v09d0 mtu 100000’ accepted by the kernel (mtu reads 100000), then ‘sys_net01.c:95: TFAIL: /sys/class/net/v09d0/mtu = 100000 out of range [1, 65535]’

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/definitions/pthread_h/6-1-buildonly.c (openposix: conformance/definitions/pthread_h/6-1-buildonly)

  • Category: UNDOC (phase 1: UNDEF)
  • Confidence: medium (phase 1: low)
  • Claim under test: pthread_self() is declared as pthread_t pthread_self(void).
  • Problem: The check does if (ptid == 0). POSIX pthread_t is opaque and may be a structure (POSIX pthread.h rationale gives a struct example; PTHREAD_NULL was added for this reason), so the compile check depends on an arithmetic pthread_t that POSIX does not require. Harmless on glibc/musl, but on a conforming implementation with a struct pthread_t it reports a compile failure that is not a conformance bug.
  • Evidence: pthread_h/6-1-buildonly.c; https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/basedefs/pthread.h.html RATIONALE “Since pthread_t is an opaque type, a definition of PTHREAD_NULL was added.”
  • Suggested action: drop the comparison (e.g. (void)ptid;) or use pthread_equal().
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): REVISED via BUILD,READ. Compiles on glibc (pthread_t=unsigned long). POSIX XBD sys/types.h: all types arithmetic ‘with the following exceptions’ incl. pthread_t (Issue 6 TC added it so it may be a struct). A struct-typed copy (my_pthread_t ptid; if (ptid == 0)) -> gcc ‘error: invalid operands to binary ==’. Not C UB: impl-defined type dependence -> UNDOC.
  • Verification conclusion: Phase-1 reasoning holds, but it is not C undefined behaviour: on an implementation with a struct pthread_t the comparison is a compile error. That is reliance on implementation-defined representation -> UNDOC. Action unchanged: drop ptid == 0 (use (void)ptid;).
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via BUILD,MUSL,SRC. glibc and musl logfile.conformance-all: ‘pthread_h/6-1-buildonly compile PASSED’ under both. pthread_t: glibc pthreadtypes.h:27 unsigned long; musl alltypes.h.in:53-57 ’struct __pthread *’ in C (unsigned long only for C++) -> ptid==0 compiles on musl only as a null-pointer compare: a third representation, confirming the check depends on the impl-defined type

UNDEF: Tests undefined or unspecified behavior

Documentation explicitly leaves the outcome open (unspecified, implementation-defined, ‘may fail’), or the test itself invokes C undefined behavior, yet the test requires one specific result. Action: drop the subcase, or reduce it to ‘any documented outcome, no crash’.

116 testcases. Sorted by path; confidence shown in each entry.

testcases/kernel/controllers/cpuctl/cpuctl_latency_check_task.c (helper for run_cpuctl_latency_test.sh)

  • Category: UNDEF (secondary: FRAGILE)
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: measures usleep() overshoot over 201 iterations and FAILs if any single overshoot is above ALLOWED.
  • Problem: actual_us = cur.tv_usec - prev.tv_usec is unsigned, so it wraps to about 4.29e9 whenever the sleep crosses a second boundary. With sleeps of up to 200ms, almost every run crosses one. actual = 1e6*actual_s + actual_us then converts a double greater than UINT_MAX to unsigned int, which is undefined behavior in C. On x86-64 it truncates to the right value by luck. On arm64, fcvtzu saturates to UINT_MAX, so delta becomes huge and the result is a spurious FAIL. A single sample above a fixed threshold under 100 hogs is also flaky. The result is never propagated (see the script entry above).
  • Evidence: cpuctl_latency_check_task.c:120-128.
  • Suggested action: compute with timespec and signed 64-bit arithmetic (or use tst_timer), or drop together with the script.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via READ,BUILD,RUN. Extracted the delta arithmetic (cpuctl_latency_check_task.c:120-123) into ub.c; prev=5.950000 cur=6.050000: actual_us=4294067296, 1e6*actual_s+actual_us=4295067296.0 > UINT_MAX; x86-64 -O2 gives actual=100000 by luck; same code with -fsanitize=float-cast-overflow -fsanitize-trap=all dies with SIGILL (rc 132) -> UB confirmed. Helper never runs on v2 hosts (test_controllers.sh TCONFs)

testcases/kernel/io/direct_io/diotest4.c (runtest: dio/dio04, dio10)

  • Category: UNDEF (secondary: FRAGILE)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: O_DIRECT error conditions, including “[3] odd count” (count=1) and “[14] non-aligned buffer” (buf+1), both required to fail with EINVAL.
  • Problem: open(2) explicitly leaves misaligned O_DIRECT handling to the filesystem: they “can either fail with EINVAL or fall back to buffered I/O”. The test hard-codes a whitelist (NFS, btrfs, FUSE, tmpfs) and otherwise requires EINVAL. Other in-tree filesystems legitimately fall back: ext4 returns dio_align 0 for data=journal/inline data/verity inodes and fs-block alignment for fscrypt inodes, so ext4_should_use_dio() picks buffered I/O; f2fs falls back for I/O that is logical-block but not fs-block aligned. On those, read/write succeed and the test TFAILs.
  • Evidence: diotest4.c:252-264, :144-157 (fs-type whitelist + runtest_f EINVAL); open(2) O_DIRECT: “In Linux alignment restrictions vary by filesystem and kernel version and might be absent entirely. The handling of misaligned O_DIRECT I/Os also varies; they can either fail with EINVAL or fall back to buffered I/O.”; /usr/src/linux/fs/ext4/file.c:55-67 ext4_should_use_dio(); /usr/src/linux/fs/f2fs/file.c:5112-5140 f2fs_should_use_dio().
  • Suggested action: query statx(STATX_DIOALIGN) (Linux 6.1+) and accept either EINVAL or a successful (buffered fallback) transfer for misaligned I/O; TCONF only when the alignment is unknown.

testcases/kernel/lib/numa_cpuset.c (helper; used by mem/ksm/ksm02, ksm04, mem/oom/oom04, oom05)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: helper write_node_cpusets() sets cpuset.mems to node nd and cpuset.cpus to that node’s online CPUs, falling back to CPU0 for CPU-less nodes.
  • Problem: gather_node_cpus() unconditionally strips the trailing comma with cpus[strlen(cpus) - 1] = '\0'. When the node has no (online) CPUs, cpus is empty, strlen()-1 wraps to SIZE_MAX and the store lands one byte before the stack buffer (C out-of-bounds write, UB). This is precisely the memory-only-node case (CXL/PMEM/HBM nodes, or all node CPUs offlined) that write_node_cpusets() explicitly tries to support with its “No CPUs in the node” branch. oom04/oom05 pick the node via get_allowed_nodes(NH_MEMS), which does not filter CPU-less nodes, so they can hit it.
  • Evidence: numa_cpuset.c:41-42 (strip), 56-63 (empty-case fallback); oom/oom04.c:58-62.
  • Suggested action: guard the strip with if (cpus[0]) (or size_t l = strlen(cpus); if (l) cpus[l-1] = '\0';).
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via BUILD,RUN,READ. HPE: harness #including numa_cpuset.c with a canary byte placed right before cpus[]; gather_node_cpus(cpus, 7) (node with no CPUs) overwrote the canary 0x43->0x00 (cpus[strlen-1] with strlen 0); node0 call leaves canary intact -> out-of-bounds write confirmed

testcases/kernel/syscalls/brk/brk01.c (runtest: syscalls/brk01)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: brk() can grow, keep and shrink the program break, and the new heap memory is writable.
  • Problem: After growing, the test writes to *(char *)cur_brk, the byte at the new break. That byte is one past the end of the data segment. It is only mapped because the kernel rounds the heap VMA up to a page boundary. inc is 2*pagesize-1, so if the starting break is at page offset 1, the new break is page-aligned and the write lands outside the heap VMA, giving SIGSEGV (or it silently hits whatever is mapped next). Usually the starting break is page-aligned and the write lands in the padding, so the test passes by luck. Either way the test does not check that the allocated range itself is writable.
  • Evidence: brk01.c:17,41,66-67; mm/mmap.c:155-156 (the heap VMA ends at PAGE_ALIGN(brk)).
  • Suggested action: Write to (char *)cur_brk - 1, or to the whole range [old_brk, new_brk).
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,VIRT. VIRT: brk01 3/3 TPASS as-is. Mutant that first moves the break to page offset 1 (brk(sbrk(0)+pagesize-off+1)), so that cur+2ps-1 is page aligned: ‘MUT: start break 0x1de61001’ then ‘TBROK: Test killed by SIGSEGV!’ -> the write at (char*)cur_brk is one byte past the heap and only works thanks to page rounding.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/epoll_wait/epoll_wait16.c (runtest: syscalls/epoll_wait16)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: with EPOLLEXCLUSIVE, one event on the target fd wakes exactly one of several waiting epoll instances.
  • Problem: epoll_ctl(2) only promises “one or more” epoll fds receive an event; “exactly one” is current kernel behaviour (__wake_up_common with nr_exclusive=1 stops at the first ep_poll_callback returning ewake=1), not a documented guarantee. ep_poll_callback returns ewake=0 for an instance whose ep->wq has no waiter, so the walk continues to the next entry; the documentation deliberately leaves room for more than one wakeup. The test FAILs if nwoken != round+1.
  • Evidence: epoll_wait16.c:12-13, :96-101; epoll_ctl(2) EPOLLEXCLUSIVE: “one or more of the epoll file descriptors will receive an event with epoll_wait(2)”; /usr/src/linux/fs/eventpoll.c ep_poll_callback (line ~1491, ewake logic).
  • Suggested action: Relax to “fewer than NWAITERS woken per event” (i.e. not all, thundering herd avoided) or “at least one”, or document that the test checks current kernel behaviour.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/fpathconf/fpathconf01.c (runtest: syscalls/fpathconf01)

  • Category: UNDEF (secondary: DOCS)
  • Confidence: low (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: “basic functionality of the fpathconf(2) system call”.
  • Problem: All nine names are queried on a regular file, and every call must return >= 0 (TST_EXP_POSITIVE). The docs do not require that for most of these names on a regular file:
    • fpathconf(3) says _PC_MAX_CANON, _PC_MAX_INPUT and _PC_VDISABLE need fd to refer to a terminal.
    • POSIX (notes 2, 3/4 and 6 in the fpathconf table) leaves it unspecified whether MAX_CANON/MAX_INPUT/VDISABLE (non-terminal), NAME_MAX/PATH_MAX/NO_TRUNC (non-directory) and PIPE_BUF (not a pipe/FIFO/directory) are supported. EINVAL is an allowed error for an unsupported association.
    • fpathconf(3) also allows -1 with errno unchanged for an indeterminate limit or an unsupported option, and the test treats that as a failure. pathconf01 was just relaxed for the same reason (commit 5b5bab8c18a7). Also, fpathconf is a libc function, not a syscall.
  • Evidence: fpathconf01.c:17-25, 34, 39; fpathconf(3): “_PC_MAX_CANON … where fd or path must refer to a terminal”, ERRORS “EINVAL The implementation does not support an association of name with the specified file”, RETURN VALUE “-1 is returned and errno is not changed”; POSIX https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/fpathconf.html notes 2/3/6.
  • Suggested action: Do as pathconf01 now does: accept EINVAL (TCONF) for the unspecified names, or use a directory fd for NAME_MAX/PATH_MAX/NO_TRUNC/PIPE_BUF and a pty for the terminal names. Accept -1 with errno 0. Fix “system call” in the description.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): REVISED via RUN,READ,GIT. HPE glibc: 9/9 TPASS (255,255,0,65535,255,4096,4096,1,1) on a regular file. POSIX notes allow EINVAL for these names on a non-terminal/non-dir fd, so the reasoning holds, but glibc/musl/bionic all return constants here (unlike pathconf01’s PC_REC* that broke Bionic, git 5b5bab8c18a7); no known libc fails -> low.
  • Verification conclusion: The POSIX argument is right (MAX_CANON/MAX_INPUT/VDISABLE on a non-terminal, NAME_MAX/PATH_MAX/NO_TRUNC/PIPE_BUF on a regular file are “unspecified”, EINVAL allowed), but all of the names fpathconf01 queries are answered with constants by glibc and, as far as known, musl and Bionic, so no supported libc fails today. Keep the suggested relaxation (TCONF on EINVAL, “libc function” in the description) but at low confidence.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: 9/9 TPASS (LINK_MAX 65535 via statfs, linux/fpathconf.c:37); musl: 9/9 TPASS (LINK_MAX 8). musl src/conf/fpathconf.c:7-34 is a constant table that ignores fd (probe fpathconf(-1,_PC_NAME_MAX)=255 errno 0; glibc EBADF). No libc returns EINVAL for these names, so low stays; under musl the test touches no kernel at all

testcases/kernel/syscalls/getgroups/getgroups01.c (runtest: syscalls/getgroups01, getgroups01_16)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: item 4, “getgroups() succeeds and gidset contains group id returned from getgid()”.
  • Problem: the kernel returns exactly the list that was last passed to setgroups(). It never adds the (e)gid. getgroups(2) explicitly leaves this unspecified. setup() calls setgroups(3, {0,1,2}) but ignores the result, and the test has no needs_root. As root the check passes only because gid 0 happens to be in that list. As non-root, setgroups fails silently and the check depends on how the login/launcher built the group list. Running under sg, under a systemd unit with Group=, or in a container with a minimal group list gives a false FAIL.
  • Evidence: getgroups01.c:154-171, :187-188; getgroups(2): “It is unspecified whether the effective group ID of the calling process is included in the returned list.”; kernel/groups.c getgroups copies current_cred()->group_info verbatim.
  • Suggested action: set needs_root, use SAFE_SETGROUPS with a known list and compare against that list, or drop item 4.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,READ. HPE as root: as-is item 4 TPASS only because setgroups({0,1,2}) contains gid 0. ‘setpriv –regid 10 –keep-groups getgroups01’ -> item 4 ‘TFAIL: getgroups(NGROUPS,gidset) ret 3, does not contain gid 10 (from getgid)’; getgroups(2) leaves egid inclusion unspecified.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/listxattr/listxattr01.c (runtest: syscalls/listxattr01)

  • Category: UNDEF

  • Claim under test: listxattr() returns the security.ltptest1 name.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/tgkill/tgkill01.c (runtest: syscalls/tgkill01)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: low
  • Claim under test: tgkill() delivers SIGUSR1 to the specified thread.
  • Problem: sigusr1_thread is a plain (non-volatile, non-atomic) pthread_t global. It is written by the signal handler running on another thread and busy-polled by the main thread (while (pthread_equal(sigusr1_thread, pthread_self())) usleep(1000);). That is a C11 data race (UB). In practice the opaque usleep()/pthread_equal() calls force a reload, so it works with current compilers, but nothing guarantees it (e.g. under LTO with an inlined pthread_equal).
  • Evidence: tgkill01.c:27-32, 82-91
  • Suggested action: Record the delivering thread’s index or tid in a volatile sig_atomic_t/_Atomic variable (or use __atomic_load_n/__atomic_store_n).
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): UNCHANGED via RUN,REPEAT,READ. HPE: TPASS, 5 runs x -i 20 all pass. objdump of installed binary: pthread_equal inlined (0 calls), loop is ‘call usleep; mov sigusr1_thread(%rip),%rax; cmp; je loop’, so the global is reloaded only because usleep() is an opaque call. Data race is real per C11 but cannot be shown to break with the current toolchain

testcases/network/nfs/nfslock01/nfs_flock_dgen.c (runtest: helper of net.nfs/nfslock01_*)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: generates a file of nlines x nchars bytes.
  • Problem: char buf[BUFSIZ] is an uninitialised local array. The loop fills only buf[0..nchars-2], and then fprintf(fp, "%s\n", buf) reads until a NUL byte. Correct output depends on buf[nchars-1] happening to be 0 (fresh stack pages), which is undefined behaviour. With garbage there, the line gets longer, nfslock01.sh’s size check fails and the test reports TBROK instead of testing anything. fopen() is also not checked for NULL.
  • Evidence: nfs_flock_dgen.c:19 (buf), 55-56 (fill loop), 58 (fprintf “%s”).
  • Suggested action: Set buf[nchars - 1] = '\0' (or use fwrite of nchars-1 bytes plus ‘’) and check fopen.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via BUILD,RUN. local: gcc -O2 build, dgen 64x1000 -> 64000 bytes (stack happened to be 0); same source with -ftrivial-auto-var-init=pattern -> 8193000 bytes, lines run into 0xFE bytes past buf[nchars-1] -> nfslock01 size check would TBROK; correctness depends on uninitialised stack

testcases/network/rpc/rpc-tirpc/tests_pack/rpc_suite/rpc/rpc_stdcall_clnt_geterr/rpc_clnt_geterr.c (runtest: net.rpc_tests rpc_clnt_geterr)

  • Category: UNDEF (secondary: WEAK)
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: clnt_geterr() copies the error status of the client handle.
  • Problem: No RPC call is made; clnt_geterr() is called on a freshly created handle and the test requires re_status == RPC_SUCCESS. The error structure of a handle that has never performed a call is not defined anywhere (it depends on libc/libtirpc internal initialisation of the private cu_error). The test therefore checks a library implementation detail, not the documented behaviour (status of the last call).
  • Evidence: rpc_clnt_geterr.c: clnt_create() then immediately clnt_geterr(); rpc(3): “clnt_geterr() A macro that copies the error structure out of the client handle”.
  • Suggested action: make a clnt_call() first (success -> RPC_SUCCESS; call to a missing procedure -> RPC_PROCUNAVAIL) and check re_status matches the returned clnt_stat.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,READ,VIRT. VIRT: TPASS as-is and with MALLOC_PERTURB_=165; libtirpc-1.3.8 src: clnt_dg_create() allocs cu via mem_alloc() == calloc(1,..) (tirpc/rpc/types.h:65) and never sets cu_error before a call, so re_status==RPC_SUCCESS(0) only through calloc zeroing, an implementation detail; no clnt_call is made so the documented ‘last call status’ is untested
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): UNCHANGED via RUN,MUSL,SRC. HPE rpc_test.sh -s rpc_svc_1 -c rpc_clnt_geterr: glibc TPASS; musl TPASS. re_status==0 comes from libtirpc mem_alloc==calloc (types.h:65, clnt_dg.c:217); musl calloc (src/malloc/calloc.c:33-45) zeroes as C requires, so no libc can differ. Detail is libtirpc’s, not libc’s

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/definitions/mqueue_h/1-1.c (openposix: conformance/definitions/mqueue_h/1-1)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: struct mq_attr members mq_flags, mq_maxmsg, mq_msgsize, mq_curmsgs are long.
  • Problem: The TEST_LIMITS macro evaluates -LONG_MIN, -(LONG_MIN+1) (fine) and LONG_MAX+1 in long arithmetic, which is signed overflow (C UB; gcc warns “integer overflow in expression”). The last check then requires the field to equal LONG_MIN, i.e. relies on two’s-complement wraparound of a UB expression. The first check (x = -LONG_MIN; x != -LONG_MIN) compares the overflowed expression with itself. Works today with gcc constant folding, but the verification is based on UB rather than on the type.
  • Evidence: mqueue_h/1-1.c TEST_LIMITS macro; POSIX mqueue.h: “long mq_flags … long mq_curmsgs”.
  • Suggested action: replace with a compile-time type check, e.g. _Static_assert(_Generic(mqs.mq_flags, long: 1, default: 0), ...) or sizeof + assignment of LONG_MAX/LONG_MIN without overflowing expressions.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via BUILD,RUN. HPE: mqueue_h_1-1.run-test PASSED rc=0. gcc -Wall: 12x ‘-Woverflow: integer overflow in expression … of type long int’ (lines 17,18,31 x4 fields): -LONG_MIN and LONG_MAX+1 are overflowing constant expressions (C11 6.6p4 constraint, UB); result relies on gcc’s wraparound folding. UBSan not available on hosts (no libubsan).

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/aio_cancel/2-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/aio_cancel/2-1)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: low
  • Claim under test: aio_cancel(fd, NULL) cancels all outstanding cancelable requests.
  • Problem: Requires aio_error()==ECANCELED for queued writes 3..7. POSIX lets the implementation decide which operations are cancelable, so a conforming implementation could cancel none of them (and return AIO_NOTCANCELED). The test encodes the glibc model: one worker per fd, queued requests cancelable, running ones not. This holds on Linux/glibc and is stable, so the risk is portability (musl, other libcs), not false FAILs on glibc.
  • Evidence: aio_cancel/2-1.c:82-91; https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/aio_cancel.html: “Which operations are cancelable is implementation-defined.”
  • Suggested action: Document the glibc dependency in the test header, or turn the per-request ECANCELED check into TCONF/UNTESTED when aio_cancel() returns AIO_NOTCANCELED for everything.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,READ. HPE: Test PASSED as-is (glibc: queued requests cancelable). Code :82-91 requires ECANCELED for every request after the blocked one; POSIX: which ops are cancelable is implementation-defined. No false FAIL possible on glibc; portability-only, low stands
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): UNCHANGED via MUSL,RUN,SRC,READ. HPE glibc: Test PASSED; musl: hangs in aio_cancel, rc=137. musl src/aio/aio.c:382-392 aio_cancel holds q->lock while waiting for each cancelled worker; a queued worker sits in pthread_cond_wait (aio.c:254), which relocks q->lock before acting on cancel (thread/pthread_cond_timedwait.c:145,168) -> deadlock (musl bug). musl also cancels queued writes, so both libcs fit the test’s model

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/aio_cancel/5-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/aio_cancel/5-1)

  • Category: UNDEF (secondary: FRAGILE)
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: An aiocb that was not cancelled is not modified.
  • Problem: (1) The test requires aio_cancel() to return AIO_NOTCANCELED and the blocked write to stay EINPROGRESS. That only holds if in-progress operations are non-cancelable, which POSIX leaves implementation-defined. musl, for example, cancels the worker thread, which is blocked in a cancellation point (send). (2) Synchronization: it polls until task #1 reports done, then relies on one 10 ms nanosleep for glibc’s worker to dequeue task #2 and start the blocking send. In glibc, the error status is published before the next request is marked running, so under heavy load task #2 can still be queued. It then gets cancelled, aio_cancel() returns AIO_CANCELED, and the test FAILs.
  • Evidence: aio_cancel/5-1.c:73-102 (the nanosleep at :76 is the only grace period); POSIX aio_cancel “Which operations are cancelable is implementation-defined.”
  • Suggested action: Document the glibc dependency. Wait until task #2 is observably blocked (e.g. poll that the receiver socket holds 2 messages and give extra margin), or accept AIO_CANCELED with TCONF/UNRESOLVED when the blocked task was cancelled.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): REVISED via RUN,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT,READ. No FAIL in 140 runs (HPE 50 + 50 ltpstress, VIRT 20 + 20 stress). glibc rt/aio_misc.c handle_fildes_io: error status of #1 set, #2 dequeued and marked running=allocated in ONE hold of __aio_requests_mutex; aio_cancel takes that mutex and treats ‘allocated’ as AIO_NOTCANCELED -> 10 ms race cannot occur on glibc. UNDEF only
  • Verification conclusion: The FRAGILE part (task #2 still queued after the 10 ms grace period) cannot happen with glibc. Once aio_error(#1) is no longer EINPROGRESS, #2 is already “allocated” under the same lock that aio_cancel needs. What remains is the portability point (implementation-defined cancelability, e.g. musl), so drop the secondary FRAGILE, use low, and limit the action to documenting the glibc dependency.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: Test PASSED; musl: hangs in aio_cancel(), rc=137 (musl deadlock, see 2-1). Probe with 1 write blocked in progress on full DGRAM socket: glibc aio_cancel=AIO_NOTCANCELED, EINPROGRESS (rt/aio_cancel.c:90-92); musl AIO_CANCELED, ECANCELED (aio.c:385-388 pthread_cancel) -> 5-1 would FAIL on musl

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/aio_read/10-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/aio_read/10-1)

  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)

HPE: Test PASSED as-is (glibc reports EBADF asynchronously). git show b451d11fc8e5 (2009): test originally required sync -1/EBADF and was flipped to ‘aio_read()!=0 -> FAIL’ to match glibc; neither version accepts both outcomes POSIX allows
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via MUSL,RUN,REPEAT,SRC. HPE glibc: Test PASSED; musl: FAIL 2/2 ‘aio_read/10-1.c bad aio_read return value()’. musl src/aio/aio.c:87-89 (fd<0 -> EBADF) + :292-296 returns -1/EBADF synchronously, which POSIX allows; glibc rt/aio_misc.c does not check the fd, so EBADF only arrives from pread in the worker. Real false FAIL

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/aio_read/11-2.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/aio_read/11-2)

POSIX allows both. glibc checks reqprio synchronously (__aio_enqueue_request), so there is no false FAIL on glibc. Also, the reqprio EINVAL condition is part of the Prioritized I/O option, which 8-1 checks via sysconf(_SC_PRIORITIZED_IO) and this test does not.

  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via MUSL,RUN,REPEAT,SRC,READ. HPE glibc: Test PASSED (rt/aio_misc.c:320-328 sync EINVAL); musl: FAIL 2/2 ‘bad aio_read return value()’. musl has no PIO: sysconf.c:44 _SC_PRIORITIZED_IO=-1, aio_reqprio never read in src/. POSIX marks reqprio EINVAL [PIO]; aio_read/8-1 (gated) is UNTESTED on musl. False FAIL

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/lio_listio/14-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/lio_listio/14-1)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: failure of an individual request does not prevent completion of the others.
  • Problem: the failing request is an aiocb with aio_fildes = -1 submitted with LIO_NOWAIT, and the test FAILs unless lio_listio() returns 0. POSIX lets EBADF be detected synchronously at submission; an implementation that does so does not queue that request and lio_listio() then returns -1 with errno EIO. Both behaviours are conforming, but only the asynchronous one passes. glibc detects it asynchronously, so Linux/glibc passes. The test also never checks that request 2 actually failed.
  • Evidence: lio_listio/14-1.c:107-108, :141-151; POSIX aio_write(): “Each of the following conditions may be detected synchronously at the time of the call to aio_write(), or asynchronously.” [EBADF]; lio_listio() ERRORS: “[EIO] One or more of the individual I/O operations failed.”
  • Suggested action: accept ret == -1 && errno == EIO as well (then check aio_error() of the good requests), and verify aio_error(aiocbs[2]) == EBADF.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,READ. HPE as-is PASS (glibc reports bad-fd request asynchronously). Mutation: request #2 given the valid fd (nothing fails) -> still ‘lio_listio/14-1.c PASSED’ rc=0: test never verifies that request 2 failed. Sync-detection (-1/EIO) rejection is from code :141-151; not testable on glibc
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): REVISED via MUSL,RUN,REPEAT,SRC,READ. HPE glibc: PASSED; musl: FAIL 2/2 ‘Error lio_listio() Resource temporarily unavailable’. musl lio_listio.c:89-104 stops at the first failing submit (sync EBADF on #2), never queues #3..#9 and returns EAGAIN, which breaks assertion 14 itself -> musl bug, true FAIL. The sync-detection concern holds; the suggested fix must also catch this
  • Verification conclusion: musl does detect the bad fd synchronously, as the finding anticipated. But musl’s lio_listio stops at the first failed submit (lio_listio.c:89-104): requests #3..#9 are never queued, and it returns -1/EAGAIN, not EIO. That violates the assertion under test (“failure of an individual request does not prevent completion of any other”), so the musl FAIL is a true positive (musl bug). The finding holds for a conforming sync-detecting libc. Corrected action: accept -1/EIO only if the other 9 requests were still queued and complete; check aio_return()==BUF_SIZE for them (the :175 check uses ‘&&’, so a never-queued zeroed aiocb with err 0 passes; use ‘||’); and verify aio_error(aiocbs[2])==EBADF.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/lio_listio/9-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/lio_listio/9-1)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: low
  • Claim under test: LIO_WRITE submits the entry as if by aio_write().
  • Problem: after the asynchronous write at aio_offset 0, the test reads the data back with plain read() at the current file offset. POSIX says that offset is unspecified once an aio operation has been enqueued. glibc uses pwrite and leaves the offset at 0, so Linux passes. An implementation that advances the offset makes read() return 0, and the test reports UNRESOLVED.
  • Evidence: lio_listio/9-1.c:101; POSIX aio_write(): “After a successful call to enqueue an asynchronous I/O operation, the value of the file offset for the file is unspecified.”
  • Suggested action: use pread(fd, check, BUF_SIZE, 0) or lseek(fd, 0, SEEK_SET) first.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION. HPE as-is PASS (glibc uses pwrite, offset stays 0). Mutation simulating an impl that advances the offset (lseek(fd, BUF_SIZE) after lio_listio) -> rc=2 ‘Error at read(): No such file or directory’ (UNRESOLVED, stale errno). Mechanism holds; no false result on glibc
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): UNCHANGED via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: Test PASSED; musl: Test PASSED. Both use pwrite for a non-O_APPEND regular file, so the offset stays 0: musl aio.c:262 (append ? write : pwrite), glibc rt/aio_misc.c:563-569. The file offset is unspecified only per POSIX; no Linux libc moves it

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_attr_destroy/1-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_attr_destroy/1-1)

  • Category: UNDEF (secondary: WEAK)
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: after pthread_attr_destroy, pthread_create with that attr returns EINVAL.
  • Problem: POSIX makes any use of a destroyed attributes object undefined behaviour, and the header comment quoted in 2-1.c says the same. The test accepts EINVAL or 0 as PASS (glibc returns 0) and fails on any other error code, even though UB permits any outcome (another errno, a crash). The assertion has no defined expected result, so the test checks nothing portable.
  • Evidence: 1-1.c: ret = pthread_create(&new_th, &new_attr, ...) after destroy; POSIX pthread_attr_destroy: “the results of otherwise referencing the object after it has been destroyed are undefined.”
  • Suggested action: Drop the test, or reduce it to “pthread_attr_destroy returns 0” (already covered by 3-1).
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,READ,GIT. HPE: PASS ‘Though returned 0 when creating a thread with a destroyed attribute…’ (glibc returns 0). Code FAILs on any errno other than EINVAL/EPERM/EAGAIN/0. POSIX pthread_attr_destroy (2024 text, fetched): ‘results of otherwise referencing the object after it has been destroyed are undefined’; Issue 7 removed EINVAL.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS ‘returned 0 … destroyed attribute’; musl: same PASS. musl pthread_attr_destroy.c:3-6 is a no-op; glibc nptl/pthread_attr_destroy.c frees iattr->extension (cpuset) so reuse of a destroyed attr with affinity would read freed memory. No libc returns the EINVAL the header asserts; UB as stated.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_attr_setdetachstate/2-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_attr_setdetachstate/2-1)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: pthread_join() and pthread_detach() on a thread created detached return an error (EINVAL is required).
  • Problem: Since POSIX.1-2008, passing a non-joinable thread to pthread_join/pthread_detach is undefined behaviour, and the EINVAL error was removed. The thread may also already have exited (it only calls pthread_exit), which ends the lifetime of its ID, a second source of UB. glibc happens to return EINVAL while the descriptor is still cached, but a crash or ESRCH would be equally conformant.
  • Evidence: 2-1.c: ret_val = pthread_join(new_th, NULL); if (ret_val != EINVAL) FAIL; and the same for pthread_detach. POSIX pthread_join: “The behavior is undefined if the value specified by the thread argument to pthread_join() does not refer to a joinable thread.” Change history: “The [EINVAL] error for a non-joinable thread is removed; this condition results in undefined behavior.”
  • Suggested action: Drop it, or replace it with a check that the detached thread’s resources are released (e.g. create many detached threads and check that none fail with EAGAIN).
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS (EINVAL: nptl/pthread_join_common.c:57-58, pthread_detach.c:42-43); musl: rc=139 SIGSEGV. musl pthread_join.c:17 a_crash() (hlt, arch/x86_64/atomic_arch.h:106-108) on a DT_DETACHED thread; if the thread already exited its map is gone. Conforming libc crashes on this UB.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_barrier_wait/3-2.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_barrier_wait/3-2)

  • Category: UNDEF (secondary: FRAGILE)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: a thread interrupted by a signal while blocked on a barrier continues normally from the completed wait after its handler returns.
  • Problem: the child’s SIGUSR1 handler loops until barrier_waited == 1. Main sets that flag only after its own pthread_barrier_wait() returns. POSIX explicitly leaves unspecified whether other threads may proceed past the barrier while a participant is still inside a signal handler. An implementation that holds main until the handler returns therefore deadlocks, and the test hangs and times out, although it is conforming. glibc lets the last arriver return, so it passes there. Synchronization is sleep() polling on plain ints written from a signal handler and another thread (sig_rcvd, barrier_waited are not volatile/sig_atomic_t).
  • Evidence: 3-2.c:41-52,126-141; the test’s own header (3-2.c:10-12) and POSIX pthread_barrier_wait.html: “Until the thread in the signal handler returns from it, it is unspecified whether other threads may proceed past the barrier once they have all reached it.”
  • Suggested action: keep the handler short (set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag and return), and have main call barrier_wait only after the handler has returned. Alternatively, add an alarm/timeout that reports UNSUPPORTED rather than hanging when main blocks.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): UNCHANGED via MUSL,RUN,REPEAT,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS 3/3 (main gets SERIAL); musl: PASS 3/3 (thread gets SERIAL). musl pthread_barrier_wait.c:93-110: last arriver returns without waiting for the instance owner, so musl, like glibc, does not hold main while the handler runs; the deadlocking implementation stays hypothetical. Finding rests on POSIX text; unchanged.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_cancel/5-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_cancel/5-1)

  • Category: UNDEF (secondary: DOCS)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: pthread_cancel() “may” return ESRCH for a nonexistent thread.
  • Problem: the test calls pthread_cancel() on a thread ID after pthread_join() has ended that thread’s lifetime. Since Issue 7 (Austin Group interpretation #142), POSIX has no ESRCH for pthread_cancel(), and using a thread ID after its lifetime is undefined behaviour. With glibc the descriptor may already be freed or reused, so the call can touch freed memory, or cancel an unrelated, newly created thread that reuses the ID. The test accepts 0 and ESRCH, so in practice it only “fails” on another errno or a crash, and it exercises UB. The header still documents the removed ESRCH error.
  • Evidence: 5-1.c:9-18,44-63; POSIX pthread_cancel.html ERRORS: only “shall not return an error code of [EINTR]”; CHANGE HISTORY Issue 7: “Austin Group Interpretation 1003.1-2001 #142 is applied, removing the [ESRCH] error condition”; RATIONALE: “If an implementation detects use of a thread ID after the end of its lifetime, it is recommended that the function should fail and report an [ESRCH] error.”
  • Suggested action: drop the test.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS ‘Returned 0’ (nptl/pthread_cancel.c:62-68 returns 0 when joinstate==EXITED, TCB in stack cache); musl: rc=139 SIGSEGV: pthread_join.c:24 munmaps the thread map, then pthread_cancel.c:99 a_store(&t->cancel,1) writes to it. The predicted use-after-lifetime UAF happens on musl.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_cond_init/4-3.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_cond_init/4-3)

  • Category: UNDEF (secondary: DOCS)
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: re-initializing an initialized condvar returns EBUSY (or 0).
  • Problem: since Issue 7, POSIX has no EBUSY for pthread_cond_init(). Re-initializing an initialized condvar is undefined behaviour. The test demands 0 or EBUSY and FAILs on any other result, although any outcome is conforming. The header still describes EBUSY as the asserted behaviour.
  • Evidence: 4-3.c:22-24,50-54; POSIX pthread_cond_destroy.html: “Attempting to initialize an already initialized condition variable results in undefined behavior.” CHANGE HISTORY Issue 7: “The [EBUSY] error for a condition variable already in use or an already initialized condition variable is removed”.
  • Suggested action: drop the test, or report non-EBUSY results as UNSUPPORTED (as pthread_cond_destroy/speculative/4-1 does) instead of FAIL.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,READ. HPE: PASS (glibc returns 0 on re-init, so it cannot fail here). Code: second init must be 0 or EBUSY else PTS_FAIL. POSIX pthread_cond_destroy page (fetched): ‘Attempting to initialize an already initialized condition variable results in undefined behavior’; Issue 7 removed EBUSY. Header still asserts EBUSY.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS; musl: PASS. Both re-init by zeroing (musl pthread_cond_init.c:5, glibc nptl/pthread_cond_init.c:32,49) and return 0; neither implements EBUSY, so the header’s assertion is exercised by no tested libc and re-init of an in-use cond would strand waiters (UB).

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_cond_timedwait/1-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_cond_timedwait/1-1)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: pthread_cond_timedwait() blocks on the condition variable.
  • Problem: the waiter calls timedwait once, without a predicate loop. If it returns 0 before main sets signaled = 1, the test prints “did not block on the cond at all” and returns PTS_FAIL. POSIX explicitly permits spurious wakeups, so a conforming implementation can fail this test. The sibling 2-1.c has the same code but returns PTS_UNRESOLVED for this case. On glibc with a single waiter this is rare in practice.
  • Evidence: 1-1.c:56-74 (vs 2-1.c:197-200); POSIX pthread_cond_timedwait.html: “Spurious wakeups from the pthread_cond_clockwait(), pthread_cond_timedwait(), or pthread_cond_wait() functions may occur.”
  • Suggested action: loop on the predicate (re-wait while signaled == 0 and rc == 0), or report UNRESOLVED like 2-1.c.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT. As-is PASS (HPE 1, VIRT 3 + 3 under stress). Mutation simulating a spurious wakeup (extra pthread_cond_signal before main sets signaled=1) -> ‘Thread1 did not block on the cond at all / Test FAILED’ rc=1. POSIX (fetched): ‘Spurious wakeups … may occur’. Real glibc spurious wakeups are rare.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): UNCHANGED via MUSL,RUN,REPEAT,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS 3/3; musl: PASS 3/3. musl pthread_cond_timedwait.c:100-102 re-waits while *fut==seq, so private condvars do not wake spuriously; :104-108 shows musl does return ‘legitimate’ spurious wakes for pshared condvars. Not observable here; phase-2 mutation stands.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_cond_timedwait/2-2.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_cond_timedwait/2-2)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: timedwait returns ETIMEDOUT when abstime passes before the cond is signalled.
  • Problem: a single pthread_cond_timedwait() call must return ETIMEDOUT, and any other result, including 0, is PTS_FAIL. The cond is never signalled, so 0 can only be a spurious wakeup, which POSIX permits. Correct usage is to re-wait with the same abstime until ETIMEDOUT. Rare on glibc, but the test FAILs a conforming outcome.
  • Evidence: 2-2.c:65-74; POSIX pthread_cond_timedwait.html: “Spurious wakeups … may occur.”
  • Suggested action: do rc = pthread_cond_timedwait(...); while (rc == 0); and then require ETIMEDOUT.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT. As-is PASS (HPE 1, VIRT 3 + 3 under stress). Mutation: one pthread_cond_signal while the thread waits (stand-in for a spurious wakeup) -> ‘Test FAILED: pthread_cond_timedwait return 0 instead of ETIMEDOUT’ rc=1. A single wait without re-wait loop FAILs a POSIX-permitted spurious return.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): UNCHANGED via MUSL,RUN,REPEAT,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS 3/3; musl: PASS 3/3 ‘stops waiting when time is out’. musl pthread_cond_timedwait.c:100-102 returns ETIMEDOUT unless the futex word changed; spurious 0 needs a racing wake. Same as 1-1: both libcs suppress spurious wakeups; finding rests on POSIX text + phase-2 mutation.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_cond_wait/1-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_cond_wait/1-1)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: pthread_cond_wait() blocks until the condition is signaled.
  • Problem: If pthread_cond_wait() returns 0 before main sets signaled = 1, the test reports PTS_FAIL (“did not block on the cond at all”). POSIX explicitly permits spurious wakeups, so that outcome is conforming. Sibling tests 2-1/3-1 handle the same case as UNRESOLVED. In practice glibc rarely wakes spuriously, so the impact is low.
  • Evidence: 1-1.c t1_func if (signaled == 0) { ... exit(PTS_FAIL); }; POSIX.1-2024 pthread_cond_wait: “Spurious wakeups from the pthread_cond_clockwait(), pthread_cond_timedwait(), or pthread_cond_wait() functions may occur.”
  • Suggested action: loop on the signaled predicate (re-wait on a spurious wakeup), or report UNRESOLVED as 2-1 does.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT. As-is PASS (HPE 1, VIRT 3 + 3 under stress). Mutation simulating a spurious wakeup (pthread_cond_signal before signaled=1) -> ‘Thread1 did not block on the cond at all / Test FAILED’ rc=1; POSIX allows spurious wakeups (text verified). Same as pthread_cond_timedwait/1-1.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): UNCHANGED via MUSL,RUN,REPEAT,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS 3/3; musl: PASS 3/3. Same mechanism as pthread_cond_timedwait/1-1 (musl pthread_cond_timedwait.c:100-102 loops on private condvars); no spurious wakeup observable on either libc.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_detach/1-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_detach/1-1)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: after pthread_detach(), the thread is no longer joinable.
  • Problem: Joins a detached thread and returns PASS only if pthread_join() returns EINVAL (0 is FAIL, anything else UNRESOLVED). POSIX.1-2024 makes this undefined behavior and lists no EINVAL error for pthread_join; EINVAL is only a RATIONALE recommendation. glibc happens to return EINVAL (IS_DETACHED check), so this passes on glibc but encodes UB.
  • Evidence: 1-1.c ret = pthread_join(new_th, NULL); ... else if (ret == EINVAL) PASS; POSIX pthread_join: “The behavior is undefined if the value specified by the thread argument to pthread_join() does not refer to a joinable thread.” ERRORS: only “may fail [EDEADLK]”.
  • Suggested action: accept any non-zero result, or drop. Detaching a joinable thread is better checked by showing that it still runs (2-2).
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS (EINVAL, nptl/pthread_join_common.c:57-58); musl: rc=139 SIGSEGV: join of a detached thread hits pthread_join.c:17 a_crash() (deliberate trap) or the self-unmapped TCB. Test encodes glibc’s EINVAL for UB.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_detach/4-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_detach/4-1)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: pthread_detach() returns EINVAL for a non-joinable thread.
  • Problem: Creates a thread with PTHREAD_CREATE_DETACHED and requires pthread_detach() to return EINVAL (ESRCH gives UNRESOLVED, anything else FAIL). POSIX.1-2024 removed EINVAL/ESRCH from pthread_detach ERRORS and makes this UB. glibc returns EINVAL, so this passes on glibc.
  • Evidence: 4-1.c if (ret != EINVAL) { ... FAIL }; POSIX pthread_detach: “The behavior is undefined if the value specified by the thread argument to pthread_detach() does not refer to a joinable thread.” ERRORS: only “shall not return an error code of [EINTR]”. RATIONALE: “it is recommended that the function should fail and report an [EINVAL] error”.
  • Suggested action: drop, or downgrade a non-EINVAL result to UNTESTED (as 4-2 does for 0).
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS (EINVAL, nptl/pthread_detach.c:42-43); musl: rc=139 SIGSEGV: pthread_detach.c:8-11 falls back to __pthread_join on a non-joinable thread -> pthread_join.c:17 a_crash(). Conforming UB outcome; test FAILs (crash) on musl.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_detach/4-2.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_detach/4-2)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: pthread_detach() returns ESRCH for a non-existent thread.
  • Problem: Joins the thread, then calls pthread_detach() on the same ID. After a join the thread ID’s lifetime has ended (XBD 2.9.2), so any use is UB. On glibc the TCB has been handed to the stack cache (tid = -1), so ESRCH comes out by luck of the cache; if the stack were unmapped this would be a use-after-free. The test tolerates 0 (UNTESTED) but FAILs on any other code, e.g. EINVAL.
  • Evidence: 4-2.c pthread_join(new_th, NULL); ret = pthread_detach(new_th); if (ret != ESRCH) FAIL; POSIX pthread_detach RATIONALE: “If an implementation detects use of a thread ID after the end of its lifetime, it is recommended that the function should fail and report an [ESRCH] error.”
  • Suggested action: drop.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): REVISED via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: rc=5 UNTESTED ‘does not return ESRCH’ (returns 0: joinstate EXITED -> pthread_detach.c:37-46 -> clockjoin returns 0; nptl_free_tcb.c:27-28 guards the double free); musl: rc=139 SIGSEGV (pthread_join.c:24 unmapped the TCB, pthread_detach.c:8 a_cas on it). Phase-1 ‘glibc gives ESRCH by luck of cache’ is wrong; never PASSes on either.
  • Verification conclusion: The UB claim holds, but the glibc detail in the finding is wrong. glibc 2.43 does not return ESRCH “by luck of the cache”. It returns 0: joinstate is still EXITED, so pthread_detach.c:37-46 calls __pthread_clockjoin_ex, which returns 0, and nptl_free_tcb.c:27-28 (TERMINATED_BITMASK) prevents a second free. The test therefore reports UNTESTED on glibc. On musl, the first join has unmapped the TCB (pthread_join.c:24) and pthread_detach.c:8 does a CAS on it, which crashes (SIGSEGV). Corrected finding: the test uses a thread ID after its lifetime has ended; it gives UNTESTED on glibc and crashes on musl, and can never PASS. Action: drop.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_join/6-2.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_join/6-2)

  • Category: UNDEF (secondary: DOCS)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: “pthread_join() SHALL fail … [ESRCH]” when it joins a thread that was already joined.
  • Problem: In POSIX.1-2024, joining a thread that is no longer joinable, or whose ID lifetime has ended, is undefined behavior. The ESRCH error was removed (Interp. 1003.1-2001 #142). ESRCH and EINVAL survive only as RATIONALE recommendations. After commits 266dabb9df22 and faa34ecaddf5 the test returns UNTESTED on 0 (glibc 2.43 behavior), but it still returns FAIL for any other value, including EINVAL, which POSIX recommends for a non-joinable thread. The header text still cites ESRCH as “SHALL fail”.
  • Evidence: 6-2.c:10-12,66-75; https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/pthread_join.html: “The behavior is undefined if the value specified by the thread argument to pthread_join() does not refer to a joinable thread.” CHANGE HISTORY: “Austin Group Interpretation 1003.1-2001 #142 is applied, removing the [ESRCH] error condition.”
  • Suggested action: Drop the test, or report UNTESTED for every outcome other than ESRCH. Fix the header to describe ESRCH as a recommendation for UB.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: rc=5 UNTESTED (second join returns 0: joinstate stays EXITED, nptl_free_tcb.c:27-28 guards free); musl: rc=139 SIGSEGV: first join munmapped the TCB (pthread_join.c:24), second join reads t->detach_state (:16). Joining an ended thread ID is UB with a crash on musl.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_join/speculative/6-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_join/speculative/6-1)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: pthread_join() on a detached thread returns EINVAL.
  • Problem: The test returns FAIL unless EINVAL comes back. POSIX.1-2024 makes joining a non-joinable thread undefined behavior; EINVAL is only “recommended”, and the [EINVAL] error was removed in Issue 7. The detached thread may also have exited already, so its ID lifetime has ended (also UB). An implementation that returns 0, ESRCH or crashes still conforms.
  • Evidence: speculative/6-1.c:50-63; pthread_join.html CHANGE HISTORY: “The [EINVAL] error for a non-joinable thread is removed; this condition results in undefined behavior.”
  • Suggested action: Drop it, or turn any non-EINVAL result into UNTESTED.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_key_create/speculative/5-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_key_create/speculative/5-1)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: creating more than PTHREAD_KEYS_MAX keys returns EAGAIN.
  • Problem: The test returns FAIL (“EAGAIN returned before the key limit was exceeded”) if EAGAIN comes before the test itself has created PTHREAD_KEYS_MAX keys. POSIX also allows EAGAIN when “the system lacked the necessary resources”, and keys used internally by libc or other libraries in the process count toward the per-process limit. An early EAGAIN therefore conforms.
  • Evidence: speculative/5-1.c:47-67; pthread_key_create(3p) ERRORS: “[EAGAIN] The system lacked the necessary resources to create another thread-specific data key, or the system-imposed limit on the total number of keys per process {PTHREAD_KEYS_MAX} has been exceeded.”
  • Suggested action: Accept EAGAIN at any i >= 1 (it is the documented outcome). Fail only when more than PTHREAD_KEYS_MAX keys succeed, or when a different error comes back.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION. HPE: PASS as-is. LD_PRELOAD of a 3-line .so whose constructor calls pthread_key_create once (like any library using TSD) -> ‘EAGAIN returned before the key limit was exceeded’ rc=1 (FAIL). POSIX (fetched): EAGAIN when ‘the total number of keys per process’ exceeds PTHREAD_KEYS_MAX, so it is conforming.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS; musl: PASS. musl PTHREAD_KEYS_MAX=128 (limits.h:66), one process-wide table (pthread_key_create.c:7) also used by C11 tss_create (tss_create.c:9); glibc 1024 (local_lim.h:64). Neither libc uses keys internally, so PASS; any library key -> early EAGAIN -> FAIL (phase-2 LD_PRELOAD mutation).

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_mutex_init/1-2.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_mutex_init/1-2)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: low)
  • Claim under test: a mutex initialized with NULL attr behaves the same as one initialized with a default attr object.
  • Problem: The behaviors compared are unlocking an unlocked mutex, unlocking a mutex owned by another thread, and relocking an owned mutex. All three are undefined for PTHREAD_MUTEX_DEFAULT unless DEFAULT maps to one of the other types. The relock subcase also uses PTHREAD_CANCEL_ASYNCHRONOUS around pthread_mutex_lock(), which is not async-cancel-safe. glibc behaves the same for both mutexes, so there is no false FAIL in practice, but the test relies on UB, and on glibc the first step leaves __nusers wrapped.
  • Evidence: 1-2.c:216-217,249,124; pthread_mutex_lock.html: for DEFAULT, “the behavior is undefined for the cases marked” (relock, unlock when not owner).
  • Suggested action: Compare observable defined properties (gettype/getprotocol/getpshared through the attr, trylock EBUSY by another thread), or document that the test relies on DEFAULT mapping to a defined type.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,READ. HPE: rc=0, ‘Results for deadlock issue: mutex 1/2 deadlock did not return 0’. Compares unlock-unlocked, unlock-by-non-owner and relock on two DEFAULT mutexes; POSIX pthread_mutex_lock table (fetched) marks these ‘undefined behavior’ for DEFAULT unless it maps to NORMAL/ERRORCHECK/RECURSIVE. glibc equal for both -> no false FAIL.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS (‘deadlock did not return 0’); musl: HANG, killed at 120 s rc=124; child in futex_do_wait (relock), main in join. musl __timedwait.c:63-70 disables cancel around the futex wait (from pthread_mutex_timedlock.c:85), so async SIGCANCEL is ignored (pthread_cancel.c:55). mutex_lock is not async-cancel-safe: musl conforms.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_mutex_init/3-2.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_mutex_init/3-2)

  • Problem: Same design as 1-2.c (UB operations on DEFAULT mutexes, async cancellation inside mutex_lock).
