  • Suggested action: As for 1-2.c.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,READ. HPE: rc=0 (same ‘deadlock did not return 0’ output as 1-2). diff vs 1-2.c from deadlk_issue on: only mtx_def(init with default attr) replaced by mtx_macro=PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER; same UB operations on DEFAULT mutexes and async cancel. See pthread_mutex_init/1-2.c.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via MUSL,BULK,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS; musl: HUNG. Rerun: glibc rc=0 in 0.16 s; musl hangs (killed at 60 s). deadlk_issue relocks a DEFAULT mutex with async cancel enabled (3-2.c:116,130; UB). musl __timedwait.c:67-69 disables cancellation around the futex wait, so the async cancel (pthread_cancel.c:55) is never acted on -> pthread_join at :307 blocks forever

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_mutex_timedlock/5-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_mutex_timedlock/5-1)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: EINVAL when the call would block and abs_timeout.tv_nsec < 0.
  • Problem: “Would have blocked” is set up by having the thread relock a DEFAULT-type mutex that it already owns (f1 locks &mutex and then timedlocks it). POSIX makes relocking a DEFAULT mutex undefined unless the type behaves like NORMAL/ERRORCHECK/RECURSIVE. pthread_mutex_timedlock also “may fail [EDEADLK] A deadlock condition was detected”, so a conforming implementation can return EDEADLK (or 0 for recursive-like behavior), and the test then returns FAIL. It passes on glibc only because glibc validates tv_nsec before the deadlock.
  • Evidence: 5-1.c:86-98; pthread_mutex_timedlock.html: “may fail if: [EDEADLK] A deadlock condition was detected.”; pthread_mutex_lock.html table: relock of DEFAULT is undefined (marked with a dagger).
  • Suggested action: Have main (or another thread) hold the mutex, as 5-3.c does, and call timedlock from a non-owner thread.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,READ. HPE: PASS as-is (glibc NORMAL checks tv_nsec first). Mutated only the mutex init to PTHREAD_ERRORCHECK_MUTEX_INITIALIZER_NP (a mapping POSIX allows for DEFAULT, per the mutex_lock table dagger) -> ‘Test FAILED: Expected return code EINVAL, got: 35’ (EDEADLK). EDEADLK is a POSIX may-fail for timedlock.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS; musl: PASS. Both default to NORMAL and both check EDEADLK for ERRORCHECK before tv_nsec: musl pthread_mutex_timedlock.c:78-80 vs __timedwait.c:41; glibc nptl/pthread_mutex_timedlock.c:78 vs :208-209. PASS depends on DEFAULT==NORMAL in both libcs; EDEADLK mapping (phase-2 mutation) FAILs.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_mutex_timedlock/5-2.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_mutex_timedlock/5-2)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: EINVAL when the call would block and tv_nsec >= 1000 million.
  • Problem: Same design as 5-1.c: the owner relocks its own DEFAULT mutex, which is UB, and an EDEADLK result is permitted.

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: pthread_mutexattr_gettype() shall fail with EINVAL for an invalid attr.
  • Problem: The attr is memset to 0 and never initialized.   • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,READ. HPE: rc=5 ‘UNTESTED: The call didn’t fail.’ (glibc returns 0 on a zeroed attr). Any result other than 0/EINVAL is FAIL. POSIX gettype page (fetched): uninitialized attr is UB; Issue 7: ‘The [EINVAL] error for an uninitialized mutex attributes object is removed’.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc and musl (pthread_mutexattr_gettype_speculative_3-1.run-test): rc=5 ‘UNTESTED: The call didn’t fail.’ Both return 0 unconditionally: musl src/thread/pthread_attr_get.c:88-92, glibc nptl/pthread_mutexattr_gettype.c:28-30 -> EINVAL path unreachable, UNTESTED on every Linux libc

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_once/3-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_once/3-1)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: if init_routine is cancelled at a cancellation point, once_control behaves as if pthread_once() was never called.
  • Problem: The thread sets PTHREAD_CANCEL_ASYNCHRONOUS and then calls pthread_once(), sleep() and perror(), none of which are async-cancel-safe; POSIX makes that undefined (only pthread_cancel/setcancelstate/setcanceltype are async-cancel-safe). The assertion is about init_routine being a cancellation point, which deferred cancellation of sleep() already exercises. Additionally init_flag is a plain int polled across threads (data race), and init functions of type void *(*)() are cast to void (*)(void) and called through it (UB in C).
  • Evidence: 3-1.c:35, 55-57, 81-82, 104; POSIX XSH 2.9.5.4 “Async-Cancel Safety”: only pthread_cancel(), pthread_setcancelstate(), pthread_setcanceltype() are async-cancel-safe; pthread_once DESCRIPTION: “if init_routine is a cancellation point and is canceled, the effect on once_control shall be as if pthread_once() was never called.”
  • Suggested action: drop the setcanceltype(ASYNCHRONOUS) call (use default deferred cancel), fix the init function prototypes to void f(void), use a semaphore/volatile flag for the handshake.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT. HPE 1x + 3x stress, VIRT 5x: all Test PASSED (glibc copes with async cancel inside sleep()). Mutant without pthread_setcanceltype(ASYNCHRONOUS) (deferred cancel, sleep() is a cancellation point): Test PASSED -> async type is unnecessary. UB only by POSIX text (man pthread_setcancelstate(3): only cancel/setcancelstate/setcanceltype are async-cancel-safe); cannot be shown by running
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): UNCHANGED via MUSL,RUN,REPEAT,SRC. HPE glibc PASS; musl PASS 6/6 (1 + ltprepeat 5). Async cancel inside sleep() works on both: musl src/thread/pthread_cancel.c:59-62 (cancel_handler calls __cancel when cancelasync), glibc nptl/pthread_cancel.c:50-54; musl undo() (pthread_once.c:3-9) resets control. UB remains by POSIX text only

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_once/6-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_once/6-1)

Mutant whose worker leaves its loop after 1000 iterations while senders still run: rc=124 timeout 2/2 on HPE and VIRT -> sender-in-sem_wait hang is real, narrow window

  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,READ. HPE: ’Test PASSED: Note*: pthread_rwlock_init() returned 0 instead of EBUSY’ rc=0. POSIX 2024 re-checked: ‘Results are undefined if pthread_rwlock_init() is called specifying an already initialized read-write lock’; Issue 7 removed EBUSY for ‘an already initialized read-write lock object’. Drop

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_rwlock_timedrdlock/6-2.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_rwlock_timedrdlock/6-2)

  • Category: UNDEF (secondary: FRAGILE)
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: after a signal handler returns, a thread blocked in timedrdlock resumes waiting “as if it was not interrupted”, and gets the lock without ETIMEDOUT.
  • Problem: Timeline: deadline = t0+2s; signal at ~t0+1; the handler sleeps 4s (until ~t0+5); main unlocks at ~t0+3, i.e. after the deadline. Had the thread not been interrupted, it would have timed out at t0+2, so “as if it was not interrupted” supports ETIMEDOUT. The test nevertheless FAILs on ETIMEDOUT and requires rc==0. POSIX does not order these: the “shall not fail with a timeout if the lock can be acquired immediately” sentence is about the call itself, not about resuming. glibc happens to re-check the lock first. Also, the main thread’s “wait for handler to be sleeping” handshake is dead code: th_fn() sets handler_state = 2 before blocking, so while (handler_state != 2 ...) exits after the first sleep(2) and the handler_state == 1 check can never trigger. Synchronization is purely sleep-based.
  • Evidence: 6-2.c:47 (TIMEOUT 2), 62-72 (handler sleeps 4s), 86 (handler_state = 2), 166-177, 184-206; https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/pthread_rwlock_timedrdlock.html: “upon return from the signal handler the thread shall resume waiting for the lock as if it was not interrupted.”
  • Suggested action: accept both 0 and ETIMEDOUT (just check the call returns and does not report EINTR), or unlock before the deadline; initialise handler_state to 1 so the handshake works.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT. HPE: PASS in 5.05 s (‘main: unlock write lock’ at ~t0+3 after the t0+2 deadline, lock taken at ~t0+5); HPE 2x+3x stress, VIRT 2x stress all PASS (glibc rechecks the lock first). Mutant without pthread_kill(): ‘Error: thread timeout in sig_handler’ rc=2, never ‘signal handler did not get called’ -> handler_state handshake is dead (th_fn presets 2)
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): UNCHANGED via MUSL,RUN,REPEAT,SRC. HPE glibc PASS; musl PASS 6/6, ~5 s. musl src/thread/pthread_rwlock_timedrdlock.c:13-21 treats EINTR as ‘retry’ and calls tryrdlock before re-waiting (lock free since t0+3); __timedwait_cp (__timedwait.c:41-48) would report ETIMEDOUT only on the next wait. Same order as glibc; ETIMEDOUT stays a conforming outcome by POSIX text

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_rwlock_timedwrlock/6-2.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_rwlock_timedwrlock/6-2)

  • Category: UNDEF (secondary: FRAGILE)
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: after a signal handler returns, timedwrlock resumes waiting and acquires the lock released during the handler.
  • Problem: Identical to pthread_rwlock_timedrdlock/6-2.c. The lock is released at ~t0+3s, after the t0+2s deadline, while the thread is still in a 4s handler. “As if it was not interrupted” would then give ETIMEDOUT, but the test FAILs on ETIMEDOUT. The handler_state handshake is dead: th_fn() pre-sets handler_state = 2.
  • Evidence: 6-2.c (TIMEOUT 2, handler sleep(TIMEOUT*2), th_fn handler_state = 2;, main if (expired == 1) FAIL); POSIX pthread_rwlock_timedwrlock: “upon return from the signal handler the thread shall resume waiting for the lock as if it was not interrupted.”
  • Suggested action: accept 0 or ETIMEDOUT, or release the lock before the deadline; fix handler_state init.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT. HPE: PASS in 5.27 s (unlock after the 2 s deadline, lock taken after the 4 s handler); HPE 2x+3x stress, VIRT 2x stress all PASS. Mutant without pthread_kill(): ‘thread: timer expired’ + ‘Error: thread timeout in sig_handler’ rc=2, the ‘signal handler did not get called’ check never fires -> same dead handshake as timedrdlock/6-2

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_rwlock_trywrlock/speculative/3-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_rwlock_trywrlock/speculative/3-1)

  • Category: UNDEF (secondary: WRONG)
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: trywrlock may fail with EINVAL on an uninitialized rwlock.
  • Problem: Using an uninitialized rwlock has been undefined since POSIX.1-2008 (the EINVAL error was removed). The logic is also self-defeating: it calls pthread_rwlock_unlock() and pthread_rwlock_destroy() on the same object before checking rc, so an implementation that does detect the uninitialized lock (returns EINVAL) would also fail the unlock and exit UNRESOLVED. The PASS-on-EINVAL branch is effectively unreachable. On glibc a zeroed static rwlock equals PTHREAD_RWLOCK_INITIALIZER, so rc is 0 and the test just passes.
  • Evidence: speculative/3-1.c:26-55; https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/pthread_rwlock_trywrlock.html (CHANGE HISTORY Issue 7: EINVAL for uninitialized rwlock removed, behaviour undefined).
  • Suggested action: drop.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,READ. HPE: ’Test PASSED: Note*: Returned 0 instead of EINVAL’ rc=0 (zeroed static rwlock == initializer on glibc). POSIX 2024: ‘Results are undefined if any of these functions are called with an uninitialized read-write lock’; Issue 7: ‘[EINVAL] error for an uninitialized read-write lock object is removed’. unlock/destroy run before rc is examined (3-1.c:33-41). Drop
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc and musl (pthread_rwlock_trywrlock_speculative_3-1.run-test): rc=0 ‘Returned 0 instead of EINVAL’. musl src/thread/pthread_rwlock_trywrlock.c:5 just CASes 0->0x7fffffff (zeroed static == initializer); no validity check in either libc -> EINVAL branch unreachable

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_rwlock_wrlock/3-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_rwlock_wrlock/3-1)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: wrlock may fail with EDEADLK when the caller already holds the write lock.
  • Problem: POSIX.1-2024 says that in this case “the call shall either deadlock or return [EDEADLK]”. Deadlock is therefore a conforming outcome, and the test hangs until the harness timeout and is counted as a failure. musl does not track rwlock owners and deadlocks here. Conversely the test accepts rc==0 (double write-acquire), which POSIX does not allow. glibc returns EDEADLK, so it passes there.
  • Evidence: 3-1.c:46-79; https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/pthread_rwlock_trywrlock.html (pthread_rwlock_wrlock): “…the calling thread already owns the read-write lock for writing or reading, the call shall either deadlock or return [EDEADLK].”
  • Suggested action: use alarm()/timed variant to treat a deadlock as PASS/UNTESTED, and stop accepting 0.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,READ. HPE: ‘main: correctly got EDEADLK / Test PASSED’. VIRT mutant where the 2nd wrlock ‘succeeds’ (rc = 0, double write acquire): ’Test PASSED: Note*: Returned 0 instead of EDEADLK’ rc=0 -> a non-conforming result passes. POSIX 2024 re-checked: ‘…already owns the read-write lock for writing or reading, the call shall either deadlock or return [EDEADLK]’ -> deadlock (musl) would time out
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: ‘main: correctly got EDEADLK / Test PASSED’ (nptl/pthread_rwlock_common.c:596-599 checks __cur_writer). musl: hangs after ‘main: attempt write lock’, killed rc=124 at LTPRUN_TIMEOUT=40: no owner tracking (src/thread/pthread_rwlock_timedwrlock.c:13-21 just waits) -> conforming deadlock reported as hang/failure

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_setcancelstate/1-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_setcancelstate/1-1)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: with PTHREAD_CANCEL_ENABLE the thread honours a cancel request (and setcancelstate returns the old state).
  • Problem: The thread switches to PTHREAD_CANCEL_ASYNCHRONOUS and then calls sleep() in a loop and pthread_testcancel(). Neither is async-cancel-safe, so per POSIX the behaviour is undefined (glibc happens to cope). Deferred cancellation would test ENABLE equally well, since sleep() is a cancellation point. The header claims the old state is returned, but oldstate is passed as NULL, which POSIX does not specify (Linux allows it). The handshake uses a plain int sem1 polled across threads.
  • Evidence: 1-1.c:42-58; man pthread_setcancelstate(3) NOTES: “POSIX.1-2001 and POSIX.1-2008 require only that pthread_cancel(3), pthread_setcancelstate(), and pthread_setcanceltype() be async-cancel-safe. In general, other library functions can’t be safely called from an asynchronously cancelable thread.” and “POSIX.1 does not specify this point [NULL oldstate]”.
  • Suggested action: drop the setcanceltype(ASYNCHRONOUS) call; pass a real oldstate and check it.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT. HPE 1x + 3x stress, VIRT 5x: all PASS. Mutant without pthread_setcanceltype(ASYNCHRONOUS): Test PASSED rc=0 (deferred cancel in sleep() is enough to test ENABLE). man pthread_setcancelstate(3) NOTES confirm only cancel/setcancelstate/setcanceltype are async-cancel-safe and NULL oldstate is a Linux extension
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): UNCHANGED via MUSL,RUN,REPEAT,SRC. HPE glibc PASS; musl PASS 6/6. Async cancel during sleep() works on both: musl src/thread/pthread_cancel.c:59-62 calls __cancel from cancel_handler when cancelasync, glibc nptl/pthread_cancel.c:50-54. UB by POSIX text only; contrast pthread_setcanceltype/1-1 where musl differs

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_setcancelstate/2-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_setcancelstate/2-1)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: a new thread’s default cancel state is ENABLE.
  • Problem: Same pattern as 1-1.c: sets ASYNCHRONOUS type and then calls sleep() (not async-cancel-safe), which is undefined behaviour. With deferred type the check would be equivalent and well-defined.
  • Evidence: 2-1.c:38-53; man pthread_setcancelstate(3) NOTES (async-cancel-safe list).
  • Suggested action: remove the setcanceltype(ASYNCHRONOUS) call.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT. HPE 1x + 3x stress, VIRT 5x: all PASS. Mutant without the ASYNCHRONOUS setcanceltype: Test PASSED rc=0 -> the default-ENABLE check works with deferred cancel and no UB; reasoning from man pthread_setcancelstate(3) NOTES holds

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_setcanceltype/1-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_setcanceltype/1-1)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: with PTHREAD_CANCEL_ASYNCHRONOUS a cancel request is acted on immediately.
  • Problem: The thread enables async cancellation and then blocks in pthread_mutex_lock(), which is not async-cancel-safe. POSIX leaves async cancellation inside such a call undefined, and it can leave the mutex internals inconsistent. The test requires the cleanup handler to run within 10s. A well-defined async-cancel test needs a pure compute loop (no library calls) in the target thread.
  • Evidence: 1-1.c:53-67, 104-124; man pthread_setcancelstate(3) NOTES: “other library functions can’t be safely called from an asynchronously cancelable thread”; “One of the few circumstances in which asynchronous cancelability is useful is for cancelation of a thread that is in a pure compute-bound loop.”
  • Suggested action: replace the mutex wait with a busy loop on a volatile flag (no library calls) after enabling async cancel.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT,READ. HPE 1x + 3x stress, VIRT 5x: all Test PASSED (cleanup handler ran). Not mutable without changing the test’s subject; man pthread_setcancelstate(3) NOTES: ‘other library functions can’t be safely called from an asynchronously cancelable thread’ - here the target is blocked in pthread_mutex_lock(), so the result relies on glibc behaviour
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via MUSL,RUN,REPEAT,SRC. HPE glibc PASS 4/4; musl FAIL 6/6 ‘Test FAILED: Cancel request timed out’. musl mutex lock waits in __timedwait(), which disables cancellation around the futex wait (src/thread/__timedwait.c:67-69, pthread_mutex_timedlock.c:85), so cancel_handler returns early (pthread_cancel.c:55); glibc sigcancel_handler (nptl/pthread_cancel.c:50-54) exits anyway

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sigaction/10-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sigaction/10-1)

  • Category: UNDEF (secondary: FRAGILE)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: assertion #10, SIGCHLD is generated when a child stops (SA_NOCLDSTOP clear).
  • Problem: PASS requires child_stopped == NUMSTOPS && child_continued == NUMSTOPS, i.e. it also demands a CLD_CONTINUED SIGCHLD for every SIGCONT. POSIX only says SIGCHLD “may” be generated when a stopped child is continued (that is assertion #11, XSI). Linux does send it, so this passes on Linux, but the check is stronger than the assertion. Also: waits use 1 s select() timeouts (a late SIGCHLD can coalesce with the next one since SIGCHLD does not queue), printf() in the handler, and failure is return -1 (exit 255) instead of PTS_FAIL.
  • Evidence: 10-1.c:113; https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/sigaction.html SA_NOCLDSTOP: SIGCHLD “shall be generated … whenever any of its child processes stop” and “may be generated … whenever any of its stopped child processes are continued”.
  • Suggested action: Check only child_stopped == NUMSTOPS (leave CLD_CONTINUED to 11-1); return PTS_FAIL.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sigaddset/2-1.c (runtest: openposix: conformance/interfaces/sigaddset/2-1)

  • Category: UNDEF (secondary: DOCS)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: sigaddset() on a sigset_t that was never initialized must not crash or hang. The header says the test passes whenever the system is able to report a result.
  • Problem: The code returns PTS_FAIL unless sigaddset() returns 0 and sigismember() then returns 1. That demands a specific outcome for behavior POSIX declares undefined, and the test reads an indeterminate automatic object. glibc and musl just OR in the bit, so it passes in practice, but the assertion contradicts both the spec and the test’s own description.
  • Evidence: testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sigaddset/2-1.c:21-33; POSIX.1-2024 sigaddset DESCRIPTION: “If such an object is not initialized in this way, but is nonetheless supplied as an argument to any of … sigaddset() … the results are undefined.”; sigsetops(3): “The results are undefined if this is not done.”
  • Suggested action: Return PTS_PASS for any return value (as the header says), or drop the test.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: ‘Test PASSED: Signal was added’ rc 0; musl: same rc 0. Both just OR in the bit without reading the rest of the set: glibc signal/sigaddset.c:27-34, musl src/signal/sigaddset.c:6-12. Claim about both libcs verified; test still demands an outcome for UB, contradicting its header

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sigaddset/4-1.c (runtest: openposix: conformance/interfaces/sigaddset/4-1)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: sigaddset() with an invalid signo (-1, -10000, INT32_MIN, INT32_MIN+1) returns -1/EINVAL.
  • Problem: POSIX lists EINVAL for sigaddset() only under “may fail”, so a conforming implementation can accept or ignore an invalid signo. The test FAILs unless EINVAL is returned. On Linux this does not cause false failures: sigsetops(3) lists EINVAL unconditionally, and both glibc and musl range-check signo. As a POSIX conformance test it is still too strict.
  • Evidence: testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sigaddset/4-1.c:39; https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/sigaddset.html ERRORS: “The sigaddset() function may fail if: [EINVAL] The value of the signo argument is an invalid or unsupported signal number.”
  • Suggested action: Accept ret==0 as PASS (or return PTS_UNSUPPORTED). Keep requiring errno==EINVAL when -1 is returned.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,READ,GIT. HPE: sigaddset_4-1 Test PASSED as-is (glibc 2.43 returns -1/EINVAL for all 4 values). opengroup.org Issue 8 sigaddset ERRORS re-fetched: ‘The sigaddset() function may fail if: [EINVAL]’ -> requiring EINVAL is stricter than POSIX; no Linux false-fail (sigsetops(3) lists EINVAL). Test written 2013 (e23ac119aa0b) from XSH6 assertion 5 wording ‘will return’.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: Test PASSED rc 0; musl: Test PASSED rc 0. Both range-check: glibc signal/sigaddset.c:27-31 (signo<=0||>=NSIG||internal), musl src/signal/sigaddset.c:7 (sig-1>=_NSIG-1 || 32..34) -> no Linux false fail; POSIX still ‘may fail’ EINVAL, so too strict as conformance test

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sigprocmask/15-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sigprocmask/15-1)

  • Category: UNDEF (secondary: DOCS, WEAK)
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: sigprocmask() returns 0 on success (assertion 15). The header says “if sigignore returns a 0”.
  • Problem: sigset_t set; is never passed to sigemptyset()/sigfillset() before sigaddset() and sigprocmask(SIG_SETMASK, &set, …). POSIX says results are undefined for an uninitialised sigset_t, so the test blocks an arbitrary stack-garbage set of signals. On Linux this cannot make the call fail (the kernel silently drops SIGKILL/SIGSTOP and ignores bits above _NSIG), so the test only checks “returns 0”. The header is copied from sigignore/4-1.
  • Evidence: sigprocmask/15-1.c:3,14-17; POSIX sigismember/sigaddset: “Applications should call either sigemptyset() or sigfillset() at least once for each object of type sigset_t prior to any other use of that object. If such an object is not initialized in this way … the results are undefined.”
  • Suggested action: add sigemptyset(&set) and fix the header.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,READ,GIT. HPE: as-is PASS. Mutant memset(&set,0xff) before sigaddset (models worst-case stack garbage) still ‘Test PASSED’ with SigBlk fffffffe7ffbfeff (all but SIGKILL/SIGSTOP and glibc-internal 32/33) -> uninitialised set is used, call cannot fail on Linux, only ‘returns 0’ is checked. Header line 8 says ‘if sigignore returns a 0’.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: Test PASSED rc 0; musl: Test PASSED rc 0. musl src/thread/pthread_sigmask.c:8-9 passes the (uninitialised) set straight to rt_sigprocmask with no validation, kernel drops SIGKILL/STOP -> call cannot fail under either libc; only ‘returns 0’ checked

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sigwaitinfo/6-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sigwaitinfo/6-1)

  • Category: UNDEF (secondary: DOCS)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: info->si_code records the cause of the signal; the test requires SI_USER for a signal generated by raise(). The header text is copied from 5-1 and talks about si_signo.
  • Problem: POSIX only requires SI_USER for kill(): “SI_USER: Signal sent by kill()”. For raise() it says “The implementation may set si_code to SI_USER if the signal was sent by the raise() or abort() functions…”, which makes SI_USER optional. On Linux, a thread-directed signal (tgkill/tkill) gets si_code = SI_TKILL (kernel/signal.c:4009 prepare_kill_siginfo, used by do_tkill at 4227). glibc’s raise() currently yields SI_USER (verified: si_code=0 on this host), but musl’s raise() uses tkill and yields SI_TKILL (-6), so the test FAILs on a conforming system.
  • Evidence: sigwaitinfo/6-1.c:3-4,48,55-58; https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/V2_chap02.html 2.4.3 SI_USER; /usr/src/linux/kernel/signal.c:4009,4227.
  • Suggested action: generate the signal with kill(getpid(), SIGTOTEST) (which must give SI_USER), or accept SI_USER and SI_TKILL; fix the header.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): REVISED via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS; musl: FAIL rc=1 ‘The cause of the signal hasn’t been stored in the si_code’. Probe: raise->sigwaitinfo si_code glibc 0, musl -6; SA_SIGINFO handler -6 on both. glibc raise also uses tgkill (nptl/pthread_kill.c:43) but sigtimedwait.c:57-62 folds SI_TKILL->SI_USER; musl raise.c:10 tkill, sigtimedwait.c no fold
  • Verification conclusion: The test fails on musl for exactly the stated reason. The finding is right. But “glibc’s raise() yields SI_USER” is wrong. glibc raise() (sysdeps/posix/raise.c:26 -> nptl/pthread_kill.c:42-43) uses tgkill, so the kernel sets SI_TKILL (kernel/signal.c:4009,4227). glibc’s sigtimedwait wrapper then rewrites SI_TKILL to SI_USER (sysdeps/unix/sysv/linux/sigtimedwait.c:57-62). musl raise.c:10 uses tkill and its sigtimedwait.c does no such rewrite. A SA_SIGINFO handler sees -6 on both libcs. Corrected text: “glibc passes only because its sigwaitinfo/sigtimedwait wrapper folds SI_TKILL into SI_USER.” The action stays the same: use kill(getpid(), SIGTOTEST), or accept SI_TKILL. Fix the header.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/strncpy/1-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/strncpy/1-1)

  • Category: UNDEF (secondary: WEAK)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: strncpy() copies at most n bytes and returns s2.
  • Problem: the destination is malloc(i - 1), and n = rand() % i can be as large as i - 1. strncpy() itself can write i-1 bytes (in bounds), but the following sample_str_2[num_bytes] = '\0' writes index i-1, one byte past the allocation. For i == 1 it is malloc(0) and writes byte 0. This heap out-of-bounds write is UB; it usually lands in malloc padding, so it passes by luck, and it fails under ASan/hardened allocators. The “bytes that follow a NUL character are not copied” part of the assertion is never exercised, because the source has no NUL before n.
  • Evidence: strncpy/1-1.c:53,59,61,63.
  • Suggested action: allocate i + 1 bytes (or num_bytes + 1). Add a source with an embedded NUL before n and check that the destination beyond it is NUL-padded.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/strncpy/2-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/strncpy/2-1)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: when the source is shorter than n, strncpy() pads with NUL up to n bytes.
  • Problem: the destination is malloc(i + EXTRA_BYTES) and strncpy() writes exactly i + EXTRA_BYTES bytes. The following sample_str_2[i + EXTRA_BYTES] = '\0' then writes one byte past the allocation, which is UB. That line is also pointless, since strncpy already NUL-padded. A content mismatch is reported as PTS_UNRESOLVED instead of FAIL.
  • Evidence: strncpy/2-1.c:54,60-67.
  • Suggested action: remove line 61 (or allocate one more byte), and return PTS_FAIL on a mismatch.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/timer_delete/1-2.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/timer_delete/1-2)

  • Category: UNDEF
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: after timer_delete(), timer_settime() on that id fails with EINVAL.
  • Problem: POSIX.1-2024 timer_settime(): “The behavior is undefined if the value specified by the timerid argument … does not correspond to a timer ID returned by timer_create() but not yet deleted by timer_delete()”. The EINVAL was made optional in Issue 6 and is only “recommended” in RATIONALE. The sibling test timer_delete/speculative/5-1.c was already relaxed for exactly this reason (“Since POSIX 2016 Edition is this behavior undefined”); 1-2 still demands EINVAL. On Linux with SIGEV_SIGNAL timers, glibc passes the kernel id through and the kernel returns EINVAL (timer_settime(2) documents “EINVAL timerid is invalid”), so there is no false failure on glibc/Linux today. The FAIL path is only unjustified under POSIX.

  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,READ,GIT. HPE PASS (kernel EINVAL). POSIX.1-2024 timer_getoverrun page (shared with timer_settime) re-fetched: ‘The behavior is undefined if the value specified by the timerid argument … does not correspond to a timer ID returned by timer_create() but not yet deleted’; EINVAL only ‘recommended’ in RATIONALE. Sibling speculative/5-1 was relaxed in d377d1cff1ec/ba58ac3254d6; 1-2 was not.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): UNCHANGED via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS ‘Test PASSED’; musl: PASS same output. Both libcs agree: SIGEV_SIGNAL timer_t = kernel id passed through (musl src/time/timer_settime.c:7-11 only decodes ids<0 = SIGEV_THREAD; glibc kernel-posix-timers.h:101-106), kernel returns EINVAL. FRAGILE: Racy, timing-dependent or environment-dependent

The test can report FAIL on a correct system because of sleep-based synchronization, scheduler or CPU assumptions, filesystem or kernel-config assumptions without detection, hardware or distro defaults. Action: add proper synchronization or detection (TCONF), or drop.

190 testcases. Sorted by path; confidence shown in each entry.

testcases/commands/unshare/unshare01.sh (runtest: commands/unshare01_sh)

  • Category: FRAGILE
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: test 6, unshare --mount --propagation shared mount --bind dir_A dir_B, makes the bind mount visible in the parent mount namespace.
  • Problem: Propagation back to the parent only happens if the mount that holds the LTP tmpdir is already shared in the parent namespace. When a mount namespace is copied, the new mount joins the peer group of the old one only if the old one has a group id; a private parent mount gives a private copy, and unshare’s --propagation shared then creates a new peer group that does not include the parent. Systemd makes / shared by default, so the test passes there, but it fails on correct kernels under non-systemd init, in containers, or with TMPDIR on a private mount. Tests 1/2 also hard-code 65534, which is /proc/sys/kernel/overflowuid and overflowgid (tunable, user_namespaces(7)), not a fixed value.
  • Evidence: unshare01.sh:150-151; fs/namespace.c:1338-1350 (clone_mnt copies mnt_group_id from the old mount; set_mnt_shared only if it has one); mount_namespaces(7) “Shared subtrees”; unshare01.sh:145-146
  • Suggested action: in setup, make the tmpdir its own shared mount (mount --bind . .; mount --make-shared .), or TCONF when findmnt shows the tmpdir mount is not shared. Read the expected ids from /proc/sys/kernel/overflow{u,g}id.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,CONTAINER. HPE: ltprun unshare01.sh 8/8 TPASS (/ is shared under systemd); ltprun unshare –mount –propagation private unshare01.sh -> ‘unshare01 6 TFAIL: unshare –mount –propagation shared mount –bind dir_A dir_B did not get bind info’ (passed 7 failed 1) on a correct kernel

testcases/cve/cve-2025-21756.c (runtest: cve/cve-2025-21756)

  • Category: FRAGILE
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: vsock keeps socket binding until destruction (fix fcdd2242c023); kernel must not taint/crash.
  • Problem: The test binds to VMADDR_CID_LOCAL, which requires the vsock loopback transport. When it is not registered (CONFIG_VSOCKETS_LOOPBACK=m and vsock_loopback not loaded, which is common on bare metal), bind() returns EADDRNOTAVAIL. vsock_bind() then reports TBROK, not TCONF. The TCONF branch keys off EINVAL (“VM socket is not supported”), but in __vsock_bind() EINVAL means “already bound” or an unsupported socket type, not that vsock is missing. The result is a false TBROK on correct kernels.
  • Evidence: cve-2025-21756.c:138-142, :155; net/vmw_vsock/af_vsock.c:730-741 (vsock_find_cid needs transport_local for CID_LOCAL), :911-912 (-EADDRNOTAVAIL)
  • Suggested action: add .needs_drivers = (const char *const []){"vsock_loopback", NULL} (or modprobe it), and map EADDRNOTAVAIL to TCONF.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,READ,VIRT. VIRT (KVM guest, vsock+virtio transport loaded, no vsock_loopback) as-is: ‘cve-2025-21756.c:38: TBROK: bind() error: EADDRNOTAVAIL (99)’. HPE: TPASS when vsock not loaded (socket() autoloads net-pf-40 incl. vsock_loopback); after rmmod vsock_loopback with vsock core loaded: same TBROK EADDRNOTAVAIL

testcases/kernel/controllers/cpuset/cpuset_memory_pressure_test/cpuset_memory_pressure_testset.sh (runtest: controllers/cpuset_memory_pressure)

  • Category: FRAGILE
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: cpuset.memory_pressure reports a non-zero rate for the cpuset whose tasks caused memory pressure, and zero for others / when disabled.
  • Problem: The metric increases only in __perform_reclaim(), i.e. when an allocating task enters direct reclaim. Tests 4-6 require a non-zero value after allocating MemAvailable-20 MB. MemAvailable is defined as memory available “without swapping”, and kswapd may free page cache fast enough that the hog never enters direct reclaim, which gives a false FAIL. The hog in sub_cpuset has mems=0 but is sized from system-wide MemAvailable. check requires 2 nodes, so that is about 2x node 0’s memory. This forces cpuset-constrained OOM, which may kill unrelated node-0 tasks; the hog’s exit status is ignored. Tests 3-4 also require the root cpuset rate to be exactly 0 while any other system task in the root cpuset could hit direct reclaim during the hog run.
  • Evidence: cpuset_memory_pressure_testset.sh:36-44 (usemem from MemAvailable), :156, :183, :229, :233 (-eq 0 -> TFAIL); /usr/src/linux/mm/page_alloc.c:4436-4447 (/* Perform direct synchronous page reclaim */ ... cpuset_memory_pressure_bump();); kernel/cgroup/cpuset-v1.c:95,144 (fmeter_markevent on task_cs(current)); Documentation/filesystems/proc.rst:1127-1129 (MemAvailable “without swapping”).
  • Suggested action: Size the hog from node-0 memory (node0/meminfo MemTotal) so it exceeds what node 0 can hold, which guarantees direct reclaim, or restrict it with a memcg limit. Accept root-cpuset noise, or move the reference tasks into a separate empty cpuset.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): UNCHANGED via RUN,READ. Cannot exercise: HPE/VIRT ‘cpuset_memory_pressure 1 TCONF: Cpuset is not supported’ (CONFIG_CPUSETS_V1 unset, both hosts have only node0 while check() needs 2 nodes). Re-read: cpuset_memory_pressure_bump() only on the direct-reclaim path (mm/page_alloc.c), hog sized from system MemAvailable; mechanism plausible but not reproducible here

testcases/kernel/controllers/cpuset/cpuset_memory_spread_test/cpuset_memory_spread_testset.sh (runtest: controllers/cpuset_memory_spread)

  • Category: FRAGILE
  • Confidence: medium

  • Problem: (1) Case 0 0 0,1 0 (spread=0, cpus=0, mems=0,1) expects all page cache on node 0, assuming CPU 0 belongs to node 0. This is never checked and is false on some topologies (CPU0 on another node, memoryless node 0). (2) Every non-target node must gain less than PAGE_SIZE*512/1024 kB (2 MB on 4K pages) of FilePages during the run. Any other file I/O on the system (journald, logs) breaks this. (3) freemem_check requires only 100000 kB MemFree per node, but the data file is 100 MiB (102400 kB). After drop_caches, normal zone fallback in the cpuset can then put pages on an unexpected node.
    1. The TCONF message uses bash array syntax ${memsinfo[*]} in a #!/bin/sh script, which fails with “Bad substitution” on dash, so the intended TCONF does not happen. TST_TOTAL=6 but test_spread_page2 reports a 7th result.

  • Suggested action: Derive the expected node from /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/node* (or pick a CPU on node 0). Raise the free-memory threshold above the file size with headroom. Make the “other nodes” tolerance relative to the 100 MB file. Fix the sh-incompatible expansion and TST_TOTAL.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): UNCHANGED via RUN,READ. Cannot exercise: ‘cpuset_memory_spread 1 TCONF: Cpuset is not supported’ on HPE/VIRT (CPUSETS_V1 unset, single node). Re-read confirms case ‘0 0 0,1 0’ assumes CPU0 on node 0, 2 MB tolerance, 100000 kB vs 100 MiB file, ${memsinfo[*]} in #!/bin/sh (:342; harmless on Fedora where sh is bash), TST_TOTAL=6

testcases/kernel/controllers/memcg/control/memcg_control_test.sh (runtest: controllers/memcg_control)

  • Category: FRAGILE
  • Confidence: low (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: a process that allocates beyond a 1-page memory limit is OOM-killed.
  • Problem: All synchronisation is by sleep. sleep 1 (line 24) is the only guarantee that mem_process has already mkfifo()‘d status_pipe before echo m > $STATUS_PIPE (line 28). If it has not, the shell creates a regular file, mem_process’s mkfifo fails with EEXIST, it reads ’m’ then EOF, and read() returning 0 leaves ch uninitialised (mem_process.c:82-90). The OOM kill is then given a fixed sleep 5 (line 29).
  • Evidence: memcg_control_test.sh:21-39; mem_process.c:100-113.
  • Suggested action: create the FIFO in the script before starting the helper (or use tst_checkpoint), and poll for the process to die with a timeout.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): REVISED via RUN,REPEAT,VIRT,MUTATION,READ. HPE ltprepeat 5: pass=5; VIRT ltprepeat 3: pass=3 (v2 path). Mutation removing the ‘sleep 1’ before ‘echo m > status_pipe’: 5/5 TPASS. If echo wins, it creates a regular file, mem_process tolerates EEXIST, reads ‘m’, allocates and is OOM-killed anyway -> same verdict; only the fixed ‘sleep 5’ wait for the kill remains timing-based
  • Verification conclusion: The mkfifo race exists but is harmless. If the shell’s echo m creates a regular file first, mem_process ignores EEXIST, reads the ‘m’ from the file, allocates and is OOM-killed, so the verdict is the same. The “ch uninitialised” path only runs after the allocation. What is left is the fixed sleep 5 for the OOM kill, which takes milliseconds in practice. Lowered to low; suggested action: create the FIFO in the script and poll for the process to exit.

testcases/kernel/controllers/memcg/functional/memcg_lib.sh (sourced by memcg functional tests)

  • Category: FRAGILE
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: check_mem_stat / test_mem_stat compare memory.stat entries against exact expected sizes right after the helper allocates.
  • Problem: Since v6.8 (kernel commit 8d59d2214c23, “mm: memcg: make stats flushing threshold per-memcg”), reading v1 memory.stat calls the non-forced mem_cgroup_flush_stats(). That flushes only when the memcg’s pending update count exceeds MEMCG_CHARGE_BATCH * num_online_cpus() (64 * ncpus). Otherwise the values may be up to one FLUSH_TIME (2 s) stale. signal_memcg_process returns as soon as memory.usage_in_bytes moves (page_counter, always exact), and the stat is read straight away. A 65-page allocation (PAGESIZES) produces only a few hundred rstat updates, which is below the threshold on hosts with more than about 4 CPUs. Stat-based checks can then see the old value (0) and FAIL. This affects memcg_stat_rss.sh, memcg_stat_test.sh and, less so, memcg_subgroup_charge.sh. It applies only to v1 hierarchies (CONFIG_MEMCG_V1).
  • Evidence: memcg_lib.sh:160-181,191-221,249-292; mm/memcontrol.c:711-715 (memcg_vmstats_needs_flush), 717-746, 755-783; mm/memcontrol-v1.c:2243 (memcg1_stat_format -> mem_cgroup_flush_stats).
  • Suggested action: poll memory.stat until it reaches the expected value or 3 s pass (in check_mem_stat), or sleep slightly over 2 s before reading; or allocate enough to exceed 64*ncpus updates.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,READ,VIRT. Tests TCONF on v2 hosts (‘memory controller mounted on cgroup v2 hierarchy’). Mechanism reproduced with a v2 analogue (same mem_cgroup_flush_stats() threshold path): touch 65 anon pages, wait for RssAnon, read memory.stat anon at once -> HPE (24 CPUs) stale in 5/20 runs (e.g. ‘immediate anon=0, after 2.5s anon=368640’); VIRT (1 CPU) 0/10 stale

testcases/kernel/crypto/af_alg07.c (runtest: crypto/af_alg07, cve/cve-2019-8912)

  • Category: FRAGILE
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: CVE-2019-8912, sockfs_setattr() must not use a stale sock->sk after the socket was released by dup2().
  • Problem: The only TPASS path is fchownat() failing with ENOENT, which on a fixed kernel happens only when the fuzzy-sync race is actually won (dup2() releases the socket after fchownat()’s path lookup but before notify_change()). If the window is not hit within the runtime (slow VMs, few real CPUs, heavy load) the loop ends with TFAIL “fchownat() failed to fail, kernel may be vulnerable” on a correct kernel. Sporadic false FAILs on fixed kernels were already reported (commit 6d2d8a711fb9 “af_alg07: add dynamic bias for ARM”). The polarity is the reverse of the usual LTP fuzzy-sync convention (no reproduction -> TPASS “nothing bad happened”).
  • Evidence: af_alg07.c:76-110; net/socket.c:673-690 (ENOENT only when sock->sk == NULL); git show 6d2d8a711fb9.
  • Suggested action: When the race was never hit, report TCONF/TINFO (“race not reproduced”) instead of TFAIL, and keep TFAIL only for a taint or a successful setattr observed inside the window.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,REPEAT,CONTAINER. HPE ltprepeat 5 af_alg07: pass=5. Pinned to one CPU (ltprun taskset -c 0 af_alg07; same as a container with –cpuset-cpus=0 on a multi-CPU host, min_cpus=2 still satisfied): 3/3 ‘Exceeded execution loops’ -> ‘af_alg07.c:110: TFAIL: fchownat() failed to fail, kernel may be vulnerable’; with LTP_RUNTIME_MUL=0.1 also 3/3 TFAIL. Fixed 7.2.9 kernel

testcases/kernel/device-drivers/block/block_dev_kernel/ltp_block_dev.c (runtest: kernel_misc/block_dev)

  • Category: FRAGILE (secondary: WEAK, DOCS)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: register_blkdev()/unregister_blkdev() equivalence classes (tc01-tc09), driven by block_dev.c.
  • Problem: tc07 deliberately calls unregister_blkdev(0, name). No major 0 is ever registered, so the kernel always takes the WARN_ON(1) branch. Every default run of block_dev therefore prints a WARNING splat and sets TAINT_W. Kernels booted with panic_on_warn panic. Later tests in the same boot that use .taint_check = TST_TAINT_W then print “Ignoring already set kernel warning taint” and silently lose their warning detection (lib/tst_taint.c:84-87). tc07 asserts nothing anyway: it passes whenever the preceding register succeeded. tc01, tc06 and tc09 likewise only check that a call returned >= 0. The header comment (“functions declared in <linux/fs.h>”) is stale: they are in linux/blkdev.h now.
  • Evidence: ltp_block_dev.c:275-296 (tc07); /usr/src/linux/block/genhd.c:303-322 (unregister_blkdev: if (!*n || strcmp((*n)->name, name)) { WARN_ON(1); }); include/linux/blkdev.h:1002-1006.
  • Suggested action: drop tc07 (or the whole unregister-with-wrong-major case), since the kernel defines it as a WARN-worthy misuse. Fix the header comment.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,BUILD,READ. Not loadable here: block_dev TCONF ‘Failed to find module ltp_block_dev.ko’ (hosts built WITH_MODULES=no, /lib/modules/*/build dangling, no kernel-devel). By source: user side runs tc07 by default (only n=8,9 skipped without -a); 7.3-rc7 genhd.c unregister_blkdev(0,..) finds no major 0 -> WARN_ON(1) -> TAINT_W; tst_taint.c:84-87 then TCONFs W for later tests

testcases/kernel/device-drivers/cpufreq/cpufreq_boost.c (runtest: kernel_misc/cpufreq_boost)

  • Category: FRAGILE (secondary: WRONG)
  • Confidence: low (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: disabling boost via cpufreq/boost or intel_pstate/no_turbo makes a CPU-bound loop measurably slower (boost-on time < 0.98 * boost-off time).
  • Problem: (1) The test compares a single wall-clock sample per state with a 2% margin, and the documented semantics do not promise any speedup. cpufreq.rst says boost=1 “does not mean that boosting is actually in use … (which still may never be used for other reasons)”. Thermal or power headroom, package load and firmware limits can all cause a TFAIL on a correct kernel. (2) find_boost_cpu() requires the per-policy file cpuN/cpufreq/boost, which was added in v6.6 (commit 218a06a79d9a). On older supported kernels with acpi_cpufreq the test therefore TCONFs “boost not supported by any CPUs” even though the global knob exists. On v6.6+ the per-policy file is created for every policy whenever the driver has set_boost (cpufreq.c:1094-1097), whether or not policy->boost_supported is set. The lookup therefore always returns the first CPU and does not do what commit d9680f1a4334 intended (selecting a boost-capable policy).
  • Evidence: cpufreq_boost.c:91-121,231-234; /usr/src/linux/Documentation/admin-guide/pm/cpufreq.rst:645-651; /usr/src/linux/drivers/cpufreq/cpufreq.c:600-616,1094-1097.
  • Suggested action: check policy boost capability properly (read cpuN/cpufreq/boost and try writing it, or compare scaling_boost_frequencies / cpuinfo_max_freq), fall back to the global knob on pre-6.6 kernels. Repeat the measurement several times and use the median, or downgrade a non-speedup to TCONF/TINFO.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): REVISED via RUN,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT,GIT. HPE (intel_cpufreq, no_turbo knob): 1+5 runs TPASS (boost 532 ms vs off 742 ms, ~30% margin vs 2% threshold); 5/5 TPASS under stress-ng on all CPUs. VIRT TCONF (VM). Not reproduced in 11 runs; pre-6.6 per-policy-file issue not testable here; on this box the margin is far above 2%
  • Verification conclusion: Not reproduced in 11 bare-metal runs, including with every CPU loaded. The turbo speedup here is about 30%, far above the 2% threshold. The single-sample design and the pre-6.6 per-policy boost lookup issue remain valid by reading but could not be shown on these hosts (intel_pstate path). Lowered to low: a false failure needs a platform with little or no turbo headroom.

testcases/kernel/device-drivers/pci/tpci_kernel/ltp_tpci.c (runtest: kernel_misc/tpci)

  • Category: FRAGILE (secondary: WRONG, WEAK)
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: exercises the PCI core API (enable, find_bus/class/device/subsys, rescan, scan_slot, match_id, (un)register_driver, assign_resource, save/restore_state, capabilities) on every PCI device that has a driver bound.
  • Problem: (1) PCI_RESOURCES runs on every driver-bound device with a prefetchable MEM BAR. Such devices include mlx5 and other NICs, GPUs and BMC VGA. For each one it calls device_release_driver() on the live device, then pci_release_resource() and pci_assign_resource(), and rebinds via device_attach() only when the reassign returned 0. If reassign fails (-ENOMEM/-EBUSY are possible, see setup-res.c), the device is left unbound and without its BAR, for example losing the test host’s network. The non-EBUSY failure is reported as TFAIL. pci_release_resource()’s return value is ignored. (2) PCI_DISABLE asserts that the device is in D3hot/D3cold after pci_disable_device(). pci_disable_device() only drops enable_cnt and clears bus mastering and never changes the power state, so this subcase can never pass. It also calls pci_release_regions() on regions owned by the bound driver. The user side skips it as “manual”, so it is dead code. (3) Several subcases cannot fail. RESTORE_STATE and UNREG_DRIVER return TPASS unconditionally. BUS_ADD_DEVICES checks if (bus) after already dereferencing it. FIND_CAP always passes and its messages are inverted: it prints “does not have” when pci_find_capability() finds PM. (4) MATCH_DEVICE requires pci_match_id(drv->id_table, dev) to match. The kernel documents that this does not see dynamic IDs, so devices bound to pci-stub (id_table = NULL) or via new_id give TFAIL on a correct kernel. (5) probe_pci_dev() only looks at PCI domain 0 and leaks the pci_get_domain_bus_and_slot() reference when the device has no driver. PCI_ENABLE and PCI_RESOURCES increment enable_cnt and never balance it.
  • Evidence: ltp_tpci.c:98-118, 146-176, 366-390, 428-475, 502-532; /usr/src/linux/drivers/pci/pci.c:2219-2242 (pci_disable_device: “This only involves disabling PCI bus-mastering”); drivers/pci/pci-driver.c:157-169 (pci_match_id “Deprecated; … will not catch any dynamic IDs”); drivers/pci/pci-stub.c:37; drivers/pci/setup-res.c:378-423.
  • Suggested action: restrict PCI_RESOURCES to driverless devices (or drop it), and always rebind when reassignment fails. Drop PCI_DISABLE. Make FIND_CAP/RESTORE_STATE/BUS_ADD_DEVICES verify something (e.g. compare config space after save/restore) or drop them. Use pci_dev_driver() plus dynid-aware matching or accept a NULL id_table. Iterate all domains (for_each_pci_dev) instead of domain 0.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,GIT,READ. tpci TCONF here (ltp_tpci.ko not built, no kernel-devel); deliberately not run. sysfs inventory: on HPE the ssh NIC eno1 (igb 02:00.0, 3 prefetchable MEM BARs) and on VIRT virtio-net plus the virtio-blk root disk (00:04.0) are driver-bound with prefetchable BARs -> PCI_RESOURCES would device_release_driver() them. Unbind added 2026-04 (13cf2ec812c9) after a UAF panic

testcases/kernel/device-drivers/zram/zram_lib.sh (runtest: helper for kernel_misc/zram01, zram02)

  • Category: FRAGILE (secondary: OBSOLETE)
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: helper creating dev_num zram devices and setting max_comp_streams/comp_algorithm/disksize/mem_limit.
  • Problem: (1) With zram-control present, zram_load sets dev_start=$(ls /dev/zram* | wc -w) and discards the id printed by hot_add. zram_add() uses idr_alloc(…, 0, 0), i.e. the lowest free id, so if existing devices are not numbered contiguously from 0 (e.g. zram1 hot-removed while zram0/zram2 remain), the test configures, mkfs’s/swapons and finally resets/hot_removes devices it did not create (possibly a live zram swap/fs, which would give EBUSY failures or worse) while its own new device is ignored. (2) zram_max_streams TCONFs on every kernel >= 4.7 and the attribute is now removed from the kernel; with LTP’s minimum of 4.4 the subtest only ever runs on 4.4-4.6, so it is effectively dead (also prints $max_stream, an unset variable, in its TFAIL).
  • Evidence: zram_lib.sh:66-75, :97-101, :118; drivers/block/zram/zram_drv.c:3084 (idr_alloc lowest id), :3189-3201 (hot_add returns device id); kernel commit 4127e13c9302 “zram: remove max_comp_streams device attr”; include/tst_kvercmp.h:13 (TST_MIN_KVER “4.4”).
  • Suggested action: record ids returned by cat hot_add and use them instead of a computed range; drop the max_comp_streams subtest (or keep only as TCONF stub) and renumber TST_CNT in zram01/zram02.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,VIRT,READ. HPE: made ids non-contiguous (hot_add zram1+zram2, hot_remove 1, decoy zram2 disksize=8M). zram02.sh computed dev_start=2: ‘created /dev/zram2~2’ though hot_add returned 1; then TFAIL comp_algorithm/disksize on the busy decoy, swapon/reset/hot_remove of zram2 (not its own), left zram1 behind. max_comp_streams TCONF on 7.2 (HPE, VIRT)

testcases/kernel/fs/proc/proc01.c (runtest: fs/proc01)

  • Category: FRAGILE (secondary: UNDOC)
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: every readable file under /proc can be opened and read without error.
  • Problem: Any open()/read() errno other than EACCES/ESRCH on any regular file under /proc is a TFAIL, unless the path is in a hand-maintained known_issues allowlist. Which errors individual procfs/sysctl/driver files return on read is not documented. It depends on kernel config, loaded drivers (nfsd, xen, rtas, sal, acpi), hugepage support, PSI, LSM stack and running services. A correct kernel with a new or less common driver therefore fails the test. The git history shows a steady stream of allowlist additions after such false failures (EOPNOTSUPP for nr_hugepages, /proc/pressure/, stable_secret EIO, nfsd clients//ctl EINVAL, apparmor/smack attr EINVAL).
  • Evidence: proc01.c:81-123 (allowlist), 346-361, 386-407; git log -- testcases/kernel/fs/proc/proc01.c (b5f924a5c029, 8a3e39f30393, 63246340d189, 168e2351c35f, 5d64780e84be, cbf52ab4816e, 80ab8bc04941).
  • Suggested action: Turn unexpected read errors from non-core proc entries into TINFO/TWARN, or limit the strict check to documented core files (proc_pid entries, /proc/meminfo, /proc/cpuinfo, …) and make the rest “does not crash or hang”. read_all (fs/read_all.c) already provides the “read everything without crashing” coverage.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): UNCHANGED via RUN,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT,GIT. Not reproduced: HPE 5/5 + 5/5 under stress-ng TPASS, VIRT 3/3 TPASS (~2081 objs, 320 MB read). git log shows the allowlist growing after false failures on correct kernels (3a3cbce7033d 2009 … 22763842080a 2021: nfsd, LSM attr, pressure, stable_secret, hugepages EOPNOTSUPP, acpi/event EAGAIN, rtas)

testcases/kernel/hotplug/cpu_hotplug/functional/cpuhotplug03.sh (runtest: cpuhotplug/cpuhotplug03)

  • Category: FRAGILE
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: Tasks get scheduled on a newly onlined CPU.
  • Problem: Spinners inherit the shell’s cpuset and affinity. On cgroup v1, offlining a CPU permanently removes it from cpus_allowed of every non-root cpuset and onlining does not add it back, so when LTP runs in a non-root v1 cpuset (containers, some systemd setups) no spinner can ever run on the re-onlined CPU and the test TFAILs on a correct kernel. The same happens if the runner’s affinity excludes CPU_TO_TEST. The migration check is limited to tst_retry’s 3 x 1 s.
  • Evidence: cpuhotplug03.sh:102-153; kernel/cgroup/cpuset-v1.c:280-298 (cpuset1_hotplug_update_tasks copies the reduced mask into cs->cpus_allowed).
  • Suggested action: TCONF unless the shell’s affinity (taskset -p $$ / Cpus_allowed_list) contains CPU_TO_TEST after re-onlining; optionally run the spinners in the root cpuset.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,VIRT,READ. HPE: ‘cpuhotplug03.sh -c 1 -l 1’ TPASS as-is; same run under ‘taskset -c 0,2-23’ (runner affinity excludes CPU_TO_TEST, as in a restricted cpuset/container) -> ‘TFAIL: No cpuhotplug_do_spin_loop processes found on CPU1’ rc=1 on a correct kernel. VIRT (1 CPU) TCONF. cgroup-v1 cpuset variant not testable (hosts are cgroup v2 only)

testcases/kernel/hotplug/cpu_hotplug/functional/cpuhotplug05.sh (runtest: cpuhotplug/cpuhotplug05)

  • Category: FRAGILE (secondary: WEAK)
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: “Does sar behave properly during CPU hotplug events?”
  • Problem: This checks the output format of the userspace sysstat sar tool, not a kernel interface. Sync is done with fixed sleep 2. Field positions 3-8 and the ‘0.00’ / non-zero heuristics depend on the sysstat version (the script already special-cases 11.7.1+). It also runs pkill sar, which kills any sar on the system. A late or partial line, or a header reprinted after the CPU comes back, gives TBROK/TFAIL with no kernel problem.
  • Evidence: cpuhotplug05.sh:94-160.
  • Suggested action: Drop, or replace with a direct check that the CPU’s line in /proc/stat disappears and reappears and its counters advance after onlining.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): UNCHANGED via RUN,READ. HPE: ‘cpuhotplug05.sh -c 1 -l 1 -d /tmp’ -> ‘TCONF: sar not found’ (sysstat not installed on Fedora 44 hosts; not installed to avoid adding units). Could not exercise the sar-format/sleep-2 heuristics; the reasoning (userspace sysstat output parsing, pkill sar) holds by reading

testcases/kernel/input/input03.c (runtest: input/input03)

  • Evidence: input03.c:92 fd_recv = SAFE_OPEN(MOUSE_DEV, O_RDONLY);, input03.c:34-48; /usr/src/linux/drivers/input/Kconfig INPUT_MOUSEDEV (“/dev/input/mice”).
