testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/mq_send/12-1.c (runtest: openposix: conformance/interfaces/mq_send/12-1)

  • Category: FRAGILE
  • Confidence: low
  • Claim under test: mq_send fails with EINTR when a signal interrupts it while blocked on a full queue.
  • Problem: The parent decides the child is blocked when a sleep(3) finishes without being interrupted by the child’s per-message SIGABRT. If the child is delayed for more than 3 s between sends (heavily loaded or throttled system), the parent signals it before it blocks. The handler then returns, the child’s next mq_send blocks forever, and the test hangs until the harness timeout. The header comment says “Test passes if errno == EINVAL” but the code checks EINTR. mq_send/5-1 shows a deterministic pipe-based approach.
  • Evidence: 12-1.c:107-112 (sleep(3) heuristic), 12-1.c:84 (child sleep(1) “give parent time”), 12-1.c:13-14 (EINVAL in comment).
  • Suggested action: Check that the child is blocked (e.g. /proc//stat state ‘S’ after the queue is full, or a pipe notification before each send as in 5-1) before signalling. Fix the comment.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): UNCHANGED via RUN,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT,MUTATION. Not reproduced: as-is 23/23 PASS (HPE 5+5 stress; VIRT 1-CPU 5+5 stress+3 stress+SCHED_IDLE). Mutant: child stalls 4 s (restarting nanosleep) before 3rd send -> parent’s sleep(3) completes, SIGABRT sent early -> rc=2 ‘Error waiting for child to exit : Interrupted system call’ UNRESOLVED (a hang needs the stall right before the blocking send).

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/mq_timedreceive/1-1.c (runtest: openposix: conformance/interfaces/mq_timedreceive/1-1)

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/mq_timedreceive/5-3.c (runtest: openposix: conformance/interfaces/mq_timedreceive/5-3)

  • Category: FRAGILE

If the parent is not yet blocked when the signal arrives, the handler runs early and mq_timedreceive later times out with ETIMEDOUT. The test then reports “errno != EINTR” FAIL. If the handler is not installed yet, the parent is killed by SIGABRT. The header admits “potential race conditions”.
  • Evidence: 5-3.c:69-78 (handler set up after fork), 5-3.c:110-112 (sleep(1); kill(getppid(), SIGABRT);).
  • Suggested action: Install the handler before fork(). Have the child send the signal only after confirming the parent is sleeping (e.g. poll /proc//stat for ‘S’), and resend periodically until the parent returns.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): REVISED via RUN,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT,MUTATION. Not reproduced: as-is 23/23 PASS (HPE 5+5 stress; VIRT 1-CPU 5+5 stress+3 stress+SCHED_IDLE). Mutant: parent delayed 1.5 s after sigaction, before mq_timedreceive -> child’s SIGABRT handled early, call times out -> rc=1 ‘errno != EINTR / Test FAILED’ (phase-1 mechanism). 1 s window after fork never slipped: lowered.
  • Verification conclusion: The mechanism is right (an early signal leads to ETIMEDOUT and a FAIL), but the parent only has to reach mq_timedreceive within 1 s of fork(), and it always did. Lowered to low.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/mq_timedsend/5-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/mq_timedsend/5-1)

  • Category: FRAGILE
  • Confidence: low (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: a blocking mq_timedsend on a full queue blocks until room is available.
  • Problem: The parent installs its SIGABRT handler only after fork(). The child relies on sleep(1) (“give parent time to set up handler”) before its first kill(getppid(), SIGABRT). If the parent has not run sigaction() within 1s, SIGABRT’s default action kills the parent with a core dump, which the run reports as SIGNALED/FAIL. Blocking is also detected only by “a 3s sleep was not interrupted”. The child ignores the return value of mq_timedsend and signals either way.
  • Evidence: 5-1.c child sleep(1); // give parent time to set up handler; the parent’s sigaction(SIGABRT) runs after fork; the heartbeat loop uses sleep(3).
  • Suggested action: Install the handler before fork() (as 5-2.c does), and have the child report the mq_timedsend result through its exit status.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): REVISED via RUN,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT,MUTATION. Not reproduced: as-is 23/23 PASS (HPE 5+5 stress; VIRT 1-CPU 5+5 stress+3 stress+SCHED_IDLE). Mutant: parent delayed 1.5 s before sigaction(SIGABRT) -> parent killed, rc=134 ‘dumped core’; the orphaned child kept running and had to be pkill’ed (it blocked our $(…) capture until the outer timeout). Consequence real, window (1 s after fork) unlikely: lowered.
  • Verification conclusion: When the parent is late, the result is worse than a FAIL: the parent dies from SIGABRT and leaves an orphaned child (and the queue /dev/mqueue/mq_timedsend_5-1_) behind. The window is the first 1 s after fork(), and it never slipped in 23 loaded runs, so lowered to low. Fix as suggested: install the handler before fork().

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_atfork/3-3.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_atfork/3-3)

  • Category: FRAGILE (secondary: WEAK)
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: pthread_atfork never returns EINTR while signals are being delivered.
  • Problem: The worker thread calls pthread_atfork() in an unbounded loop for 1 second, and every call registers another handler triple that is never freed. A standalone reproduction of that loop on this machine (glibc, x86_64) made 50.6M registrations in 1s with max RSS 1933 MB. On small-memory or memory-limited systems (cgroups, containers, embedded), that can trigger the OOM killer (reported as SIGNALED/FAIL) before ENOMEM is returned. The value of the check is also low: pthread_atfork is pure userspace, so EINTR cannot come from the kernel.
  • Evidence: 3-3.c test(): while (do_it) { count_ope++; ret = pthread_atfork(prepare, parent, child); ...} with main sleep(1). Measured with a small standalone C probe: “50659328 calls, maxrss 1933 MB”.
  • Suggested action: Cap the number of iterations (e.g. 10000, as 3-2 does) or stop on ENOMEM, or drop the test.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT,CONTAINER. VIRT: real test peaks 55 MB (1.35M ops) / 74 MB (1.8M ops) memcg in 1 s; in a systemd-run scope with MemoryMax=64M it is OOM-killed rc=137 2/2 (kernel ‘Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process pthread_atfork_’). Unlimited: HPE 6/6, VIRT 5/5 stress PASS. Phase-1’s 1.9 GB figure is ~20x too high (signals slow the loop).
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via MUSL,RUN,REPEAT,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS 3/3 (~1.57M ops/s); musl: PASS 3/3 (~491k ops). systemd-run scope MemoryMax=32M: glibc rc=137 OOM-killed, musl PASS (114k ops); 64M both PASS. Unbounded growth in both: musl pthread_atfork.c:42 malloc per call, glibc posix/register-atfork.c:44 dynarray emplace.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_cancel/2-2.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_cancel/2-2)

  • Category: FRAGILE
  • Confidence: low (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: TSD destructors run when a thread is canceled.
  • Problem: after pthread_cancel(), main does a fixed sleep(5) and then checks cleanup_flag (a plain int). It never joins the thread. A slow or loaded system that has not finished unwinding within 5 s gives a false FAIL, and every run costs 5 s. pthread_join() would give a deterministic happens-before and no fixed delay.
  • Evidence: 2-2.c:98-105 (no pthread_join anywhere).
  • Suggested action: replace sleep(5) with pthread_join(new_th, NULL), then check the flag.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): REVISED via RUN,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT. Not reproduced: HPE 6/6 plain PASS; VIRT 3/3 plain + 8/8 under ltpstress (1 CPU) PASS. Thread uses PTHREAD_CANCEL_ASYNCHRONOUS and sleeps, so unwinding takes microseconds against a fixed 5 s budget; false FAIL needs >5 s stall. Mechanism real but unlikely -> low. Cost (5 s/run) and missing join stand.
  • Verification conclusion: The missing pthread_join() is real, but the thread is canceled asynchronously and unwinding takes far less than the 5 s sleep. A false FAIL needs a stall of more than 5 s, which even the loaded 1-CPU guest did not produce. Lowered to low. The suggested fix (join, then check the flag) is still right and also saves 5 s per run.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_cancel/2-3.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_cancel/2-3)

  • Category: FRAGILE
  • Confidence: low (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: TSD destructors run after all cancellation cleanup handlers return.
  • Problem: (1) same fixed sleep(5) instead of pthread_join() as 2-2. (2) The ordering is derived from CLOCK_REALTIME timestamps taken in the cleanup handler and in the destructor. CLOCK_REALTIME can be stepped backwards (NTP or settimeofday) between the two calls, which gives “Destructor called before Cleanup Handler” on a correct system. A sequence counter (or CLOCK_MONOTONIC) states the ordering exactly.
  • Evidence: 2-3.c:42,51 (CLOCK_REALTIME), 120-143.
  • Suggested action: record order with a counter (e.g. order = ++seq) and use pthread_join.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): REVISED via RUN,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT. Not reproduced: HPE 6/6 plain, VIRT 3/3 plain + 8/8 ltpstress PASS. Same 5 s sleep as 2-2. CLOCK_REALTIME ordering: cleanup and destructor timestamps are microseconds apart, so a backwards clock step must land in that window; real but very narrow (not induced: stepping the clock on shared hosts is unsafe).
  • Verification conclusion: Both mechanisms are real but narrow. (1) The sleep(5) is the same as in 2-2. (2) The two CLOCK_REALTIME reads are microseconds apart in one unwinding thread, so an NTP or settimeofday step would have to land between them. A clock step was not attempted because the hosts are shared. Lowered to low. Keep the suggested fix: a sequence counter plus pthread_join.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_cond_broadcast/1-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_cond_broadcast/1-1)

  • Category: FRAGILE
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: pthread_cond_broadcast() unblocks all threads blocked on the condvar.
  • Problem: after the broadcast, main does sleep(1) and returns PTS_FAIL if waken_num < 3. Each woken thread must reacquire the mutex and increment a plain int within that second. On an overloaded or heavily throttled guest this gives a false FAIL. The sibling tests 2-1/2-2/4-1 use the same pattern but report UNRESOLVED instead of FAIL, and 1-2 uses join + a 180 s watchdog.
  • Evidence: 1-1.c:104-118.
  • Suggested action: join the threads, with a generous watchdog (e.g. alarm(30)), instead of a fixed sleep(1). Alternatively, report UNRESOLVED like the sibling tests.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): UNCHANGED via RUN,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT. Not reproduced: HPE 6/6 plain, VIRT 3/3 plain + 8/8 under ltpstress (1 CPU) PASS. Code re-checked: after broadcast, sleep(1) then FAIL if waken_num < 3 (plain int) - a false FAIL needs 3 threads to miss a 1 s window; siblings report UNRESOLVED for the same timeout. Window real but wide; kept medium for the FAIL-vs-UNRESOLVED inconsistency.

The rest of the test already uses alarm(5) plus join and reports UNRESOLVED on timeout.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_cond_wait/3-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_cond_wait/3-1)

  • Category: FRAGILE
  • Confidence: low (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: pthread_cond_wait() returns 0 on successful completion.
  • Problem: Main sleeps 2 s and then broadcasts. It never confirms that thread1 is blocked in pthread_cond_wait(): there is no t1_start wait and no mutex handshake, unlike 1-1/2-1. If thread1 is scheduled late, the broadcast is lost, thread1 blocks forever, and alarm(5) exits PTS_UNRESOLVED. run-tests.sh treats that as a non-pass. signaled is also written without the mutex.
  • Evidence: 3-1.c test_main sleep(2); ... signaled = 1; pthread_cond_broadcast(...).
  • Suggested action: wait for t1_start, then lock/unlock the mutex before broadcasting (as 2-1 does), or set signaled under the mutex and have the waiter loop on it.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): REVISED via RUN,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT,MUTATION. Not reproduced: HPE 6/6 plain, VIRT 3/3 plain + 8/8 ltpstress PASS. Mutation sleep(3) at thread1 start (thread misses the 2 s window) -> ‘Error: failed to wakeup thread’ rc=2 (UNRESOLVED, not FAIL) after alarm(5). Mechanism real, needs a >2 s thread start delay; outcome is UNRESOLVED -> low.
  • Verification conclusion: The lost-wakeup mechanism is real: there is no t1_start handshake, and a late thread blocks until alarm(5). It needs a thread start delay of more than 2 s, and it yields UNRESOLVED, not FAIL. Lowered to low. Keep the fix: wait for t1_start and do a mutex handshake, or set signaled under the mutex.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_setschedparam/1-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_setschedparam/1-1)

  • Category: FRAGILE

  • Problem: Switches the thread to SCHED_FIFO and reports PTS_FAIL on any error, including EPERM. Unprivileged callers (RLIMIT_RTPRIO 0, no CAP_SYS_NICE) and root in a cgroup without RT budget (CONFIG_RT_GROUP_SCHED) get EPERM on a correct system. Built and run as non-root here: “Error at pthread_setschedparam: rc=1”, exit PTS_FAIL.
  • Evidence: 1-1.c:22-30; man pthread_setschedparam(3) ERRORS: “EPERM The caller does not have appropriate privileges to set the specified scheduling policy and parameters.”; man sched(7) (RLIMIT_RTPRIO, CAP_SYS_NICE).
  • Suggested action: return PTS_UNTESTED/UNRESOLVED on EPERM, or use a policy that needs no privileges (e.g. SCHED_OTHER priority 0 round-trip) as the main check.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN. HPE as root: Test PASSED rc=0. VIRT as uid 65534 (ulimit -r = 0, no CAP_SYS_NICE): ‘Error at pthread_setschedparam: rc=1’ (EPERM) rc=1 = PTS_FAIL on a correct system. RT_GROUP_SCHED case not reproducible here (# CONFIG_RT_GROUP_SCHED is not set on Fedora 44)

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sem_unlink/2-2.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sem_unlink/2-2)

  • Category: FRAGILE
  • Confidence: low (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: destroying the semaphore is postponed until every process using it has called sem_close/_exit/exec.
  • Problem: Each child reconnects by name with sem_open(SEM_NAME, 0) in common(). The parent assumes all three children have done so after sleep(1) and then calls sem_unlink. If a child is scheduled late (loaded or slow system), its sem_open fails with ENOENT and the child exits via UNRESOLVED (exit 2). The parent then sees a non-zero exit status and reports FAILED(“Child … exited abnormally”), a false FAIL. The children could instead use the inherited sem pointer (named semaphore mappings survive fork), or signal readiness through a second semaphore or pipe.
  • Evidence: testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sem_unlink/2-2.c:91-96, 190-198, 221-243
  • Suggested action: Replace sleep(1) with explicit readiness synchronization, or have the children use the inherited mapping.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): REVISED via RUN,MUTATION,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT. Not reproduced: HPE 1+5+5 stress, VIRT 3+3 stress = 17/17 PASS. Mutant with sleep(2) before common() in child 3 (child misses the 1 s window): ‘unresolved: got 2 (No such file or directory) … Failed to reconnect’ then ‘FAILED: Child exec exited abnormally’ rc=1 -> mechanism real, but needs >1 s fork-to-sem_open delay; lowered
  • Verification conclusion: The false-FAIL mechanism is real (a late child gets ENOENT and the parent reports FAIL), but it needs a child to take more than 1 s from fork() to sem_open(), which did not happen even under full stress-ng load on 24 or 1 CPUs. Keep as FRAGILE, low; fix as suggested (inherited mapping or readiness sync).

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sem_wait/7-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sem_wait/7-1)

  • Category: FRAGILE
  • Confidence: low (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: a sem_wait blocked on a locked semaphore is interrupted by a signal and returns EINTR. Linux documents this: sem_wait(3) ERRORS EINTR, and signal(7) says sem_wait fails with EINTR when SA_RESTART is not set.
  • Problem: The parent uses sleep(1) and then kill(pid, SIGABRT), assuming the child has installed its SIGABRT handler and is blocked in sem_wait. If the child has not reached sigaction() yet (slow fork or exec, loaded machine), SIGABRT’s default action kills it. WEXITSTATUS() of a signaled status is 0, which equals CHILDFAIL, so the parent reports FAIL. The child also tests errno without checking sem_wait’s return value. sem_timedwait/9-1.c does the same thing correctly with tst_process_state_wait3(pid, ‘S’, …).
  • Evidence: testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sem_wait/7-1.c:54-89
  • Suggested action: Wait with tst_process_state_wait3(pid, ‘S’, …) (or a pipe handshake) before kill(), and check WIFEXITED.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): REVISED via RUN,MUTATION,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT. Not reproduced: HPE 1+5+5 stress, VIRT 3+3 stress = 17/17 PASS. Mutant with sleep(3) in the child before sigaction(): SIGABRT default kills the child, parent returns PTS_FAIL rc=1 with no message (WEXITSTATUS 0 == CHILDFAIL) -> false FAIL path confirmed, but needs >1 s from fork to sigaction(); lowered
  • Verification conclusion: Confirmed that a child that has not installed its handler within 1 s is reported as FAIL rather than UNRESOLVED; the window is 1 s and was not hit under load. Use tst_process_state_wait3() and WIFEXITED as suggested.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/shm_open/38-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/shm_open/38-1)

  • Category: FRAGILE
  • Confidence: medium (phase 1: low)
  • Claim under test: shm_open fails with EMFILE when the process runs out of file descriptors.
  • Problem: The test opens descriptors in a loop until shm_open fails, and it does not lower RLIMIT_NOFILE first. Under container or CI setups with very large nofile limits (up to fs.nr_open = 1048576), it opens up to a million tmpfs fds. It can then hit ENFILE or ENOMEM (memcg) before EMFILE, which is a FAIL. It is also slow.
  • Evidence: testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/shm_open/38-1.c:27-38
  • Suggested action: setrlimit(RLIMIT_NOFILE) to a small value (for example 32) before the loop.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,CONTAINER. VIRT: ulimit -n 1048576 -> ‘Test PASSED: 1048573 files open’ in 2.0 s (no ENFILE). Same nofile inside ‘systemd-run –scope -p MemoryMax=64M’: shm_open_38-1 OOM-killed by memcg (‘Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process … (shm_open_38-1)’) rc=137. Container-style nofile=1M plus a memcg limit breaks the test; setrlimit(RLIMIT_NOFILE) to a small value fixes it

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/shm_open/8-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/shm_open/8-1)

  • Category: FRAGILE
  • Confidence: medium (phase 1: low)
  • Claim under test: shm_open returns the lowest-numbered unused fd.
  • Problem: The test requires fd2 == fd1 + 1, assuming the descriptor right after mkstemp()’s is free. If the harness leaks an fd above a gap (for example fds 0-2, a hole at 3, inherited fd 4), mkstemp gets 3 and shm_open gets 5, a false FAIL even though 5 is the lowest free fd. The robust form is to close a known low fd and check that shm_open reuses it.
  • Evidence: testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/shm_open/8-1.c:40-58
  • Suggested action: Use dup() to find a free fd, close it, and expect shm_open to return that number.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN. VIRT: ltprun sh -c ‘exec 3<&- 4 ’Test FAILED’ rc=1 although shm_open returned the lowest free fd; with fd 3 simply open (no hole) -> Test PASSED. Needs a harness that leaks an fd above a gap, so the trigger is uncommon

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sigqueue/1-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sigqueue/1-1)

SIGRTMIN’s default action then terminates the child, WEXITSTATUS() of a signalled status is 0, and the test reports FAIL.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sigqueue/11-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sigqueue/11-1)

  • Evidence: sigqueue/11-1.c:24; /usr/src/linux/include/linux/threads.h PID_MAX_LIMIT.

  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,READ,CONTAINER,VIRT. HPE as-is PASS (ESRCH). VIRT: unshare –pid –fork –mount-proc, ns_last_pid=999998, ‘sleep 60 &’ got pid 999999 -> sigqueue_11-1 rc 1 ‘sigqueue() did not return -1 on ESRCH’. Both hosts pid_max=4194304 (/usr/lib/sysctl.d/50-pid-max.conf); HPE pid counter went 899847 -> 1052692 during this session, i.e. it crossed 999999 naturally.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sigqueue/2-2.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sigqueue/2-2)

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sigqueue/3-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sigqueue/3-1)

  • Category: FRAGILE

  • Claim under test: sigqueue() to a process with a different uid fails with EPERM.

When started as an unprivileged user inside a container or PID namespace where pid 1 runs under the same uid (rootless podman/docker –user), sigqueue(1, 0) succeeds and the test FAILs. kill_ok_by_cred() allows it when the uids match.

Control: as nobody in init pid ns -> rc 0. Needs a non-default setup, so medium.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sigsuspend/4-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sigsuspend/4-1)

  • Category: FRAGILE
  • Confidence: low (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: after sigsuspend() returns, the original mask (SIGUSR1 blocked) is restored.
  • Problem: the parent waits sleep(1) and then sends SIGUSR1. If the child has not run sigaction(SIGUSR1) yet (slow fork/scheduling), SIGUSR1’s default action kills it and the parent reports FAIL (“Did not exit normally”). If the signal arrives after sigprocmask() but before sigsuspend(), it stays pending and works, so only the window before line 88 matters.
  • Evidence: sigsuspend/4-1.c:88-96,118-132.
  • Suggested action: block SIGUSR1 and install the handler before fork().
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): REVISED via RUN,MUTATION,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT. Not reproduced: HPE 11/11 PASS (1+5 plain, 5 ltpstress), VIRT 6/6 PASS (3 plain, 3 stress). Mechanism proven by mutation: sleep(2) before the child’s sigaction -> ‘Test FAILED: Did not exit normally’ rc=1. Trigger needs a >1 s stall between fork() and sigaction(), unlikely in practice, so confidence lowered.
  • Verification conclusion: The mechanism is real: a SIGUSR1 sent before the handler is installed kills the child and gives a false FAIL. Triggering it needs more than 1 s between fork() and sigaction(), which did not happen even with stress-ng on a 1-CPU guest. Keep it as low-confidence FRAGILE. The fix (install the handler and block SIGUSR1 before fork) is still the right one.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sigsuspend/6-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sigsuspend/6-1)

  • Category: FRAGILE
  • Confidence: low (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: sigsuspend() returns -1 after a caught signal.
  • Problem: SIGUSR1 is never blocked before sigsuspend(), and the parent only sleep(1)s before kill(). If the signal arrives after sigaction() but before sigsuspend(), the handler runs early and sigsuspend() blocks forever (HUNG). If it arrives before sigaction(), the child dies and the test reports UNRESOLVED.
  • Evidence: sigsuspend/6-1.c:46-53,67-70.
  • Suggested action: block SIGUSR1 before fork() (sigsuspend with an empty mask unblocks it atomically).
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): REVISED via RUN,MUTATION,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT. Not reproduced: HPE 11/11 PASS, VIRT 6/6 PASS (incl. stress-ng). Mutation sleep(2) between sigaction and sigsuspend (SIGUSR1 never blocked) -> handler runs early, sigsuspend blocks forever, rc=124 (HUNG). Real but needs a >1 s stall after fork; confidence lowered.
  • Verification conclusion: The HUNG outcome is demonstrated, but it needs a stall of more than 1 s after fork(), which was not observed in 17 runs (including stress). Confidence lowered to low. Block SIGUSR1 before fork().

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sigtimedwait/1-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sigtimedwait/1-1)

  • Category: FRAGILE
  • Confidence: low (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: sigtimedwait() waits for the full timeout interval when no signal becomes pending.
  • Problem: it FAILs if a 1 s timeout takes more than 1.1 s of wall-clock time. That is a 100 ms upper margin on a sleeping call, measured with gettimeofday() (CLOCK_REALTIME, which NTP/clock steps can move). POSIX only requires waiting at least the interval (it may be rounded up to the clock resolution), and scheduling latency on loaded or virtualised systems can exceed 100 ms. The lower bound is the only strict requirement.
  • Evidence: sigtimedwait/1-1.c:32,94-117; POSIX sigtimedwait: the timeout is “the time interval specified in the timespec structure”, based on CLOCK_MONOTONIC.
  • Suggested action: measure with CLOCK_MONOTONIC and check only elapsed >= timeout (or allow a generous upper bound).
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): REVISED via RUN,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT. Not reproduced: HPE 11/11 PASS (incl. 5 under stress-ng on all 24 CPUs), VIRT 6/6 PASS (1 CPU, incl. stress). A >100 ms overshoot of a 1 s sleeping wait needs a large stall or a CLOCK_REALTIME step; confidence lowered. Also note the lower bound accepts 0.9 s, i.e. an early return passes.
  • Verification conclusion: A 100 ms overshoot on a 1 s sleeping wait was not reached, even on a stressed 1-CPU guest. It would take a multi-100 ms stall or a CLOCK_REALTIME step (gettimeofday), so confidence is lowered to low. The fix (CLOCK_MONOTONIC, check only elapsed >= timeout) still stands. The current check also accepts a return that is 100 ms early (lower bound 0.9 s), which POSIX does not allow.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sigwait/6-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sigwait/6-1)

  • Category: FRAGILE (secondary: UNDEF)
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: when several threads are blocked in sigwait(), one process-directed signal wakes only one of them.
  • Problem: (1) Main sends SIGUSR1 right after pthread_create() and only sleep(1)s before requiring n_awaken == 1. If no thread has reached sigwait within 1 s (loaded host), n_awaken is 0 and the test FAILs. (2) In the wake-up loop, up to four threads run n_awaken++ on a volatile int concurrently. volatile does not make ++ atomic, so this is a data race (C11 UB), and a lost increment leaves n_awaken < NTHREADS forever. The for (; n_awaken < NTHREADS; sched_yield()) kill(...) loop then spins until the harness timeout (HUNG).
  • Evidence: sigwait/6-1.c:83,101,146-166.
  • Suggested action: use a barrier or semaphore so all threads are about to call sigwait before kill(), then wait for the first wake with a condvar or semaphore instead of sleep(1). Make the counter atomic (or protect it with a mutex), and wake the rest by joining with per-thread pthread_kill.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): UNCHANGED via RUN,MUTATION,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT. Not reproduced: HPE 41/41 PASS (1+20 plain, 20 ltpstress, 24 CPUs), VIRT 6/6. Mutations: sleep(2) before sigwait -> ‘0 threads were awaken FAILED’ rc=1; widening n_awaken++ to load/usleep(2ms)/store -> lost increment, wake loop spins, rc=124 (HUNG). The race window is real but narrow (two threads woken back-to-back), so confidence kept at medium.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sigwait/6-2.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sigwait/6-2)

  • Category: FRAGILE
  • Confidence: low
  • Claim under test: a thread-directed signal wakes only the target thread among several sigwait()ers.
  • Problem: correctness relies on ch[0] having run sigwait() within sleep(1) of pthread_kill(). The signal stays pending for ch[0], so the result is right but may come late, and n_awaken may still be 0 at the check, giving a false FAIL under load. n_awaken and last_awaken are plain globals written by threads and read by main without synchronisation.
  • Evidence: sigwait/6-2.c:82-83,101-103,148-163.
  • Suggested action: wait on a semaphore posted by the woken thread (sem_timedwait with a generous timeout) instead of sleep(1).
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): UNCHANGED via RUN,MUTATION,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT. Not reproduced: HPE 11/11 PASS, VIRT 6/6 PASS (incl. stress-ng). Mutation sleep(2) before sigwait in every thread -> ‘0 threads were awaken … FAILED: Unexpected number of threads awaken’ rc=1. Needs ch[0] to stall >1 s before sigwait; stays low.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sigwaitinfo/3-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sigwaitinfo/3-1)

  • Category: FRAGILE (secondary: UNDEF)
  • Confidence: low (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: sigwaitinfo() suspends until a signal in set becomes pending.
  • Problem: the child installs a SIGUSR1 handler but never blocks SIGUSR1, and the parent sends it after a fixed sleep(1). (a) If the signal arrives after sigaction() but before sigwaitinfo(), the handler consumes it and sigwaitinfo() waits forever (HUNG). (b) If it arrives before sigaction(), the child is killed and the parent reports FAIL. (c) While waiting, POSIX says an unblocked caught signal “shall be handled asynchronously and the wait shall be interrupted” (EINTR is a “may fail”). The child maps a -1 return to exit 2, which the parent reports as FAIL. Linux happens to dequeue the signal in do_sigtimedwait() before delivery, so it passes when timing cooperates. sigwaitinfo(2) NOTES: “In normal usage, the calling program blocks the signals in set via a prior call to sigprocmask(2)”.
  • Evidence: sigwaitinfo/3-1.c:40-58,69-72,89-92; POSIX sigtimedwait/sigwaitinfo DESCRIPTION; /usr/src/linux/kernel/signal.c do_sigtimedwait().
  • Suggested action: block SIGUSR1 before fork() (drop the handler), so the signal stays pending until sigwaitinfo() consumes it.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): REVISED via RUN,MUTATION,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT. Not reproduced: HPE 11/11 PASS, VIRT 6/6 PASS (incl. stress-ng). Mutation sleep(2) between sigaction and sigwaitinfo -> handler consumes SIGUSR1, sigwaitinfo waits forever, rc=124 (HUNG). Needs a >1 s stall after fork; confidence lowered. Fix (block SIGUSR1 before fork) still right.
  • Verification conclusion: Same assessment as sigsuspend/6-1: the mechanism is real and the window needs a stall of more than 1 s, which was not reproduced. Lowered to low. The fix (block SIGUSR1 before fork, drop the handler) stands.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/strftime/2-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/strftime/2-1)

  • Category: FRAGILE
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: the E and O modifiers select alternative representations.
  • Problem: the test calls setlocale(LC_TIME, ““) (the runner’s environment locale) and then requires byte counts that only hold for locales without alternative eras or digits: %EC == 2, %EY == 4, %Od/%OH/%Om/… == 2, %Ou/%Ow == 1. POSIX defines %EC as”the name of the base year (period) in the locale’s alternative representation” and %O* as “the locale’s alternative numeric symbols”. In a locale with era or alt_digits data (e.g. ja_JP.UTF-8: %EC gives an era name like “令和”, %Od gives kanji numerals), these lengths differ and the test FAILs on a correct libc. It passes only because CI usually runs in C/POSIX or en_US. The test also never checks that an alternative representation is produced at all.
  • Evidence: strftime/2-1.c:25,42-197; POSIX strftime() DESCRIPTION, “Modified Conversion Specifiers”.
  • Suggested action: use setlocale(LC_TIME, “C”) or “POSIX” (where E/O must fall back to the unmodified specifier) and compare against the unmodified output; or skip when the locale defines era/alt_digits.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN. HPE (LANG=en_US.UTF-8) PASS. Same binary with LC_ALL=ja_JP.UTF-8 (glibc-langpack-ja 2.43 extracted, LOCPATH, nothing installed): ‘EC Bytes 6 令和 Test Failed: %EC doesn’t equal to 2 bytes’ rc=1 on correct glibc. date +%EC/%EY confirms 令和/令和08年.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS (en_US); glibc LC_ALL=ja_JP.UTF-8 (LOCPATH langpack): FAIL ‘%EC Bytes 6 令和’. musl: PASS in any locale: musl src/time/strftime.c:249 skips E/O modifiers (no era/alt_digits); glibc time/strftime_l.c:886 uses _nl_get_era_entry. Test passes on a libc that ignores E/O -> fragile on glibc and vacuous on musl

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/timer_create/9-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/timer_create/9-1)

  • Category: FRAGILE
  • Confidence: medium (phase 1: low)
  • Claim under test: per-process timers are disarmed and deleted by exec.
  • Problem: it hardcodes execl(“/bin/sleep”, …) and returns PTS_FAIL when execl() fails. On systems without /bin/sleep (Android: /system/bin; some minimal containers without the /bin symlink) this is a false FAIL instead of UNRESOLVED. The logic is otherwise sound: a surviving timer would SIGALRM-kill sleep.
  • Evidence: timer_create/9-1.c:69-72.
  • Suggested action: use execlp(“sleep”, …) and map execl failure to PTS_UNRESOLVED.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN. HPE as-is PASS. In a private mount ns with /dev/null bind-mounted over /usr/bin/sleep (unshare -m) execl(/bin/sleep) fails and the test prints ‘Test FAILED’ rc=1 instead of UNRESOLVED. Mechanism proven; only bites where /bin/sleep is absent (Android, minimal roots).

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/timer_getoverrun/2-3.c (runtest: openposix: conformance/interfaces/timer_getoverrun/2-3)

  • Category: FRAGILE
  • Confidence: low
  • Claim under test: overrun count equals extra expirations with smallest possible interval (2*resolution).
  • Problem: Overruns are computed at signal delivery (sigprocmask unblock) from the elapsed time since the first expiry (kernel/time/posix-timers.c:295 hrtimer_forward_now). With a 2ns interval, the upper bound “overruns < expected + fudge” (fudge = 50ms worth) is effectively an assertion that nanosleep(2s) wakes up and the process gets to sigprocmask within 50ms. That is scheduling latency, not POSIX semantics; on a loaded VM it can be exceeded and produce a false FAIL. The tolerance has already been increased once for this reason (568e5c094556).
  • Evidence: 2-3.c:97-103,121-123,155; kernel/time/posix-timers.c:290-322.
  • Suggested action: measure the actual elapsed time with clock_gettime() just before unblocking and derive the upper bound from it, or drop the upper bound.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): UNCHANGED via RUN,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT,GIT. All PASS: HPE 11/11, VIRT 6/6. Excess over expected 499999999: HPE idle ~59-68k (~0.13 ms), HPE stress max 548500 (~1.1 ms), VIRT stress max 1725145 (~3.5 ms) vs fudge 25000001 (50 ms): >10x margin. Mechanism real but unlikely. 568e5c094556 widened it for low timer precision (qemu-arm64 4 ms), not for load.

testcases/realtime/func/async_handler/async_handler.c (realtime profile: func/async_handler async_handler -c 100)

  • Category: FRAGILE
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: The latency from pthread_cond_signal() until the waiting SCHED_FIFO 89 thread runs is below 100us.
  • Problem: The verdict line “Result: FAIL” is printed if any single one of 1,000,000 samples exceeds pass_criteria (100us). Nothing checks for a PREEMPT_RT kernel, CPU isolation, or turned-off RT throttling. On a stock kernel, one SMI, softirq burst or RT-throttling period (95% bandwidth by default) is enough to fail it, and that is not a kernel bug. The signaller also holds a PI mutex while signalling at the same priority as the handler. The measured value therefore includes mutex-handoff and usleep(10) polling effects, not only wakeup latency.
  • Evidence: async_handler.c:48-50 (1e6 iterations, PASS_US 100), :142-144 (any delta > pass_criteria sets ret=1), :128-141 (usleep polling); profiles/default:22.
  • Suggested action: Base the verdict on a percentile, or TCONF/skip unless running on PREEMPT_RT (/sys/kernel/realtime), or document that the test is only meaningful on a tuned RT system.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,VIRT. Stock non-RT 7.2 kernels (PREEMPT_DYNAMIC, no PREEMPT_RT): VIRT ‘Max: 126 us Avg: 4.0454 us Criteria: latencies < 100 Result: FAIL’ rc=1 (39 s); HPE 2/2 ‘Max: 378 us / 328 us, Avg 3.5-3.6 us, Result: FAIL’ rc=1. A single outlier among 1e6 samples fails it, with the average at ~4 us.

testcases/realtime/func/hrtimer-prio/hrtimer-prio.c (runtest: realtime profiles/default func/hrtimer-prio)

  • Category: FRAGILE (secondary: DOCS)
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: FIFO busy threads cannot increase hrtimer wakeup latency of a higher-priority timer thread.
  • Problem: PASS requires the maximum of 10000 nanosleep(10us) overshoots to be <= 10us while 2*NCPU FIFO60 busy threads run. A 10us worst-case bound over 10000 samples is not achievable on typical stock (non-PREEMPT_RT), virtualised or power-managed systems, and there is no detection/TCONF for such environments, so the test reports FAIL without any kernel bug. The header refers to an -rt-era “softirq_hrtimer”/“softirqd-hrtimer” thread at prio 98 that no longer exists (hrtimers expire in hard irq context).
  • Evidence: hrtimer-prio.c:23-28, :48-53 (DEF_CRITERIA 10us, 10000 iterations), :133-143, :155 (2*NPROCESSORS_ONLN busy threads), :213 (max_delta <= pass_criteria).
  • Suggested action: Gate on PREEMPT_RT or use a percentile/relative criterion (busy vs idle baseline); fix the header.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,VIRT,STRESS. HPE (24 CPU, 48 FIFO60 busy threads) 3/3 ‘Maximum: 214/205/213 us Criteria: Maximum wakeup latency < 10 us Result: FAIL’; VIRT idle: 25 us FAIL, 10 us PASS, 11 us FAIL; VIRT under stress-ng 2/2 FAIL. Nothing gates on PREEMPT_RT. Also the message says ‘< 10 us’ but the check is <= (10 us printed as PASS).

testcases/realtime/func/matrix_mult/matrix_mult.c (runtest: realtime profiles/default func/matrix_mult “-c 0.75”)

  • Category: FRAGILE
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: running matrix multiplications concurrently on all CPUs gives a speedup > 0.75 * NCPU.
  • Problem: numcpus is sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN), not the process affinity. Under a restricted cpuset/taskset, set_affinity() walks CPU ids until sched_setaffinity succeeds and returns -1 once the allowed CPUs are used up, so the test exits with an error. Even with full affinity, the 0.75*NCPU speedup requirement is unattainable on SMT machines (siblings share execution units) and with per-core turbo/thermal limits, giving FAIL on healthy hardware.
  • Evidence: matrix_mult.c:125-145 (set_affinity), :156-159 (exit on failure), :286 (savg > cavg*criteria), :304-306 (numcpus = _SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN, criteria = 0.75*numcpus).
  • Suggested action: Use get_numcpus()/affinity-aware CPU selection and count physical cores, or relax the criterion.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,REPEAT,CONTAINER,VIRT. HPE (12 cores/24 threads): 4/4 runs Result: FAIL, speedup Avg 12.41-12.99 vs required 18.00 (0.75*24 logical CPUs); systemd-run –scope -p AllowedCPUs=0-3: ‘Thread 4: Can’t set affinity.’ rc=1. VIRT (1 CPU): PASS only because concurrent Avg = 0 us -> multiplier ‘inf’ (worker finishes before main takes start time)

testcases/realtime/func/prio-wake/prio-wake.c (runtest: realtime profiles/default func/prio-wake)

  • Category: FRAGILE
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: low)
  • Claim under test: after pthread_cond_broadcast, waiters wake (acquire the mutex) in priority order.
  • Problem: Workers (one per online CPU, increasing FIFO priorities) all wake on broadcast; glibc’s condvar does a plain futex wake of all waiters, each then re-acquires the PI mutex. The master unlocks right after the broadcast; on SMP the woken threads run on different CPUs and reach pthread_mutex_lock in an order determined by wakeup/IPI latency. A lower-priority thread that arrives while the mutex is free takes it via the userspace fast path even though a higher-priority thread is still on its way. POSIX only requires priority ordering among threads already blocked on the mutex at unlock time, so an out-of-order record is not a kernel/libc bug. The unlocked (-l0) variant additionally relies on usleep(1000) for workers to reach cond_wait.
  • Evidence: prio-wake.c:121-125 (broadcast then immediate unlock), :152-158 (order recorded under mutex), :222-227 (strict order check); POSIX pthread_mutex_unlock: “If there are threads blocked on the mutex object … the scheduling policy shall determine which thread shall acquire the mutex” (only blocked threads).
  • Suggested action: Pin all workers to one CPU (making the order deterministic), or accept the result only as informational.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT. HPE (24 CPUs, idle): prio-wake 5/5 FAIL (‘FAIL: Thread 19 woken before 24’, ‘Thread 16 woken before 23’, …); HPE under stress-ng (no idle CPUs): 5/5 PASS; VIRT (1 CPU): 3/3 PASS -> wake order depends on cross-CPU wakeup latency on SMP, exactly the phase-1 mechanism; deterministic FAIL on idle SMP bare metal
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via RUN,REPEAT,MUSL,SRC. HPE glibc: 1/5 pass, 4/5 FAIL (varying ‘Thread 5 woken before 8’…); musl: 5/5 FAIL rc=23, deterministic: woken strictly in arrival order 1..24 (23 FAIL lines). musl src/thread/pthread_cond_timedwait.c:152-157,183-208 wakes broadcast waiters one at a time in wait order via barrier chain, ignoring priority (musl limitation vs POSIX cond_broadcast ‘scheduling policy shall determine the order’)

testcases/realtime/func/pthread_kill_latency/pthread_kill_latency.c (runtest: realtime profiles/default func/pthread_kill_latency “-c 20”)

  • Category: FRAGILE (secondary: UNDEF)
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: pthread_kill() to a FIFO89 thread blocked in sigwait() is delivered within 20us.
  • Problem: FAIL if any single sample out of 10000 exceeds 20us. The receiver sleeps between samples (sender polls with usleep(100)), so wakeup includes cross-CPU IPI and idle-state exit, which routinely exceed 20us on stock, virtualised or power-managed systems; there is no PREEMPT_RT, idle-state or hypervisor detection. Same class as hrtimer-prio. Separately, sigset_t set is never sigemptyset()-initialised before sigaddset()/pthread_sigmask()/sigwait(), so the blocked/waited set contains stack garbage (UB; sigwait may return for other signals and sig is never checked). The exit status is the failure count, so 256 failures exit 0.
  • Evidence: pthread_kill_latency.c:58-60 (10000 iterations, THRESHOLD 20), :117,130-137 (uninitialised set), :159-174 (any delta > 20us counts as failure), :250-268 (usleep polling), :308 (return fail).
  • Suggested action: sigemptyset(&set) first; check sig; use a percentile or an RT-only threshold (TCONF/warn on non-PREEMPT_RT); exit(!!fail).
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT,READ. HPE plain 5/5 FAIL (Failures 2-19, Max 24-326 us), HPE stress 5/5 FAIL (Failures 63-138, Max 54-234 us), VIRT 2/3 FAIL (Max 26/28 us vs 20 us); exit status = failure count (rc=13,19,138 observed, wraps at 256). sigset_t set never sigemptyset()’d (read)

testcases/realtime/func/sched_latency/sched_latency.c (runtest: realtime profiles/default func/sched_latency “-d 1 -t 5 -c 100”)

  • Category: FRAGILE
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: periodic FIFO89 wakeups (5ms period, 1ms load) are never late by more than 100us.
  • Problem: Any single late wakeup out of 10000 (>100us) or a missed period sets FAIL. This is a hard real-time bound on whatever kernel/hardware runs it; VMs (steal time), deep C-states, SMIs and non-PREEMPT_RT configs can exceed it without any bug. No environment detection or TCONF.
  • Evidence: sched_latency.c:58-64 (10000 iterations, PASS_US 100), :146-163 (missed period -> ret=1), :178-191 (delay > pass_criteria -> ret=1).
  • Suggested action: Gate the hard bound on PREEMPT_RT (tst_check_preempt_rt-like probe) or report as informational/percentile on stock kernels.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT. HPE plain 3/5 FAIL (Max 102/128/371 us > 100), HPE stress 3/5 FAIL (Max 124-285 us), VIRT 3/3 FAIL (Max 6804 us, 3684 us, and one run Max 58 us but FAIL via PERIOD MISSED path) on stock PREEMPT_LAZY 7.2 kernels with no bug -> hard 100us bound without RT detection

WEAK: Low verification value

The test only checks that a call succeeds, is trivial, duplicates another test, or covers far less than it claims. It is unlikely to catch a regression. Action: strengthen, merge into the duplicate, or drop.

563 testcases. Sorted by path; confidence shown in each entry.

testcases/commands/mv/mv_tests.sh (runtest: commands/mv01_sh)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: Test #1 mv dir1 dir2 moves the tree and removes the old directory; Test #2 mv -b file1 file2 keeps a backup of file2 with its original content.
  • Problem: Two of the checks are ineffective. In test1 the “old directory removed” check is [ -f tst_mv.old ] (line 108); -f is false for a directory, so this branch can never TFAIL even if the directory were still there. In test2 both tmpfile1 and tmpfile2 are created empty by touch (line 121) and MD5_backup is computed from tmpfile2 (line 139), not from tmpfile2~; the MD5s are therefore always equal (empty content vs empty content) and the TPASS condition reduces to -f tmpfile2~. The backup content is never verified.
  • Evidence: testcases/commands/mv/mv_tests.sh:108, :121, :123, :139, :145
  • Suggested action: use [ -e tst_mv.old ]/-d; give tmpfile1 and tmpfile2 different content and compare MD5 of tmpfile2~ with MD5_old and MD5 of tmpfile2 with tmpfile1.

testcases/cve/cve-2017-2618.c (runtest: cve/cve-2017-2618)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: SELinux off-by-one in selinux_setprocattr() (fix 0c461cb727d1) does not crash the kernel when “” is written to /proc/self/attr/fscreate.
  • Problem: setup only checks that /proc/self/attr/fscreate exists. That file exists whenever CONFIG_SECURITY is enabled, whatever the LSM. The write goes to the first LSM that implements setprocattr. With SELinux not built in, disabled or not first (AppArmor, Smack or no LSM), the write fails with EINVAL in another LSM or the default hook, so selinux_setprocattr() never runs. The write’s return value is ignored and the test reports TPASS “Bug not reproduced” without covering the code under test. On Debian, Ubuntu and SUSE (AppArmor) this is a false PASS.
  • Evidence: cve-2017-2618.c:22-24, :33; security/security.c:3891-3900 (security_setprocattr dispatches to the first hook only)
  • Suggested action: TCONF unless SELinux is enabled (e.g. /sys/fs/selinux/enforce exists, or tst_selinux_enabled()), or check that the write returns 1 and TCONF on EINVAL.

testcases/cve/meltdown.c (runtest: cve/cve-2017-5754)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: CPU/kernel does not let userspace speculatively read kernel memory (Meltdown, CVE-2017-5754), probing saved_command_line.
  • Problem: The probe address comes from /proc/kallsyms. When the kernel hides symbol values (kptr_restrict=2, or lockdown confidentiality) kallsyms prints all-zero addresses, find_symbol_in_file() parses 0, and the test falls back to /boot/System.map-$(uname -r), whose addresses are link-time (pre-KASLR). With KASLR active the test then probes an unrelated address, recovers garbage, and reports TPASS “I was not able to read your kernel memory” without ever exercising the vulnerability. A zero address from kallsyms should be treated as “hidden” and the System.map fallback only used when KASLR is disabled (or TCONF instead).
  • Evidence: testcases/cve/meltdown.c:254-293 (find_symbol_in_file / find_kernel_symbol), :302-306; kernel/ksyms_common.c:28 kallsyms_show_value() returns false for kptr_restrict=2, and kernel/kallsyms.c s_show() then prints a zero address.
  • Suggested action: TCONF when kallsyms reports address 0 and KASLR is enabled (e.g. “nokaslr” absent from /proc/cmdline), rather than trusting System.map.

testcases/kernel/containers/pidns/pidns32.c (runtest: containers/pidns32)

  • Category: WEAK (secondary: FRAGILE)

  • Claim under test: “check for the maximum amount of nested containers”.

The final TST_EXP_EQ_LI(*level-1, MAXNEST) is tautological: the counter always ends at 33 unless a SAFE_CLONE failed, which already TBROKs. Additionally, if the test is started inside a non-initial pid ns (containerised CI), the 32 clones exceed the limit and the test TBROKs on a correct kernel.
  • Evidence: pidns32.c:30, 61; include/linux/pid_namespace.h:15 (MAX_PID_NS_LEVEL 32); kernel/pid_namespace.c:88-89 (level > MAX_PID_NS_LEVEL -> -ENOSPC). Commit 878d81e6c0cd shows the pre-fix version did only 31 nests yet passed the same counter check, i.e. the check cannot fail.
  • Suggested action: Compute the starting level (e.g. count NSpid entries in /proc/self/status), create nested ns up to MAX_PID_NS_LEVEL, then TST_EXP_FAIL the next clone with ENOSPC.

  • Evidence: cgroup_regression_test.sh:93-108,162-192,236-277,287-315,354-372; cgroup_regression_5_1.sh:9; /usr/src/linux/kernel/cgroup/cgroup.c:1847-1859; /usr/src/linux/kernel/cgroup/cgroup-v1.c:1059-1075; /usr/src/linux/kernel/sched/debug.c:763; grep -rn slt_result /usr/src/ltp -> only this file.

testcases/kernel/controllers/cgroup_xattr/cgroup_xattr.c (runtest: controllers/cgroup_xattr)

  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: since 3.7 xattrs (trusted., security.) can be set/read on cgroupfs files.
  • Problem: The test does not use the LTP cgroup library; it parses /proc/cgroups, groups enabled controllers by hierarchy id and does its own mount -t cgroup -o xattr,<all ctrls of that hierarchy> into the tmpdir. On a cgroup-v2 host every controller has hierarchy 0, so one mount with all controllers is attempted and rebind_subsystems returns -EBUSY for any controller that has child csses on the default hierarchy (cgroup.c:1853-1855) -> “Can’t mount” for all -> TCONF “Nothing mounted”. So the test never runs on current distros. On v1 hosts the mount reuses the already-mounted system hierarchy (cgroup1_root_to_use name/subsys match), and the recursive walk then sets trusted.test xattrs on every file of every system cgroup (systemd slices included). The “BUG WORKAROUND … Only mount those subsystems which are not mounted yet” comment (lines 262-269) describes a filter the code does not implement (it never looks at /proc/mounts), and the “see setup()” comment on the security. key (line 67) is stale (setup only touches trusted.). Since 3.15 xattr support comes from kernfs on every cgroup mount regardless of the xattr option, so the xattr mount option is irrelevant.
  • Evidence: cgroup_xattr.c:242-313,378-424; /usr/src/linux/kernel/cgroup/cgroup.c:1853-1859, 2186 (KERNFS_ROOT_SUPPORT_USER_XATTR); /usr/src/linux/kernel/cgroup/cgroup-v1.c:987-988.
  • Suggested action: rewrite on top of tst_cgroup (operate inside the LTP test cgroup on whichever hierarchy is mounted, v2 included) and drop the self-mounting code and stale comments; or drop the test.

testcases/kernel/controllers/cpuctl/run_cpuctl_test.sh (runtest: controllers/controllers via test_controllers.sh)

testcases/kernel/device-drivers/block/block_dev_user/block_dev.c (runtest: kernel_misc/block_dev)

The comment says this waits for “kernel fix where register_blkdev() & unregister_blkdev() checks the input device name parameter against NULL”. No such fix exists or is planned: these are in-kernel APIs with no NULL contract. __register_blkdev() does strscpy(p->name, name) and unregister_blkdev() does strcmp(name), so both oops (and tc09’s “kernel should silently ignore this” is wrong). Two of nine reported results are therefore always TCONF, and running with -a crashes the machine.

testcases/kernel/fs/acl/acl_file_ops01.c (runtest: fs/acl_file_ops01)

  • Category: WEAK (secondary: DOCS)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: “chmod(2) should update ACL_USER_OBJ, ACL_GROUP_OBJ and ACL_OTHER entries” and “chown(2) should change owner/group without affecting ACL entries; ACL permissions preserved after ownership change”.
  • Problem: Both subtests install a minimal ACL (only USER_OBJ/GROUP_OBJ/OTHER). On every listed filesystem (ext2/3/4, xfs, btrfs) ->set_acl() calls posix_acl_update_mode(), which runs posix_acl_equiv_mode(); for a minimal ACL that returns 0, *acl = NULL, the mode bits are rewritten and the system.posix_acl_access xattr is removed. The library’s acl_get_file() (acl_lib.h) then gets ENODATA and synthesizes the three entries from st_mode (acl_from_mode()). Consequently subtest 1 can only fail if chmod(0777) fails to change st_mode, and subtest 2 can only fail if chown() changes st_mode (it never does for a 0644-style file, and chown() succeeds unconditionally for root). posix_acl_chmod() and the “ACL survives chown” property are never exercised; a kernel that corrupted extended ACLs on chmod/chown would still pass. The docparse text claims ACL-entry level coverage that the test does not provide.
  • Evidence: acl_file_ops01.c:67-75 and 128-136 (minimal ACL), acl_lib.h acl_get_file() ENODATA -> acl_from_mode(); /usr/src/linux/fs/posix_acl.c posix_acl_update_mode() (if (error == 0) *acl = NULL;), called from fs/ext4/acl.c:252, fs/xfs/xfs_acl.c:262, fs/btrfs/acl.c:115. acl(5) “Correspondence between ACL entries and file permission bits”: for an ACL with a mask entry chmod changes the ACL_MASK entry, not ACL_GROUP_OBJ.
  • Suggested action: Add an ACL_USER (and ACL_MASK) entry so the xattr is actually stored; in subtest 1 verify after chmod(0777) that USER_OBJ/OTHER became rwx and that ACL_MASK (not GROUP_OBJ) was updated and the named-user entry is intact (posix_acl_chmod()); in subtest 2 verify the named-user and mask entries are preserved after chown(). Reword the description accordingly.

testcases/kernel/fs/fsstress/fsstress.c (runtest: none directly; used by testcases/network/nfs/nfs_stress/nfs06.sh)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: filesystem stress (xfstests fsstress port); nfs06.sh reports TFAIL if an fsstress process exits non-zero.
  • Problem: fsstress only generates load. Every op records errno and prints it only with -v; nothing is verified (write_f fills with a byte pattern that is never read back). In the multi-process mode used by nfs06 (-p $THREAD_NUM) the parent reaps children with while (wait(&stat) > 0 ...) and never looks at stat, then return 0, so even a child crashing with SIGSEGV/SIGBUS gives exit status 0. nfs06’s “fsstress process failed” check therefore only catches setup errors (chdir/mkdir failure, bad options). Expected for a load generator, but the PASS of nfs06 means “the machine did not hang”, nothing more. (Minor: doproc() compares the return value of stat64() with EIO, which can never match; only reachable with XFS error injection, compiled out by -DNO_XFS.)
  • Evidence: fsstress.c main(): while (wait(&stat) > 0 && !should_stop) continue; … return 0;; write_f()/dread_f(): e = write(...) < 0 ? errno : 0; used only in if (v) printf; nfs06.sh:30-41.
  • Suggested action: make the parent return non-zero if any child did not exit 0 (WIFSIGNALED or non-zero WEXITSTATUS); optionally count unexpected errnos (EIO, EFSCORRUPTED) and fail on them.

testcases/kernel/fs/lftest/lftest.c (runtest: fs/lftest01)

testcases/kernel/fs/racer/fs_racer.sh (runtest: fs/fs_racer)

  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: shuffles, deletes and recreates 20 files from many concurrent workers “to test for race conditions in the filesystem code”.
  • Problem: There is no verification and no LTP result. The script starts 24 background workers, sleeps for -t seconds (runtest: 5), killalls them and always exit 0. A failure can only show up as a kernel oops/hang seen outside the test. Environment dependencies: it launches workers as ./fs_racer_*.sh, so it does nothing (and still exits 0) unless the runner’s cwd is testcases/bin. It uses $TMPDIR/race without tst_test.sh, so an unset TMPDIR means /race on the root fs. It needs killall (psmisc) without checking for it; if killall is missing, the workers keep running after the test. fs_racer_file_create.sh runs three concurrent dd of up to 2,000,000 KiB each, with no free-space check, which can fill a tmpfs /tmp.
  • Evidence: fs_racer.sh:32-34, 67-68, 77-90, 92-100 (always exit 0); fs_racer_file_create.sh MAX_SIZE=2000000, bs=1k.
  • Suggested action: Port to tst_test.sh: use TST_NEEDS_TMPDIR, TST_NEEDS_CMDS=killall (or track PIDs and kill them directly), call the workers via PATH, cap dd sizes, and add at least a TPASS/“system survived” check, ideally with a dmesg/taint check. Otherwise drop it in favour of fsstress-based runs.

  • Problem: The only assertion is that the userspace top -b process is still alive one second after offlining a CPU. This tests procps robustness, not kernel behaviour; its output is discarded.

  • Suggested action: Drop, or replace with a /proc/stat or /sys/devices/system/cpu/online consistency check during hotplug.

testcases/kernel/io/direct_io/diotest2.c (runtest: dio/dio02, dio08, dio14, dio18, dio22)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: combinations of direct/buffered read and write, “for each iteration” writing and reading back data; larger iteration counts and offsets are run as separate runtest entries.
  • Problem: runtest() seeks to offset + iter * bufsize where iter is the loop bound, not the loop index i. Every iteration therefore writes/reads the same single block at offset+iter*bufsize; the -i 1000 variants (dio14/18/22) only repeat one block 1000 times instead of exercising a 65 MB region. The check itself is valid, but the coverage is far narrower than the runtest variants suggest. diotest3/6 use per-child offsets correctly.
  • Evidence: diotest2.c:100 and :109 (lseek(fd_w, offset + iter * bufsize, SEEK_SET), same for fd_r), loop index i at :98.
  • Suggested action: use offset + i * bufsize, or drop the large-iteration runtest variants.

testcases/kernel/io/writetest/writetest.c (runtest: fs/writetest01, fs_readonly/test_robind55)

  • Category: WEAK (secondary: DOCS)
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: “verify that writes to disk occur without corruption” by writing N 1 MB blocks of rand() data and reading them back.
  • Problem: the file is written and immediately re-read without fsync(), O_DIRECT, or dropping caches, so the verify pass is served from the page cache and says nothing about on-disk integrity; the default (and the runtest entry) is a single 1 MB block. The write-pass result is also reported as a TPASS even though it only checks that write() returned BLOCKSIZE. The only real value is as a smoke test that write/read of a file in the tmpdir works, which many other tests already cover (e.g. fs/fs_inod, ltp-aiodio aiocp compare).
  • Evidence: writetest.c:20-27 (description), 83-108 (no fsync), 119-159 (verify from cache), runtest/fs:61.
  • Suggested action: either add fsync()+posix_fadvise(DONTNEED)/O_DIRECT re-read and a larger default so the description is true, or reword the description to “buffered write/read-back sanity check”; consider dropping in favour of aiocp/fs tests.

testcases/kernel/ipc/pipeio/pipeio.c (runtest: syscalls/pipeio_1 .. pipeio_8)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: stress named/unnamed pipes with N writers of fixed-size records and one reader, in blocking and “non-blocking” mode, checking record integrity.
  • Problem: (1) the non-blocking variants (pipeio_2/4/7/8, without -b) are effectively identical to the blocking ones: pipeio sets O_NONBLOCK, but all I/O goes through lio_read_buffer()/lio_write_buffer() which loop on EAGAIN/EINTR and on short transfers until the full size is done (lib/tlibio.c:663-690, 1091-1115), so the “partial read” TFAIL branch at pipeio.c:688 is unreachable and no non-blocking semantics are actually verified. (2) The periodic progress line for -v/-p is emitted with tst_resm(TFAIL, ...) (pipeio.c:702), so any run with those options fails regardless of data (not used by runtest). (3) A child whose write fails exits(1), but the parent only notices via EOF, prints TWARN “children have died prematurely” and still reports TPASS if no data mismatch was seen (pipeio.c:679-682, 852-862).
  • Evidence: pipeio.c:553, 664, 688-697, 702, 679-682; lib/tlibio.c:663-690, 1091-1115.
  • Suggested action: drop the duplicated non-blocking runtest entries (or implement real non-blocking reads with explicit EAGAIN counting), change line 702 to TINFO, and propagate child exit status to TFAIL.

testcases/kernel/mem/cpuset/cpuset01.c (runtest: mm/cpuset01)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: Regression for OOM when cpuset.mems of a task bound with MPOL_BIND is changed while it allocates (fixed in 2.6.35).
  • Problem: mem_hog_cpuset() forks the hog children and then immediately sends SIGUSR1 to all of them (lines 122-141), so each hog runs for at most a few mmap/memset iterations. Meanwhile the parent writes cpuset.mems just twice, back to back, with no synchronization against the hogs (lines 66-67). The window where mems changes while hogs allocate is tiny and non-deterministic. The original reproducer kept allocating while mems was toggled repeatedly. TPASS is printed unconditionally after tst_reap_children().
  • Evidence: cpuset01.c:63, 66-71, 122-141.
  • Suggested action: Keep the hogs running (signal them only after the parent has toggled mems in a loop for some time/iterations), e.g. use a checkpoint to start toggling once hogs are allocating.

testcases/kernel/mem/hugetlb/hugemmap/hugemmap01.c (runtest: hugetlb/hugemmap01)

  • Category: WEAK (secondary: FRAGILE)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: mmap() of a hugetlbfs file succeeds and the number of free huge pages decreases.
  • Problem: TPASS is printed as soon as mmap() returns non-MAP_FAILED. The “free pages decreased” check is only a TWARN. TEMPFILE is opened with O_CREAT (no O_TRUNC) every iteration and only unlinked in cleanup(), so with -i 2 the huge page is still in the file’s page cache. Free pages then do not decrease and the test reports TWARN (non-zero exit) on a correct kernel. Coverage overlaps hugemmap04/hugemmap09 and many libhugetlbfs ports.
  • Evidence: hugemmap01.c:42, 55-65, 84-87.
  • Suggested action: Use tst_creat_unlinked()/O_TRUNC per iteration and turn the free-count check into a real TPASS/TFAIL, or drop as a duplicate.

testcases/kernel/mem/hugetlb/hugemmap/hugemmap04.c (runtest: hugetlb/hugemmap04)

  • Category: WEAK (secondary: FRAGILE)
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: mmap() of the largest possible hugetlbfs mapping succeeds.
  • Problem: “Largest possible” is taken as HugePages_Free, which ignores HugePages_Rsvd. If anything else holds reservations, the mmap fails with ENOMEM on a correct kernel. The free-decrease check is TWARN only. As in hugemmap01, TEMPFILE persists across -i iterations, so the second iteration TWARNs because page 0 is already instantiated. Otherwise it only checks mmap() success.
  • Evidence: hugemmap04.c:299-335; mm/hugetlb.c hugetlb_acct_memory() reserves against free minus reserved pages.
  • Suggested action: Use Free - Rsvd, use an unlinked/truncated file per iteration, and make the counter check a real assertion. Or merge into hugemmap01.

testcases/kernel/mem/hugetlb/hugemmap/hugemmap32.c (runtest: hugetlb/hugemmap32)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: Freeing a gigantic hugepage does not produce “Bad page state” (ba9c1201beaa, a01f43901cfb).
  • Problem: run_test() writes “1” to the gigantic nr_hugepages file and only checks that the write did not error. It never reads the value back. set_max_huge_pages() returns 0 when alloc_pool_huge_folio() fails (goto out), so on a system that cannot find 1GB of contiguous memory at runtime (common even after drop_caches/compact) no gigantic page is allocated or freed. The taint check then trivially passes and the test reports TPASS without exercising the free path. If gigantic pages were preallocated (org_g_hpages >= 1), writing 1 allocates nothing new, though writing 0 does free them.
  • Evidence: hugemmap32.c:31-38; /usr/src/linux/mm/hugetlb.c:3863-3870 (allocation failure -> goto out, returns 0).
  • Suggested action: After writing 1, read nr_hugepages back and TCONF if it is below 1 (or max(1, org)) before writing 0 and checking taint.

testcases/kernel/mem/mmapstress/mmapstress05.c (runtest: mm/mmapstress05)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: “mfile_insque”: mmapping file portions in front of / behind an existing mapping such that “None of the mmaps can be concatenated”.
  • Problem: The test only checks that three MAP_FIXED PROT_READ file mmaps succeed and then unmaps them. It never reads the mapped data (the file has ‘a’ pages at each offset) and does not verify anything about VMA layout. The description refers to IRIX mfile objects (MMU_NARROWPTEPG) that have no Linux counterpart.
  • Evidence: mmapstress05.c:282-301 (only return values checked), :126-131 (description).
  • Suggested action: at least verify the mapped pages contain ‘a’ (and optionally inspect /proc/self/maps for 3 VMAs), or merge into another mmap test / drop.

testcases/kernel/mem/mmapstress/mmapstress08.c (runtest: mm/mmapstress08)

  • Category: WEAK (secondary: DOCS)
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: exercises IRIX “as_anon_get” by burning level-2 page tables (one 4K page per 4MB, 1024 PTEs per table), then unmapping.
  • Problem: Only checks that 256 hinted (non-MAP_FIXED) anonymous mmaps and one 1GB munmap succeed; pages are never touched, so no page tables are actually populated, and the 1024-PTEs-per-table assumption is wrong on x86_64 (512 entries, 2MB per PTE table). Hints are not checked against the returned address, so mappings may land elsewhere while the final munmap blindly unmaps 1GB above brk. x86-only gating is arbitrary.
  • Evidence: mmapstress08.c:21-28, :49, :86-100.
  • Suggested action: touch each page and verify returned addresses, drop the IRIX text; or drop the test as low-value.

testcases/kernel/mem/mtest05/mmstress.c (runtest: mm/mtest05)

  • Category: WEAK (secondary: DOCS)

  • Claim under test: race conditions between simultaneous read/write/COW faults (32 threads), fork-exit and fork-exec-exit.
  • Problem: Tests 1-4 only touch pages; nothing ever reads back written data or compares file contents, and thread_fault() always pthread_exit(NULL) so the th_status == 1 failure branch is unreachable. The only detectable failure is a crash (SIGSEGV/SIGBUS handler exits with TBROK). test4’s text says “READ faults … /dev/zero” but it passes COW_FAULT (MAP_PRIVATE, PROT_WRITE, writes).
  • Evidence: mmstress.c:219-233 (no verification), :423 (unreachable), :514-519 (test4 uses COW_FAULT).
  • Suggested action: verify page contents after join (shared file should contain ‘a’, private mapping file must be unchanged), fix test4 description.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,READ. HPE: mtest05 6x TPASS as-is. Mutation: thread_fault() write fault replaced by a read (no page is ever written) -> still TEST 1-6 Passed, rc=0: nothing verifies data; thread_fault() only ever pthread_exit(NULL) (line 233) so th_status==1 branch is dead; test4 passes COW_FAULT despite READ text

Largely duplicated by mmap21 / mmapstress tests.

testcases/kernel/mem/mtest07/shm_test.c (runtest: mm/shm_test01)

  • Category: WEAK (secondary: FRAGILE)

  • Claim under test: shmat/shmdt/IPC_RMID stress from many threads with readers and writers.
  • Problem: The “reader” thread writes ‘Y’ and the “writer” thread reads into a dummy variable; contents are never compared, so only syscall success is verified. Not on the LTP API (plain exit(0)/exit(-1), no TPASS/TFAIL). Uses hard-coded SysV keys 1969..1983 in the (global) IPC namespace: if any existing segment uses such a key with a smaller size or other owner, shmget() fails with EINVAL/EACCES and the test exits -1 with no kernel bug.

testcases/kernel/mem/oom/oom02.c (runtest: mm/oom02)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: OOM behaviour under MPOL_BIND, MPOL_INTERLEAVE and MPOL_PREFERRED.

Because set_mempolicy() from the MPOL_BIND case was applied to the test process and is never reset, the INTERLEAVE and PREFERRED cases actually run again under MPOL_BIND and report TPASS with the policy name in the log. On the most common NUMA setup (2 nodes) 2/3 of the claimed coverage is not exercised. oom03’s “MEMCG & mempolicy” block has the same behaviour.

That is about 10MB in total, with no memory pressure, swapping or sharing. It only checks that anonymous memory keeps what was written to it, which every other mm test already covers implicitly. The core logic is the same as in stack_space.c. Minor: a child that cannot malloc exits “OK”, and dumpbuf(buf - csize) reads out of bounds when chunk 0 fails (failure path only).

testcases/kernel/mem/vmtests/stack_space.c (runtest: mm/stack_space)

  • Claim under test: “Test VM for set of stack-space intensive programs”.

testcases/kernel/power_management/runpwtests04.sh (runtest: power_management_tests/runpwtests04)

testcases/kernel/pty/ptem03.c (runtest: pty/ptem03)

  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: “send a break to both master and slave”.

testcases/kernel/pty/ptem06.c (runtest: pty/ptem06)

  • Category: WEAK (secondary: DOCS)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: “set baudrate to B0 (which means hang up)”.
  • Problem: Only checks that TCSETS with CBAUD=B0 succeeds. For a pty B0 has no hangup effect (pty has no set_termios hangup handling; the “hang up” semantics belong to hardware UART drivers), and the test does not check any effect on the master side (no POLLHUP, no EIO). The description promises something the test neither triggers nor verifies.
  • Evidence: test lines 27-30; drivers/tty/pty.c pty_set_termios only propagates termios/winsize.

testcases/kernel/pty/pty01.c (runtest: pty/pty01)

  • Category: WEAK (secondary: WRONG)
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: Data written to the master is read from the slave and data written to the slave is read from the master.
  • Problem: The slave keeps the default termios (ICANON|ECHO, OPOST|ONLCR). The first write “Linux Test Project” on the master is echoed by the slave line discipline back to the master as “Linux Test Project” and is queued on the master before the test ever writes on the slave. The second SAFE_READ(masterfd, string_len + 1) therefore returns the echo, not the slave’s write; the comparison passes regardless of whether the slave->master path delivered correct data (the slave’s own output simply remains unread). The comment about “kernel converts newline into carriage return + newline” is accidentally true for both. So half of the claimed coverage is not verified.
  • Evidence: test lines 29-42; /usr/src/linux/drivers/tty/n_tty.c echo path (n_tty_receive_char -> echo_char, commit_echoes writes to tty->ops->write of the slave = master read queue); default termios tty_std_termios in drivers/tty/tty_io.c (c_lflag includes ECHO).
  • Suggested action: clear ECHO on the slave (or drain the echoed line from the master) before the slave->master half, or compare with two distinct strings.

testcases/kernel/sched/cfs-scheduler/hackbench.c (runtest: sched/hackbench01, sched/hackbench02)

  • Category: WEAK (secondary: WRONG)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: “hackbench tests the Linux scheduler” (groups of 20 senders spraying 20 receivers over socketpairs/pipes).
  • Problem: This is a benchmark with no verification: data is not checked, the elapsed time is only printed. Worker failures are also not propagated in process mode: reap_worker() does wait(&status); if (!WIFEXITED(status)) exit(1);, so a worker that hits barf() (write/read/poll error -> exit(1)) is WIFEXITED and ignored, and main exits 0. Only death by signal (e.g. SIGPIPE) or a hang is detected.
  • Evidence: hackbench.c:89-93 (barf -> exit(1)), 221-235 (reap_worker checks WIFEXITED only), 374 (exit(0)).
  • Suggested action: check WIFEXITED(status) && WEXITSTATUS(status) == 0 in reap_worker; ideally port to the new API with a TPASS/TFAIL verdict, or document it as a stress/benchmark that only detects crashes and hangs.

testcases/kernel/sched/hyperthreading/ht_enabled/smt_smp_enabled.sh (runtest: hyperthreading/smt_smp_enabled)

  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: “tests whether HT/SMP is supported or not”.
  • Problem: No kernel behaviour is tested. ht_enabled checks CPUID.1:EDX bit 28 (HTT) and EBX[23:16]>=2, which is set on any multi-core package, not “SMT enabled”; then the script emits TPASS “SMT is enable” when /proc/cpuinfo “cpu cores” is 1 and TPASS “SMP System” when >=2. These are statements about the hardware, not kernel checks. Offline CPUs yield TCONF but exit 1 (a failure). Multi-valued “cpu cores” output breaks the [ ] tests.
  • Evidence: smt_smp_enabled.sh:36-77; ht_enabled/ht_utils.c is_ht_cpu() (CPUID HTT bit).
  • Suggested action: drop (with the whole runtest/hyperthreading file); if SMT coverage is wanted, test /sys/devices/system/cpu/smt/{control,active} per Documentation/ABI/testing/sysfs-devices-system-cpu.

testcases/kernel/sched/pthreads/pth_str03.c (runtest: sched/pth_str03)

  • Category: WEAK (secondary: WRONG)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: “create a tree of threads does calculations, and returns result to parent”.
  • Problem: Each node adds its children’s sum to its own, and main prints child_info[0].sum, but the value is never compared with the expected total (sum of 0..num_nodes-1 = total*(total-1)/2), so the “calculation” part verifies nothing. The summation is also racy: after joining info_p->threads[child] (creation order) it reads info_p->child_ptrs[child]->sum (registration order in synchronize_children), which can belong to a sibling that has not been joined yet, so a correct check would intermittently fail. Apart from that the test is identical to pth_str01.
  • Evidence: pth_str03.c:404-427 (join threads[child], read child_ptrs[child]->sum), 210 (sum initialised), 657-659 (sum only printed); synchronize_children child_ptrs[child_count++] assignment.
  • Suggested action: join all children first, then sum, and compare the root sum with total*(total-1)/2 (TFAIL on mismatch); otherwise drop as a duplicate of pth_str01.

testcases/kernel/sched/sched_stress/sched_driver.c (runtest: sched/sched_stress via sched_stress.sh)

  • Claim under test: scheduler stress: run throughput tests (tc4-tc6) at varying priorities while long-term (tc0, tc2) and short-term (tc1, tc3) load runs.
  • Problem: There is no pass/fail criterion: timings and percent deltas are printed and main always returns 0 (only fork/fopen errors exit non-zero). With the runtest arguments -s 0.9 -t 0.02 -p 2, available_user_process_slots() returns 2 (process_slots < processes in ps), workslots = (int)(2*0.9) = 1, long_term_slot_total = short_term_slot_total = 0, so the /4 loops never start tc0-tc3 and the “stress” is just sequential runs of tc4-tc6. The argv passed to tc0 is broken anyway ("sched_tc0 -t" as argv[0], " -p1" with leading space). Header says priorities 50-64; code uses 55-75. runtest comment says “2 minutes” but -t 0.02 h is 72 s.
  • Evidence: sched_driver.c main (workslots/long_term_slot_total), available_user_process_slots(), start_long_term_testcases(), start_short_term_testcases(); runtest/sched:17-18; sched_stress.sh:33.
  • Suggested action: drop the sched_stress suite, or define a verdict (e.g. all children exit 0 within a bound) and fix the slot arithmetic so the load generators actually run.

testcases/kernel/sched/sched_stress/sched_tc4.c (runtest: sched/sched_stress via sched_stress.sh -> sched_driver)

  • Category: WEAK (secondary: FRAGILE, WRONG)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: “short-term disk I/O bound process” whose elapsed time is reported to sched_driver for throughput comparison.
  • Problem: The whole sched_stress suite has no pass/fail criterion: sched_driver only prints elapsed times and %delta, and sched_stress.sh ends with rm -rf ..., so the runtest entry always exits 0 regardless of what the children do. In sched_tc4 the elapsed time is (time()-time())/100.0 (sched_tc4.c:149-154): the AIX original used times() ticks, the Linux port switched to time() seconds but kept the /100, so the logged number is 100x too small. The device read comes from RAWDEV=$(df / | grep dev | awk '{print $1}') (sched_stress.sh), which yields “overlay”/“tmpfs”/an LV path on many systems; open() then fails and the helper exits via sys_error, silently (the driver still “passes”).
  • Evidence: sched_tc4.c:149-154, :195-206; sched_stress.sh:30-35; sched_driver.c measure_test() (only reads the number back, no threshold).
  • Suggested action: Either give sched_stress a real criterion (e.g. TFAIL when a helper exits non-zero, detect a real block device or drop the raw-device case) or drop the suite as a legacy AIX benchmark port.

testcases/kernel/sched/sched_stress/sched_tc5.c (runtest: sched/sched_stress)

testcases/kernel/security/cap_bound/cap_bounds_rw.c (runtest: capability/cap_bounds)
