testcases/kernel/security/kallsyms/kallsyms.c (runtest: mm/kallsyms)

  • Category: WEAK (secondary: UNDEF)
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: user space cannot write to any kernel address listed in /proc/kallsyms.
  • Problem: /proc/kallsyms shows real addresses only when kallsyms_show_value() allows it (kptr_restrict=0/1 with CAP_SYSLOG). With kptr_restrict=2 (a common hardening setting), or under an LSM that denies CAP_SYSLOG, every address reads as 0. The test then just writes to NULL ~100k times and reports TPASS, with no check that any non-zero address was read. Also sscanf(line, "%lx %c %s", ..., name) writes into char name[128], but KSYM_NAME_LEN is 512 and Rust-enabled kernels have longer symbols, so it can overflow (C UB). The name is only used for messages.
  • Evidence: kallsyms.c:45-49, 83-86, 185-190; kernel/kallsyms.c:847,901 (show_value); include/linux/kallsyms.h:18 #define KSYM_NAME_LEN 512.
  • Suggested action: TCONF if all addresses are 0 (or temporarily set kptr_restrict=0); use a KSYM_NAME_LEN-sized buffer or %*s.

testcases/kernel/security/umip/umip_basic_test.c (runtest: kernel_misc/umip_basic_test)

  • Category: WEAK (secondary: DOCS)
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: “check if Intel UMIP is working” by executing SGDT/SIDT/SLDT/SMSW/STR in a child.
  • Problem: On any kernel >= 5.10 (all supported ones) every subtest passes as long as the child is not killed by SIGSEGV (lines 121-148). That outcome is identical whether UMIP is enforced and the kernel emulates the instruction, or UMIP is not enforced at all and the CPU executes it natively, so the test cannot tell “UMIP working” from “UMIP off”. The emulation returns fixed, documented dummy values (UMIP_DUMMY_GDT_BASE 0xfffffffffffe0000, UMIP_DUMMY_IDT_BASE 0xffffffffffff0000, SMSW returns CR0 image, SLDT/STR return fixed selectors) which the children never inspect; val is discarded. Also .min_kver = "4.1" is wrong: UMIP support landed in 4.16 and emulation for 64-bit in 5.4, and the “Got SIGSEGV -> TPASS” branch is dead on all supported kernels.
  • Evidence: test lines 35-80 (results discarded), 115-149; /usr/src/linux/arch/x86/kernel/umip.c:44-66 (dummy values), 198-216 emulate_umip_insn().
  • Suggested action: have the children print/return the stored value and compare against the kernel dummy values (or at least check SGDT/SIDT base equals the UMIP dummy base); drop the pre-5.4/5.10 branches and bump min_kver.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/adjtimex/adjtimex01.c (runtest: syscalls/adjtimex01)

  • Claim under test: adjtimex() works when setting offset, frequency, maxerror, esterror, status, timeconst and tick, and with ADJ_OFFSET_SINGLESHOT.
  • Problem: The test writes back the values it just read (with all SET_MODE bits) and only checks that the return value is a clock state from TIME_OK to TIME_ERROR. It never reads the parameters back to confirm they were applied. A kernel that ignored every write would pass. There is no docparse description.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/cachestat/cachestat01.c (runtest: syscalls/cachestat01)

  • Category: WEAK (secondary: WRONG)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: cachestat() counts cached and dirty pages correctly for files of 1..2^15 pages on every filesystem.
  • Problem: setup() computes (1lu << num_shift) * page_size / 1024, which is in KiB, and compares it with tst_device->size, which is in MiB (include/tst_device.h: “Device size in megabytes”). On the default 300 MB device with 4 KiB pages the loop stops at num_shift=7, so only files of 1..64 pages are tested. With 64 KiB pages it stops at num_shift=3, so only 1..4 pages are tested. Larger files, which would exercise the xarray walk across multiple nodes and large folios, are never tested.
  • Evidence: cachestat01.c:74-79; include/tst_device.h:18.
  • Suggested action: Compare in matching units, e.g. ((1lu << num_shift) * page_size) >> 20 >= tst_device->size, perhaps with a margin for fs metadata.

  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: capset() works with LINUX_CAPABILITY_VERSION_1/2/3.

  • Evidence: capset01.c:41-46.
  • Suggested action: Drop a capability (e.g. clear CAP_NET_RAW from pE), capset(), then capget() and check that the bit is gone. Run this for each version.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/chmod/chmod09.c (runtest: syscalls/chmod09)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: chmod() through /proc/self/fd/N of an O_PATH|O_NOFOLLOW symlink fd fails with EOPNOTSUPP, and neither the symlink nor its target changes mode (5d1f903f75a8), on all filesystems (.all_filesystems = 1, .mntpoint = “mntpoint”).

Each .all_filesystems iteration therefore formats and mounts a device that is never used and repeats the same check on the tmpdir filesystem. Filesystem-specific symlink setattr paths are never exercised.
  • Evidence: chmod09.c:15-16,24,48-49,63-64; fs/attr.c:457-458 (the check is in generic notify_change, so the result is fs-independent today, but the test claims per-fs coverage).

  • Claim under test: basic chown() on a file succeeds.

It never stats the file, and no ownership change takes place. chown02, chown03 and chown05 already cover successful chown() with stat() verification of uid/gid and mode.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/clock_getres/clock_getres01.c (runtest: syscalls/clock_getres01)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: clock_getres() works for 10 clock ids (and a NULL res) across libc/syscall/time64 variants, and fails with EINVAL for clock id -1.
  • Problem: (1) In the success cases the returned resolution in tspec is never examined: not that it is non-zero, not that it is <= 1 s, and not that the COARSE clocks report a resolution at least a tick. The test checks only the return value. (2) Any EINVAL from a success case becomes TCONF “NO SUPPORTED”. This is reasonable for the *_ALARM clocks (alarm_clock_getres() returns -EINVAL without an RTC), but it also hides a regression where CLOCK_REALTIME or CLOCK_MONOTONIC wrongly return EINVAL. Those clocks are mandatory, see clock_getres(2) / POSIX.
  • Evidence: clock_getres01.c:69-88.
  • Suggested action: Allow the EINVAL-to-TCONF path only for the *_ALARM clocks (and, if needed, the Linux-specific clocks on very old kernels). For success with a non-NULL res, check that 0 < res <= 1 s.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): UNCHANGED via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: 44/44 TPASS; musl: 44/44 TPASS, identical (incl. *_ALARM and -1). musl src/time/clock_getres.c:20 is a plain syscall, glibc goes via vDSO; the finding (res never examined, EINVAL->TCONF for every clock) is about test logic and unaffected

  • Problem: The test sleeps until now+10ms and only checks that the call returned 0. It never reads the clock afterwards, so an absolute sleep that returns early (or at once) still passes. Also, when the call fails it prints TFAIL and then, because there is no return, TPASS too.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/exit_group/exit_group01.c (runtest: syscalls/exit_group01)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: exit_group() ends the child and all its running threads.
  • Problem: The child calls exit_group() immediately after pthread_create(); there is no barrier ensuring the workers ever ran (counters may all be 0). The only real check is the exit status 4. check_counters() runs after waitpid(), which by definition returns only once the whole thread group has exited (group leader is a delayed zombie), so the counters cannot change; and even if they did the result is a TFAIL with no TPASS counterpart. The “all threads ended” claim is effectively unverified.
  • Evidence: exit_group01.c:44-50, :83-99, :52-76.
  • Suggested action: Have the child wait until every worker counter is non-zero before calling exit_group(); verify thread termination via e.g. the threads’ tids no longer existing (kill(tid,0)/ /proc//task) or keep the counter check but sample over a window and print TPASS.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/fanotify/fanotify12.c (runtest: syscalls/fanotify12)

  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: FAN_OPEN / FAN_OPEN_EXEC (plus ignore masks) produce the expected sequence of event masks for open() then execve() of marked files.
  • Problem: The verification loop while (FAN_EVENT_OK(event, len) && event_num < tc->event_count) exits silently when the buffer runs out. If fewer events than event_count arrive (e.g. the execve event with FAN_OPEN|FAN_OPEN_EXEC is never generated), the earlier events produce TPASS and nothing reports the missing event, so the test passes. Extra events beyond event_count are also never checked. (If the child fails, generate_events() returning 0 also jumps to cleanup without any result, though SAFE_* in the child reports TBROK itself.)
  • Evidence: fanotify12.c:187-217 (no post-loop check of event_num vs event_count or of remaining len); compare fanotify13.c:368 which does check for a missing expected event.
  • Suggested action: after the loop, TFAIL if event_num < tc->event_count, and TFAIL if FAN_EVENT_OK(event, len) still holds (unexpected extra events).

testcases/kernel/syscalls/fanotify/fanotify19.c (runtest: syscalls/fanotify19)

The post-loop check only detects extra events.
  • Evidence: fanotify19.c:199-257.
  • Suggested action: after the loop, TFAIL for each test_number < tc->event_count (“didn’t get event”), as fanotify15/16 do.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/fcntl/fcntl24.c (runtest: syscalls/fcntl24, fcntl24_64; same issue in fcntl25, fcntl26)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: high

Kernel commit 387e3746d01c (“locks: eliminate false positive conflicts for write lease”, v5.3) replaced it with i_readcount/i_writecount. On current kernels write leases work on tmpfs/ramfs/overlayfs. The tests now skip on common TMPDIR setups (tmpfs /tmp, overlayfs containers), and a real overlayfs lease regression would pass silently. fcntl24/25/26 are also line-for-line copies that differ only in the open() flags.
  • Evidence: fcntl24.c:121-128 (TCONF on NFS/RAMFS/TMPFS), 146-149 (overlayfs EAGAIN -> TINFO); fs/locks.c:609-634 lease_open_conflict() uses i_writecount/i_readcount only; git describe --contains 387e3746d01c = v5.3-rc1.
  • Suggested action: limit the tmpfs/ramfs skip and the overlayfs EAGAIN exception to kernels < 5.3 (tst_kvercmp); merge fcntl24/25/26 into one new-API test with three open-mode tcases.

  • Claim under test: fork() must keep failing once the merged anonymous VMA exceeds 16 TB (dup_mmap length overflow, 7edc8b0ac16c).
  • Problem: TFAIL needs a fork() failure followed by a success at i >= 16K. fork() only fails here through VM_ACCOUNT in dup_mmap() under heuristic overcommit (mode 0, pages > RAM+swap). With vm.overcommit_memory=1, __vm_enough_memory() always returns 0, so fork() never fails, prev_failed is never set, and the test prints TPASS without exercising the bug. The same happens if the 1 GB mmaps do not merge into one VMA. The test neither sets overcommit_memory nor checks that any fork() failed.
  • Evidence: fork14.c:58-93; mm/util.c:969-976; mm/mmap.c:1758.
  • Suggested action: Add .save_restore for /proc/sys/vm/overcommit_memory = 0, and report TCONF (not TPASS) if no fork() failure was observed before i reached LARGE.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/io_pgetevents/io_pgetevents01.c (runtest: syscalls/io_pgetevents01)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium (phase 1: low)

Because the sigset is emptied with sigemptyset() its first 16 bytes are zero, so the kernel reads {NULL, 0} and never installs a mask. The test therefore exercises only io_getevents() semantics; the sigmask part (the reason io_pgetevents exists) is untested. io_pgetevents02 has the same mixup (its “invalid sigmask” case still validly gets EFAULT from copy_from_user).
  • Evidence: io_pgetevents01.c:43,59; include/lapi/io_pgetevents.h:19-24; /usr/src/linux/fs/aio.c:2329-2350 (copy_from_user(&ksig, usig, sizeof(ksig))).
  • Suggested action: pass a struct __aio_sigset {&sigmask, _NSIG/8} and ideally add a case that checks the mask is applied during the wait.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION. HPE: as-is TPASS. Work copy adding sigaddset(&sigmask, SIGUSR1) to the ‘sigmask’: ‘TFAIL: io_pgetevents() failed: EINVAL’ -> kernel reads the sigset_t as struct __aio_sigset {sigmask=0x200, sigsetsize=0} (fs/aio.c copy_from_user + set_user_sigmask size check). With an empty set it reads {NULL,0}: mask never applied.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): UNCHANGED via MUSL,BULK,RUN,BUILD. HPE glibc: PASS (rc 0); musl: ‘TCONF: test requires libaio and it’s development packages’ (rc 32), 2/2 runs. Artefact of the musl build env: HAVE_LIBAIO undef in /root/ltp-musl/include/config.h (no libaio in /usr/x86_64-linux-musl); ci/alpine.sh installs it, so upstream musl CI builds it. Nothing learned about the finding

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: kill() with a negative pid kills the whole process group.
  • Problem: The child creates 5 group members and calls kill(-getpgrp(), SIGKILL). The parent checks only that this child died with SIGKILL. A kernel that delivered the signal only to the caller would also pass. The 5 grandchildren are never waited for or checked, and if they survived they would leak as pause()d orphans.

  • Suggested action: Collect the grandchildren’s pids (e.g., the group leader forks them and the test reaps them via a subreaper or checks /proc or kill(pid,0)==ESRCH after the leader’s wait), or merge with kill08.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/kill/kill10.c (runtest: syscalls/kill10)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: low
  • Claim under test: signal flooding between many processes works (every manager hears from every child).
  • Problem: The test has no TFAIL path. The master prints TPASS once child_signal_counter reaches num_pgrps, so a lost or misrouted signal shows up only as an endless pause()/alarm(1) loop that ends in a harness timeout. The handshake flags (create_procs_flag, signal_parents_flag, confirmed_ready_flag, child_signal_counter) are plain ints written from signal handlers. This works only because the polling loops call external functions. There is a sleep(1) “to let all the children pause”.
  • Evidence: kill10.c:256-264, 494-500, 537, 566-577, 710-713.
  • Suggested action: Convert to the new API with a bounded wait that reports TFAIL, and use volatile sig_atomic_t flags; or drop it as low-value legacy stress.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,VIRT,READ. HPE+VIRT: kill10 ‘TPASS All 2 pgrps received their signals’. grep: the only result calls are tst_resm(TPASS) l.263 and TBROK for option/setup errors; no TFAIL path, lost signals only spin in alarm(1)/pause() loops (l.257-261, 495-499, 581-585, 711-712) until harness timeout; flags are plain int (l.198-200). Finding holds.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/landlock/landlock06.c (runtest: syscalls/landlock06)

  • Category: WEAK (secondary: DOCS)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: LANDLOCK_ACCESS_FS_IOCTL_DEV access works, by creating a pipe and checking that ioctl() can be run on it.
  • Problem: Both fds (a regular file and /dev/zero) are opened before the ruleset is enforced, and the only ioctls issued are FIONREAD on a regular file plus FIOCLEX/FIONCLEX/FIONBIO/FIOASYNC. The uapi docs list these as always allowed regardless of IOCTL_DEV, and they would also be allowed on a pre-opened fd. The test therefore passes with or without the access right, and it never checks that a driver ioctl on a device opened after enforcement, outside the allowed hierarchy, is denied. The description says it creates a pipe, but the code creates a regular file named “fifo” with SAFE_TOUCH.
  • Evidence: landlock06.c:24-57; include/uapi/linux/landlock.h:309-322 (“the following common IOCTL commands continue to be invokable independent of the LANDLOCK_ACCESS_FS_IOCTL_DEV right”).
  • Suggested action: After enforcement, open a char device outside the allowed path and verify that a device ioctl (e.g., TCGETS on /dev/tty or a /dev/null driver ioctl) fails with EACCES, and that the same ioctl is allowed on a device inside the allowed hierarchy. Keep the always-allowed checks, and fix the description.

Its 2 cases are a subset of lseek02’s 15 (EBADF x3, EINVAL x3, ESPIPE x9); only difference is Makefile CFLAGS -D_FILE_OFFSET_BITS=64, which on 64-bit maps lseek to the same syscall. Only adds coverage of _llseek on 32-bit ABIs. Finding holds.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/lsm/lsm_set_self_attr01.c (runtest: syscalls/lsm_set_self_attr01)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: lsm_set_self_attr() rejects NULL ctx, too-small/too-big size, non-zero flags and an invalid attr.
  • Problem: Every case only checks that the return is -1 (TST_EXP_EXPR(... == -1)). The errno is never checked, even for the four cases that the common code rejects before any LSM hook runs (flags -> EINVAL, size < sizeof(lsm_ctx) -> EINVAL, size > PAGE_SIZE -> E2BIG, NULL -> EFAULT). Commit 5b884412ecd3 dropped the errno checks because LSMs return different errnos, but that only applies to the hook dispatch. Also, the “attr is invalid” case passes size=page_size, while ctx is a guarded buffer of LSM_CTX_SIZE_DEFAULT (4096+header) bytes. On 64K-page systems memdup_user() therefore faults into the guard page and returns EFAULT, so the invalid-attr path is never reached and the case still passes.
  • Evidence: lsm_set_self_attr01.c:73-76,229-231; security/security.c:3826-3835 (flags/size/E2BIG/memdup_user checks before the hook loop at :3844); include/lapi/lsm.h:18-21.
  • Suggested action: Use TST_EXP_FAIL with EINVAL/EINVAL/E2BIG/EFAULT for the first four cases. For the invalid-attr case, pass the real ctx length (ctx_orig->len) so the hook is reached, and accept any errno only there.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/madvise/madvise01.c (runtest: syscalls/madvise01)

  • Category: WEAK (secondary: FRAGILE)
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: madvise() succeeds for a list of advice values.
  • Problem: This is a success-only smoke test, and every EINVAL is reported as TCONF “not supported”. So EINVAL regressions are hidden for advice that must be supported (MADV_REMOVE on tmpfs, MADV_DONTNEED, MADV_COLD/PAGEOUT on >=5.4, MADV_FREE). Nothing checks what the advice actually did. In addition, MADV_HWPOISON runs as root on the shared tmpfs mapping. With CONFIG_MEMORY_FAILURE=y this really calls memory_failure() on every page (10 pages per iteration), which permanently poisons host pages and prints “Memory failure” to dmesg. With -i N it repeats each iteration. That is a host side effect for a “returns 0” check.
  • Evidence: madvise01.c:46,102-104; mm/madvise.c:1462-1492 (madvise_inject_error -> memory_failure(pfn, MF_ACTION_REQUIRED|…|MF_SW_SIMULATED)).
  • Suggested action: Drop MADV_HWPOISON from the list (or use MADV_SOFT_OFFLINE / a dedicated test). Turn EINVAL into TCONF only for advice that has a real config dependency (KSM, THP, HWPOISON); report TFAIL otherwise.

  • Claim under test: MADV_WILLNEED on swapped-out shmem brings pages into swap cache so that accessing them causes no page faults (regression for 55231e5c898c5, 66383800df9c).

The only check that can fail is the generic kernel taint check, which always gives a TPASS. On a kernel with the original bug the test still passes. The header comment still says “two checks are performed” and that a SwapCached increase is “expected”.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/madvise/madvise08.c (runtest: syscalls/madvise08)

  • Category: WEAK (secondary: DOCS)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: memory marked MADV_DONTDUMP is left out of a core dump, and “the same memory then marked with MADV_DODUMP” is included again.
  • Problem: Each subtest forks a fresh child from the parent. MADV_DONTDUMP is only applied in the first child, so the second child’s mapping never has VM_DONTDUMP. In that child, MADV_DODUMP is a no-op, and the DODUMP subtest just checks the default behaviour (anonymous private memory is dumped). A broken MADV_DODUMP that fails to clear VM_DONTDUMP would still pass. The header text describes a sequence (DONTDUMP then DODUMP on the same memory) that the code never runs.
  • Evidence: madvise08.c:250-268 (each run_child forks from the untouched parent and calls a single madvise), :286-300; mm/madvise.c MADV_DODUMP only clears VM_DONTDUMP.
  • Suggested action: In the DODUMP child, call madvise(MADV_DONTDUMP) first and then madvise(MADV_DODUMP) before abort(). Alternatively apply DONTDUMP in the parent before the second fork.

  • Suggested action: rewrite to the new API. After each call, check that VmLck grew to roughly VmSize (MCL_CURRENT), or that a new mmap is locked (MCL_FUTURE). Call munlockall() between cases.

That check is obsolete given the LTP minimum kernel, and it is also buggy: it compares the first characters as chars, so a release such as “10.0” gives ‘1’-‘2’ < 0 and the whole test TCONFs.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/mmap/mmap09.c (runtest: syscalls/mmap09)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: truncating an mmapped file (shrink, grow, to 0) “works correctly”.
  • Problem: The only assertion is that ftruncate() returns 0, which it does on any open writable file whether or not it is mapped. The test never accesses the mapping afterwards, so it does not check any mmap-related semantics: SIGBUS beyond the new EOF, zero-filled tail after growing, or data kept below the new size.
  • Evidence: mmap09.c:37-42.
  • Suggested action: after each ftruncate, check the mapping (SIGBUS past EOF with sigsetjmp, ‘A’ below the new size, zeros after a grow), or drop.

That case calls tst_brk(TCONF) when KSM is missing, which also skips the following anon+KSM case. On kernels without CONFIG_KSM the test never maps /dev/zero. The description still talks about “an option”. The pass condition is only “did not crash”.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/mmap/mmap12.c (runtest: syscalls/mmap12)

  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: mmap(MAP_POPULATE) “should succeed … The file should be read into RAM, and pages should be present.”
  • Problem: The present-bit check on /proc/self/pagemap only prints TINFO; a missing page never causes a failure. The only real assertion is that a freshly ftruncate()d sparse file reads as zeros, which any mmap test covers. mmap(2) does allow MAP_POPULATE to fail silently, so the docparse claim “pages should be present” is not a hard guarantee either. The test therefore checks almost nothing specific to MAP_POPULATE.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/msgctl/msgctl12.c (runtest: syscalls/msgctl12)

  • Category: WEAK (secondary: WRONG)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: msgctl() IPC_INFO, MSG_INFO and MSG_STAT work.
  • Problem: The test only checks that each call does not return -1. It never checks the msginfo contents (e.g. msgmax/msgmnb/msgmni against /proc/sys/kernel/msg*), or that MSG_STAT returns a valid msqid and fills msqid_ds. On failure, verify_msgctl() prints TFAIL and then falls through to an unconditional TPASS (no return). MSG_STAT is called on the highest used index returned by IPC_INFO. That index can belong to another user’s queue, so a non-root run can get a spurious EACCES. msgctl06 already covers MSG_INFO + MSG_STAT_ANY more thoroughly.
  • Evidence: msgctl12.c:38-44 (TFAIL without return, then TPASS); msgctl12.c:50 (index_q = max index of the whole namespace).
  • Suggested action: use TST_EXP_POSITIVE/TST_EXP_PASS. Compare IPC_INFO fields with /proc/sys/kernel/msgmax, msgmnb, msgmni. Check that MSG_STAT returns msg_q’s id when applied to msg_q’s own index. Otherwise merge into msgctl06.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/msgget/msgget05.c (runtest: syscalls/msgget05)

  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: when msg_next_id names an id already in use, msgget() still succeeds and allocates another id.
  • Problem: The only assertion is queue_id[1] != queue_id[0]. That always holds: the IPC idr can never return an index that is in use (ipc/util.c:255 ipc_idr_alloc() calls idr_alloc(start=ipcid_to_idx(next_id), end=ipc_mni) and takes the next free slot). So the test effectively checks only that msgget() did not fail. It does not check that msg_next_id was reset to -1 after the allocation (the documented behavior that msgget04 does check).
  • Evidence: msgget05.c:28-41; ipc/util.c:207-208,253-256; Documentation/admin-guide/sysctl/kernel.rst (msg_next_id).
  • Suggested action: add TST_ASSERT_INT(NEXT_ID_PATH, -1) after the allocation, or merge into msgget04 as a second subcase.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/msync/msync01.c (runtest: syscalls/msync01)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: msync() succeeds on part of a mapped region “and successfully synchronize[s] the memory region”.
  • Problem: The test writes through a MAP_SHARED mapping, calls msync(MS_ASYNC), then read()s the same file. On Linux the mapping and read() share the same page cache folio, so the read sees the data whether or not msync() did anything; msync(MS_ASYNC) is effectively a no-op on modern kernels. The only real check is that msync() returns 0. Also, err_flg is never reset between -i iterations.
  • Evidence: msync01.c:103-138; mm/msync.c:58-62 (“if the flag is MS_ASYNC (w/o MS_INVALIDATE) … nothing left to do”); msync(2) NOTES (since 2.6.19 MS_ASYNC is a no-op).
  • Suggested action: merge into msync04 (which checks dirty state via /proc/kpageflags), or drop. At minimum, describe it as a “return value only” smoke test.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/msync/msync02.c (runtest: syscalls/msync02)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: msync(MS_INVALIDATE) on a shared mapping succeeds and the mapping then holds the data written to the file.
  • Problem: The data is written with write() after mmap(). Because the page cache is unified, the mapping already shows that data before msync() is called, so the memcmp passes even if msync(MS_INVALIDATE) is a no-op (which it is on Linux, apart from the EBUSY check for locked VMAs). Only the return value is effectively tested.
  • Evidence: msync02.c:94-101, 138-143; mm/msync.c (MS_INVALIDATE only triggers -EBUSY for VM_LOCKED).
  • Suggested action: reword as a return-value smoke test, or drop/merge with msync03 (EBUSY path) and msync04.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/munlock/munlock01.c (runtest: syscalls/munlock01)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: munlock() works with various valid addresses and lengths.
  • Problem: The test only checks that munlock() returns 0 after a successful mlock(). It never checks that the pages are actually unlocked (VmLck in /proc/self/status, or mincore/pagemap). It is a line-for-line mirror of mlock01, which already does mlock() of the same sizes from malloc’ed memory.
  • Evidence: munlock01.c:31-33; mlock/mlock01.c (same tcases).
  • Suggested action: read VmLck before and after munlock and require it to drop. Or merge mlock01/munlock01 into one test that checks VmLck goes up and then down.

E.g. if nftw passed FTW_D instead of FTW_DP under FTW_DEPTH, test11A would PASS. test_func14 is fully vacuous because test14A walks d333 and no d333 path is in badlist. test_func15 passes if d666/errs is never reported at all.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/pipe/pipe09.c (runtest: syscalls/pipe09)

  • Category: WEAK (secondary: DOCS)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: “Check that two processes can use the same pipe at the same time.”
  • Problem: the parent forks child 1, waits for it to exit (SAFE_WAITPID), then forks child 2 and waits for it too, then reads. The two writers never run concurrently, so the test only checks that 50+50 one-byte writes from two sequential processes end up in the pipe, already covered by pipe01/pipe10/pipe11. There is no interleaving or concurrency check.
  • Evidence: pipe09.c:101-153 (waitpid(fork_1) at :123 before fork #2 at :128)

testcases/kernel/syscalls/pselect/pselect03.c (runtest: syscalls/pselect03)

  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: “basic test for pselect() returning without error”.

The test accepts any ret >= 0 and never checks that the regular file is reported readable. It verifies nothing beyond “the syscall exists”, which pselect01/pselect02 already cover.
  • Evidence: pselect03.c:27-31; select(2) DESCRIPTION, nfds
  • Suggested action: call pselect(fd + 1, …) and require ret == 1 && FD_ISSET(fd, &readfds) (regular files are always readable), or drop the test.

TPASS : TFAIL. local_flag is never set to FAILED anywhere, and no return value is checked. The test only fails if the kernel crashes or hangs. The parent synchronises with pause() for SIGALRM, and the result is always TPASS.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/rt_sigaction/rt_sigaction01.c (runtest: syscalls/rt_sigaction01)

  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: rt_sigaction() changes the action for a signal and saves the previous action in oact, for SIGRTMIN..SIGRTMAX with SA_RESETHAND/SA_SIGINFO/SA_NOMASK.
  • Problem: The only assertion is that rt_sigaction() returns 0. After kill(getpid(), sig) the handler just prints TINFO. Nothing checks that the handler actually ran, that SA_RESETHAND restored SIG_DFL, or that oldaction holds the previously installed handler and flags. A broken kernel that accepted the call but ignored the action would pass. test_flags lists the same combination three times.
  • Evidence: rt_sigaction01.c set_handler() and main loop (if (TEST_RETURN == 0) TPASS); handler() only calls tst_resm(TINFO).

  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): NEW (second finding, secondary category UNDEF/high; primary kept) via MUSL,BULK,RUN,SRC. Secondary to WEAK/medium (unaffected). HPE glibc: PASS; musl: ‘timeout: the monitored command dumped core (rc 139, no TPASS)’ 2/2. lapi/rt_sigaction.h:65-83 sig_initial() takes restore_rt from oact.sa_restorer of libc sigaction(); glibc copies it back (x86_64/libc_sigaction.c:29), musl does not (src/signal/sigaction.c:56-58): probe shows 0xa5a5.. garbage -> handler return jumps there
  • Verification conclusion: New finding in include/lapi/rt_sigaction.h (shared by rt_sigaction01/02/03, rt_sigprocmask01, rt_sigsuspend01 via safe_rt_signal.h): on x86_64 the SA_RESTORER address is scraped from libc’s struct sigaction, which only glibc fills in. Under musl it is uninitialised stack, so every test that actually delivers a signal crashes (02/03 only test error paths and pass). Action: provide LTP’s own rt_sigreturn trampoline on x86_64 (as already done for arc/sparc) instead of relying on glibc filling oact.sa_restorer.

  • Claim under test: two processes contend for a binary semaphore (“fighting for control”).
  • Problem: Nothing checks mutual exclusion. Both processes run semdown/usleep/semup 1000 times through SAFE_SEMOP, and the only TPASS is TST_EXP_POSITIVE(semctl(IPC_RMID)). A kernel that let both processes into the critical section at once would still pass. The fixed key 9142 with IPC_CREAT (no IPC_EXCL) can also attach to a leftover or foreign set.
  • Evidence: semop04.c:50-59 (no shared state checked), :68 (fixed key), :82 (only result).
  • Suggested action: use a shared counter/flag (e.g. mmap MAP_SHARED) incremented inside the critical section and assert it never exceeds 1; use IPC_PRIVATE.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/set_tid_address/set_tid_address01.c (runtest: syscalls/set_tid_address01)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: “Verify the basic functionality of set_tid_address() syscall.”
  • Problem: The test only checks that the return value is the caller’s TID. The syscall’s real purpose is never exercised: it stores clear_child_tid, and on thread exit the kernel zeroes *tidptr and does a futex wake. A kernel that ignored tidptr completely would still pass.
  • Evidence: set_tid_address01.c:12-16; set_tid_address(2): “When a thread whose clear_child_tid is not NULL terminates, then, if the thread is sharing memory with other threads, then 0 is written at the address specified in clear_child_tid and the kernel performs the following operation: futex(clear_child_tid, FUTEX_WAKE, …)”.
  • Suggested action: Strengthen it. Create a thread or a CLONE_VM child that calls set_tid_address(&shared) and exits, then check that the shared word becomes 0 (or wait on it with FUTEX_WAIT).

testcases/kernel/syscalls/setgid/setgid01.c (runtest: syscalls/setgid01, setgid01_16)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium (phase 1: low)
  • Claim under test: “Calls setgid() with current gid and expects success.”
  • Problem: The call is a no-op (gid == current rgid), so only the 0 return is checked. Changing the gid is covered with verification by setgid03 (root -> nobody, checked with getgid()).
  • Evidence: setgid01.c:17-25; setgid03.c:93-100.
  • Suggested action: Merge into setgid03 as an extra subcase, or drop.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,READ,VIRT. VIRT as-is ‘setgid01.c:19: TPASS: SETGID(gid) passed’ where gid = getgid() (no-op). No post-check; setgid03 covers root->nobody with getgid() verification

testcases/kernel/syscalls/setgroups/setgroups01.c (runtest: syscalls/setgroups01, setgroups01_16)

  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: “Check the basic functionality of the setgroups() system call.”
  • Problem: The test calls SETGROUPS(1, list) with list taken from getgroups(), or zeros when there are none, and only checks ret >= 0. It never checks the resulting group list. setgroups02 does the same call and verifies it with getgroups().
  • Evidence: setgroups01.c:134-144; setgroups02.c:170-181.
  • Suggested action: Drop it as a duplicate of setgroups02, or add a getgroups() comparison.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/setpgrp/setpgrp01.c (runtest: syscalls/setpgrp01)

  • Category: WEAK

  • Claim under test: setpgrp() succeeds when the caller is not a process group leader.
  • Problem: The test only checks that setpgrp() returns 0. It never checks that getpgrp() == getpid() afterwards. setpgrp02 does the same call in a forked child and also verifies the pgrp changed.
  • Evidence: setpgrp01.c:252-262; setpgrp02.c:316-324.
  • Suggested action: Drop it as a duplicate of setpgrp02.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/setsockopt/setsockopt03.c (runtest: syscalls/setsockopt03, cve/cve-2016-4997)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: CVE-2016-4997 (compat IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE target_offset out-of-bounds) does not crash the kernel.
  • Problem: run() always reports TPASS (“We didn’t cause a crash”) whatever setsockopt() returned, and the test has no .taint_check. A non-fatal OOB write or a WARN on a vulnerable kernel goes unnoticed. The test also passes without touching the vulnerable code: when CONFIG_IP_NF_IPTABLES (legacy ip_tables) is missing, setsockopt returns ENOPROTOOPT, and on a native 64-bit build it is not the compat path (only a TINFO is printed).
  • Evidence: setsockopt03.c:47-51, 71-73, 76-85 (no taint_check); compare setsockopt05/06/08/09, which use .taint_check = TST_TAINT_W | TST_TAINT_D.
  • Suggested action: Add .taint_check = TST_TAINT_W | TST_TAINT_D. TCONF on ENOPROTOOPT. TCONF, or at least report differently, when not in compat mode.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/setuid/setuid01.c (runtest: syscalls/setuid01, setuid01_16)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium (phase 1: low)
  • Claim under test: “Verify that setuid(2) returns 0 and effective uid has been set successfully as a normal or super user.”
  • Problem: The test only calls setuid(getuid()), which changes nothing, and checks for a 0 return. It never checks the effective uid, even though the description says so. The real transitions are covered by setuid03/04 and setreuid04.
  • Evidence: setuid01.c:125-133.
  • Suggested action: Add a geteuid() check, or merge into another test and drop.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,READ,VIRT. VIRT as-is ‘setuid01.c:25: TPASS: setuid(0) passed’ = setuid(getuid()) no-op; doc block claims ‘effective uid has been set successfully’ but no geteuid() check exists (source has only TST_EXP_PASS(SETUID(uid)))

testcases/kernel/syscalls/shutdown/shutdown01.c (runtest: syscalls/shutdown01)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: SHUT_RD / SHUT_RDWR disable recv() on the socket.
  • Problem: For SHUT_RD and SHUT_RDWR the test calls SAFE_RECV(0, client_sock, buff, MSGSIZE, 0). With len==0 safe_recv() accepts any non-negative return value (lib/safe_net.c:291), so the expected end-of-file (recv() returning 0) is never asserted. A broken SHUT_RD would only be noticed indirectly by a blocking recv() hanging until the test timeout (reported as TBROK timeout, not TFAIL).
  • Evidence: shutdown01.c:91-92; lib/safe_net.c:276-297.
  • Suggested action: use TST_EXP_EQ_SSZ(recv(…, MSG_DONTWAIT), 0) for the SHUT_RD/SHUT_RDWR cases.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/splice/splice02.c (runtest: syscalls/splice02)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: low)
  • Claim under test: data spliced from stdin pipe into a file has the right size and content.
  • Problem: In the content loop, to_check for the last block is st.st_size % page_size. When the file size is a multiple of the page size (always true for the default 16 * pipe size), that is 0, so the last page is never compared.
  • Evidence: splice02.c:95-96; default size at splice02.c:126-127.
  • Suggested action: use min(page_size, st_size - block*page_size) for to_check.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION. HPE: as-is TPASS. Copy that pwrite()s a wrong byte at st_size-1 (last page) after splicing: still ‘TPASS: splice() system call passed’. Control copy corrupting a byte one page earlier: ‘TFAIL: 1 unexpected bytes found’ -> last page (to_check = st_size % page_size = 0) is never compared

testcases/kernel/syscalls/splice/splice06.c (runtest: syscalls/splice06)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: splice() read/write of /proc/sys files (pipe-max-size, domainname).
  • Problem: setup() calls file_write_num(PATH_KERN_DOMAINNAME, PIPE_MAX_INIT_SIZE). The intended path is clearly PATH_FS_PIPE_MAX_SIZE, so domainname is overwritten with “65536” right after being set to “LTP_INIT”, and pipe-max-size is never initialised. All functional mismatches are reported with tst_brk(TBROK | TERRNO), not TFAIL (with a meaningless errno). The string checks compare only strlen(buf_file) bytes, so a truncated read/write (e.g. “LTP”) still passes.
  • Evidence: splice06.c:173-204,207-212.
  • Suggested action: fix the path in setup, report mismatches as TFAIL, and compare full strings (strcmp after trimming the trailing newline).

testcases/kernel/syscalls/statfs/statfs01.c (runtest: syscalls/statfs01)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: statfs() works on all available filesystems.
  • Problem: The test only asserts that statfs() returns 0. It never checks any returned field, e.g. f_type against the known magic of tst_device->fs_type, f_bsize > 0, f_bfree <= f_blocks, or f_namelen. A kernel returning garbage would pass.
  • Evidence: statfs01.c:27-32.
  • Suggested action: verify at least f_type against the expected magic and basic consistency of block/inode counts (cf. fstatfs tests).

testcases/kernel/syscalls/statx/statx10.c

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium
  • Found in phase 3 verification (not flagged by the phase-1 reading).
  • Verdict: NEW (WEAK, medium) [category before this check: OK/high]
  • Method: MUSL, BULK, RUN, SRC, BUILD
  • Ran:
ltprun-musl statx10; ltprun-glibc statx10   (bare-metal host, musl and glibc builds)
  • Observed:
musl : statx10.c:50: TCONF: glibc statx struct miss stx_dio_mem_align field
glibc: PASS
config.h musl: /* #undef HAVE_STRUCT_STATX_STX_DIO_MEM_ALIGN */
  • Conclusion: New (minor) finding: the test #ifdefs on the libc struct and TCONFs, although LTP’s lapi already provides struct ltp_statx with stx_dio_mem_align/stx_dio_offset_align for exactly this case. Under musl (or any libc with an older struct statx) the STATX_DIOALIGN check is skipped, and the TCONF text blames glibc. Action: use struct ltp_statx (sx.data.stx_dio_*) like the statmount tests and drop the #ifdef.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): NEW via MUSL,BULK,RUN,SRC,BUILD. HPE glibc: PASS; musl: ‘TCONF: glibc statx struct miss stx_dio_mem_align field’ (rc 32). musl 1.2.5 struct statx (include/sys/stat.h:129-150) lacks stx_dio_, so HAVE_STRUCT_STATX_STX_DIO_MEM_ALIGN is undef; the test ignores the existing lapi/stat.h:99-116 struct ltp_statx fallback (used by statmount/listmount*). Not a false FAIL, but zero coverage and wrong text

testcases/kernel/syscalls/string/string01.c (runtest: syscalls/string01)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: Functionality of strchr, strrchr, strcat, strcmp, strcpy, strlen, strncat, strncmp and strncpy.

The strncmp check is also partly ineffective: for {yat, tiat, 8, 0, 1} (first 8 bytes equal, expected 0) any positive return is accepted, because the fallback only fails when n < a_res.
  • Evidence: string01.c:172-185 (a_res table), 397-408 (fallback logic)
  • Suggested action: Drop from syscalls (libc test suites cover these functions), or at least fix the strncmp tolerance to check the sign of the result.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): UNCHANGED via MUSL,RUN. HPE glibc: ‘string01 1 TPASS : Test passed’; musl: same. Pure libc string test under both; the strncmp tolerance flaw is in the test’s fallback logic and no libc difference surfaced

testcases/kernel/syscalls/symlink/symlink02.c (runtest: syscalls/symlink02)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: Basic functionality of symlink().
  • Problem: It only checks that symlink() returns >= 0 (and TST_EXP_POSITIVE accepts any non-negative value, although 0 is the only valid success). It never verifies that a link was created or what it points to. symlink04 covers the same call with an lstat()/S_ISLNK check, and symlink05/readlink tests verify the contents.
  • Evidence: symlink02.c:17-25; symlink04.c:41-49
  • Suggested action: Merge into symlink04 or drop. At minimum use TST_EXP_PASS and readlink() the result.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/sysconf/sysconf01.c (runtest: syscalls/sysconf01)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: sysconf() returns values for 55 SC* names and EINVAL for an invalid name.
  • Problem: This is a glibc test: most SC* values are compile-time glibc constants and never reach the kernel. Any value other than -1 counts as TPASS, so nothing is validated (e.g. _SC_PAGESIZE is not compared with getpagesize(), _SC_OPEN_MAX not with RLIMIT_NOFILE). _SC_MEMORY_PROTECTION is tested twice (lines 139 and 142).
  • Evidence: sysconf01.c:44-76, 139-142
  • Suggested action: Drop, or reduce to the kernel-backed names (_SC_PAGESIZE, _SC_OPEN_MAX, _SC_CHILD_MAX, SC_NPROCESSORS*, _SC_PHYS_PAGES) and compare them with the kernel sources (getrlimit, sysinfo, /sys/devices/system/cpu).
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE same source, different values, all PASS/TCONF: _SC_ARG_MAX glibc 2097152 (rlimit/4, linux/sysconf.c:56-63) vs musl 131072 (constant, conf/sysconf.c:192-193); XOPEN_XCU_VERSION 4 vs 700; COLL_WEIGHTS_MAX 255 vs 2; RE_DUP_MAX 32767 vs 255; STREAM_MAX 16 vs TCONF; musl 20 TCONFs. Libc constants, nothing validated

testcases/kernel/syscalls/sysfs/sysfs01.c (runtest: syscalls/sysfs01)

testcases/kernel/syscalls/sysfs/sysfs03.c (runtest: syscalls/sysfs03)

testcases/kernel/syscalls/timer_getoverrun/timer_getoverrun01.c (runtest: syscalls/timer_getoverrun01)

  • Claim under test: “base timer_getoverrun() functionality”.

The only other check is EINVAL after timer_delete. timer_settime03 covers overrun capping, but no test checks a normal small overrun count.
  • Evidence: timer_getoverrun01.c:125-143
  • Suggested action: Arm a periodic timer with SIGALRM blocked, sleep for N intervals, and check that timer_getoverrun() returns about N-1 after the signal is accepted (sigwait).

testcases/kernel/syscalls/timerfd/timerfd02.c (runtest: syscalls/timerfd02)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: low)
  • Claim under test: TFD_CLOEXEC / TFD_NONBLOCK set the corresponding fd flags (and flags=0 sets neither).
  • Problem: The flags=0 subcase checks (fcntl(F_GETFD) & 0) == 0, which is always true, so it cannot detect a spurious FD_CLOEXEC. The positive subcases are fine.
  • Evidence: timerfd02.c:188, 198
  • Suggested action: For flags=0, check (F_GETFD & FD_CLOEXEC) == 0 and (F_GETFL & O_NONBLOCK) == 0.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION. HPE: as-is 6/6 TPASS; work copy creates the flags=0 timerfd with TFD_CLOEXEC|TFD_NONBLOCK -> still 6/6 TPASS (‘SAFE_FCNTL(fdesc, tcase->check) & tcase->expected == tcase->expected (0)’), so a spurious FD_CLOEXEC is never detected

testcases/kernel/syscalls/times/times01.c (runtest: syscalls/times01)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: “Phase I” times(2) test.
  • Problem: It only checks that times() does not return -1. The struct tms contents are never examined. times03 already calls times() and validates user/system/children times, so this test adds nothing.
  • Evidence: times01.c:13-23; times/times03.c
  • Suggested action: Drop (covered by times03).

testcases/kernel/syscalls/ulimit/ulimit01.c (runtest: syscalls/ulimit01)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: basic functionality of ulimit(3) UL_GETFSIZE and UL_SETFSIZE.
  • Problem: All three checks are TST_EXP_POSITIVE on the return value. The test never reads the limit back (UL_GETFSIZE or getrlimit(RLIMIT_FSIZE)) after UL_SETFSIZE(value - 1), and does not compare the return value with the requested limit, so a ulimit() that returns a positive number without changing anything would pass.
  • Evidence: ulimit01.c:20-31; ulimit(3): “UL_SETFSIZE Set the limit on the size of a file … returns the new limit”.
  • Suggested action: after UL_SETFSIZE(current-1), check that the return value is current-1 and that getrlimit(RLIMIT_FSIZE).rlim_cur == (current-1)*512 (skip if current was unlimited).
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): NEW (second finding, secondary category UNDEF/medium; primary kept) via MUSL,BULK,RUN,SRC. Secondary to WEAK/medium. HPE musl, stdout to file: ‘TBROK: Test killed by SIGXFSZ!’ 2/2; to pipe: 3 TPASS; glibc: 3 TPASS. musl src/legacy/ulimit.c:15,18 has no RLIM_INFINITY case: GET gives 2^55-1, SET writes 512*that = 0xffff..fe00 (finite); kernel fs/read_write.c:1714-1718 reads it as negative loff_t -> SIGXFSZ on next write. glibc resource/ulimit.c:50-64 maps infinity<->LONG_MAX
  • Verification conclusion: New secondary finding: the test round-trips an unlimited RLIMIT_FSIZE through ulimit(UL_GETFSIZE)/ulimit(UL_SETFSIZE). POSIX (Issue 7, obsolescent; removed in POSIX.1-2024) does not say how an infinite limit is encoded, and musl turns it into a huge finite limit that the kernel’s signed comparison treats as negative, so the test kills itself whenever its output goes to a regular file. Under glibc the ‘value - 1’ call is a no-op (still infinity), which also supports the WEAK finding. Action: set an explicit finite limit (e.g. via setrlimit, then ulimit to a smaller value) and verify it with getrlimit().

testcases/kernel/syscalls/vhangup/vhangup02.c (runtest: syscalls/vhangup02)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: vhangup(2) succeeds for a privileged process (no doc block; old header).
  • Problem: The child calls setsid() before vhangup(), which detaches it from any controlling terminal. vhangup() then only performs the CAP_SYS_TTY_CONFIG check and calls tty_vhangup_self(), which does nothing when there is no controlling tty. The test therefore only verifies that a root process gets return value 0; the hangup itself is never exercised or observed. It is the success-side mirror of vhangup01 and adds very little coverage.
  • Evidence: vhangup02.c:26-33; linux fs/open.c:1579-1586 (vhangup -> tty_vhangup_self(), no-op without current tty).
  • Suggested action: either open a pty and make it the controlling terminal (TIOCSCTTY), call vhangup() and verify that reads/writes on the old fd fail with EIO / POLLHUP, or merge into vhangup01 as a trivial success subcase.

testcases/kernel/syscalls/writev/writev02.c (runtest: syscalls/writev02)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: writev() with an invalid iovec on a sparse file returns EFAULT and leaves the data previously written at offset 8k intact.
  • Problem: The EFAULT check is fine, but the integrity check cannot detect anything: the data written at offset 8192 is buf2, which is memset to 0 (indistinguishable from a hole or from zero-filled garbage), and the failing writev() is issued at offset 0 with an 8192-byte iovec, so even a buggy partial write could only touch bytes 0..8191, never the checked range 8192..16383. Old-API test with no docparse.
  • Evidence: writev02.c:108-109 (both buffers zeroed), 125-126 (8k write at 8192), 144-145 (writev at 0 with CHUNK=8192), 153-161 (compare at 8192).
  • Suggested action: fill the pre-written data with a non-zero pattern and verify both that bytes 0..8191 stay a hole/zero and that the file size is unchanged; merge with writev05 and convert to the new API (or fold the EFAULT case into writev01).

testcases/kernel/syscalls/writev/writev05.c (runtest: syscalls/writev05)

  • Category: WEAK (secondary: DOCS)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: “same as writev02” but the valid write is at the beginning of the file; writev() with an invalid iovec returns EFAULT and the file is not modified.
  • Problem: Writes 8192 zero bytes at offset 0, then a failing writev() of 8192 bytes at offset 0, then only checks that read() at offset 8192 returns 0 bytes. A writev of CHUNK=8192 bytes at offset 0 can never extend an 8192-byte file, and the content of 0..8191 (zeros, same as what garbage-free failure would leave) is never compared, so the only meaningful assertion is the EFAULT errno, which duplicates writev02. The header’s “sparse files” claim is wrong: the file has no hole.
  • Evidence: writev05.c:120-128, 153-166; writev02.c:144-151.
  • Suggested action: drop and keep one EFAULT test (writev02 fixed, or a writev01 subcase), or pre-fill with a non-zero pattern and verify content and size.

  • Claim under test: regression for the userstacktrace preempt count leak (kernel commit 1dbd195 “tracing: Fix preempt count leak”).
  • Problem: The script enables the stack tracer, the userstacktrace option and a page-fault event 10 times (the loop just rewrites the same values) and then prints TPASS unconditionally. A preempt-count leak normally appears as “BUG: scheduling while atomic” or similar warnings, not as an oops, and the old shell API checks neither dmesg nor taint, so a reproduced bug still PASSes. On architectures without exceptions/page_fault_kernel (only x86 and riscv have it), the else branch reads and writes events/kmem/mm_kernel_pagefault, which does not exist in mainline. The writes fail silently, no page-fault event is enabled, and the test still reports TPASS.
  • Evidence: ftrace_regression01.sh:46-80; /usr/src/linux: page_fault_kernel only in arch/x86/mm/fault.c and arch/riscv/mm/fault.c; no mm_kernel_pagefault anywhere in include/ or mm/.
  • Suggested action: port to the shell loader (tst_run_shell) with .taint_check or read /proc/sys/kernel/tainted before/after, TCONF when neither event exists, and generate user page faults while tracing is on.

testcases/kernel/tracing/ftrace_test/ftrace_stress/ftrace_tracing_cpumask.sh (runtest: worker of tracing/ftrace-stress-test)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: stress writing random CPU masks to tracing_cpumask.
  • Problem: CPU ids are drawn with tst_random 1 $range, so CPU 0 (and CPU 32k within each group) is never selected. On more than 32 CPUs the final mask=... overwrites the comma-joined multi-word mask with just the last partial group. The kernel’s cpumask_parse_user also treats the first comma group as the highest word, so even the intended layout is reversed. With 1 CPU, tst_random 1 0 is called with an empty range. The worker does no checking.
  • Evidence: ftrace_tracing_cpumask.sh lines 7-60; kernel/trace/trace.c tracing_cpumask_write() -> cpumask_parse_user().
  • Suggested action: generate masks with a simple loop over 0..nr_cpus-1 and write them in kernel bitmap order, or drop the worker.

Literal [ -n “LTP_IPC_PATH” ] is always true (dead check confirmed), but mutation ‘unset LTP_IPC_PATH’ before it -> TBROK ‘LTP_IPC_PATH is not defined’ from tst_res_ (tst_reinit, tst_test.c:201), rc=2: shell tst_res itself needs the var, so the property is still enforced; typo, no coverage loss

testcases/misc/crash/crash02.c (runtest: crashme/crash02)

  • Category: WEAK (secondary: DOCS, FRAGILE)
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: Robustness under random syscalls with random arguments; -n sets the number of syscalls tried (default 1000).
  • Problem: (1) sysno = rand() % MAX_SYSCALLS with a hard-coded 465 assumes the x86_64 table. Syscalls above 465 are never exercised. On arches whose numbers start at an offset (mips o32 4000+, n64 5000+) every call is ENOSYS. (2) exit, exit_group, rt_sigreturn, munmap and similar calls are not blacklisted. Any of them ends the single child early: rt_sigreturn with a garbage frame raises SIGSEGV, and exit/exit_group simply exit. Only one child runs per iteration, so far fewer than num_tries syscalls are made and the reported counts do not mean what they say. (3) Pass/fail is only “the parent survived”: signals and errors are counted as TINFO. (4) runtest/crashme describes crash02 as “Fork as many children as possible … can hang the system by using up all pids”, which is the old test’s description, not this rewrite (commit 16cd67ef1f85).
  • Evidence: crash02.c:16, :63, :24-36 (blacklist), :94-114 (single child, unconditional TPASS); runtest/crashme:10-12.
  • Suggested action: Pick syscall numbers from the arch’s real range (lapi/syscalls tables). Re-fork the child when it dies until num_tries is reached, or blacklist exit/exit_group/rt_sigreturn. Fix the runtest comment.

testcases/misc/math/float/float_bessel.c (runtest: math/float_bessel)

  • Category: WEAK (secondary: WRONG)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: j0/j1/y0/y1/lgamma give correct results, checked against “expected data” files, computed by 20 threads per function (README, tfloat.h “expected data”).
  • Problem: The expected data are not fixed reference values. main.c:generate() runs the genbessel generator at test start, in the test’s tmpdir. The generator computes them with the same libm functions on the same machine (genj0.c: tabR[i] = j0(Inc * i)). thread_code.c then compares j0(x) with j0(x). This can only catch non-determinism or thread-unsafety in libm. It can never catch a wrong result. For lgamma, the sign file is never compared (thread_code.c skips the exponent/sign check when fident is “lgamma”). The generator (genlgamma.c) declares a local int signgam = 0 that shadows libm’s signgam, so the sign file is all zeros anyway. lgamma is also called through an unprototyped double (*)() with an extra &tmp argument.
  • Evidence: main.c:82-94, :166-174 (runtime generation); bessel/genj0.c:46-52; thread_code.c:661-690 (strcmp “lgamma” skips the sign check); bessel/genlgamma.c:41,56 (shadowing signgam).
  • Suggested action: Ship real reference tables with the source (or compare against long double / known identities), or reword the test as a “libm thread-safety/determinism” stress test. Drop the dead lgamma sign file or fix it (use lgamma_r and check the sign).

testcases/network/nfs/nfslock01/nfslock01.sh (runtest: net.nfs/nfslock01_*)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: two processes lock lines of one file simultaneously and write to them, so NFS byte-range locking works.
  • Problem: Process 0 locks and writes only odd lines, process 1 only even lines. The F_SETLKW ranges [offset, offset+nchars) of the two processes never overlap, so no lock ever blocks or contends. A server or client that granted conflicting locks, or ignored locks entirely, would produce the same file. The test only checks that the lock/unlock calls return 0 and that disjoint writes land, not mutual exclusion.
  • Evidence: nfs_flock.c:71-105 (offset computation, odd/even only); nfs_flock_func.c lock_reg; nfslock01.sh:62-83.
  • Suggested action: Add an overlapping-range check, e.g. one process holds a write lock on the whole file while the other must see F_GETLK report it (lock_test() already exists) or get EAGAIN with F_SETLK, ideally from rhost as a second client.

VIRT: same as rpc_svcfd_create: rc=0 with fd0 inherited pipe, /dev/null, pipe, connected socketpair; rc=1 ‘could not retrieve remote addr’ only for unconnected TCP socket on fd0; svc_destroy is reached on a non-socket handle and only ‘checked’ by not crashing -> vacuous rather than fragile in practice
  • Verification conclusion: The test is vacuous rather than fragile: svc_destroy() runs on a handle built around a non-socket, and it is only checked by not crashing. Use a real connected socket.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): UNCHANGED via RUN,MUSL,SRC. HPE rpc_test.sh -c rpc_svc_destroy: glibc TPASS; musl TPASS. fd0 table identical under glibc and musl (rc=0 for /dev/null, pipe, socketpair; rc=1 ‘svc_fd_create: could not retrieve remote addr’ for unbound and bound-unconnected TCP). Logic is libtirpc svc_vc.c:236-252 (getsockname ENOTSOCK -> return handle), libc-independent; musl adds nothing

The result type is xdr_int, which allocates nothing; clnt_freeres() just runs xdr_int() in XDR_FREE mode, which returns TRUE unconditionally.   • Evidence: rpc_clnt_freeres.c “test_status = !clnt_freeres(clnt, (xdrproc_t) xdr_int, …)”; rpc(3) clnt_freeres: “frees any data allocated by the RPC/XDR system when it decoded the results”; xdr_int(3) has nothing to free.
  • Suggested action: require cs == RPC_SUCCESS and use a result type that allocates (xdr_wrapstring with a NULL out pointer against rpc_svc_1 STRPROCNUM), checking the pointer is handled; or drop as trivial.

  • Problem: test2’s limit ssh_num=$(echo "$pids" | wc -w) counts $pids, which is declared local and never assigned (the live list is $RHOST_PIDS). ssh_num is always 0, so the “Do not make ssh connection over the specified quantity” cap never applies and connections are spawned without limit for NS_DURATION seconds. Also, test_ssh_connectivity() only prints TFAIL and returns 0, so test1/2/3 go on and print “TPASS Test finished successfully” even when SSH is unreachable. test2 never checks whether any individual login succeeded.
  • Evidence: ssh-stress.sh:148 (local pids), :172 (echo "$pids" | wc -w), :104-110 (no non-zero return), :143/:206/:247 (unconditional TPASS).
  • Suggested action: use $RHOST_PIDS for the count; make test_ssh_connectivity return 1 and have callers || return.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): REVISED via RUN,MUTATION. HPE as-is: test2 TPASS ‘(64 connections)’ in NS_DURATION=10 with CONNECTION_TOTAL=10, ‘Max connections reached’ never printed. Mutation pids->RHOST_PIDS: 8x ‘Max connections reached’, TPASS ‘(18 connections)’ -> cap bug real. But test_ssh_connectivity’s TFAIL is still counted, so an unreachable sshd fails the run (TFAIL+TPASS), not a vacuous pass.
  • Verification conclusion: The cap bug is real: test2 spawns ~6x CONNECTION_TOTAL logins. The other half of the finding is overstated: test_ssh_connectivity() calls tst_res TFAIL, which is recorded, so an unreachable sshd still fails the run (it just also prints TPASS). Remaining issues are low verification (no per-login result checked, misleading TPASS after TFAIL) plus the cap bug -> WEAK medium. Action: use $RHOST_PIDS; return 1 from test_ssh_connectivity and || return in callers.

testcases/network/tcp_cmds/tc/tc01.sh (runtest: net.tcp_cmds tc01)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: reproducer for sch_teql NULL pointer dereference (fixed by 1ffbc7ea9160).
  • Problem: detection is dmesg | grep -q 'RIP:.*sch_teql'. “RIP:” is printed only by x86 (arch/x86/kernel/dumpstack.c); arm64 prints “pc : teql_destroy+… [sch_teql]”, and ppc/s390 print other formats. On non-x86 an oops kills tc, EXPECT_FAIL is satisfied, the grep misses, and the test reports TPASS on a buggy kernel. Old dmesg content is also not cleared or bounded, so an earlier oops in the same boot gives a false TFAIL.
  • Evidence: tc01.sh:36-42; /usr/src/linux/arch/x86/kernel/dumpstack.c:140 (RIP: %04x:%pS); /usr/src/linux/arch/arm64/kernel/process.c:223 (pc : %pS).
  • Suggested action: grep for an arch-neutral marker (e.g. sch_teql together with “Oops”/“BUG:”/“Call trace”), check the kernel taint before/after, and record the dmesg position before triggering.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/behavior/timers/1-1.c (openposix: conformance/behavior/timers/1-1)

  • Category: WEAK (secondary: WRONG)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: TIMER_MAX timers can be created with timer_create(CLOCK_REALTIME).
  • Problem: The loop bound is sysconf(_SC_TIMER_MAX). glibc does not define TIMER_MAX on Linux, so sysconf returns -1 (“no determinate limit”) and the loop runs zero times; the test prints PASSED without creating a single timer. The -1 case is not handled at all (no UNSUPPORTED/ fallback to _POSIX_TIMER_MAX).
  • Evidence: 1-1.c:24-31; getconf TIMER_MAX -> “undefined” on glibc; POSIX sysconf(): returns -1 without changing errno when the variable has no limit.
  • Suggested action: when sysconf returns -1, create at least _POSIX_TIMER_MAX (32) timers, or report UNTESTED; otherwise drop (timer_create01..05 in syscalls cover creation).
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION,MUSL,SRC. HPE glibc: timers_1-1 ‘Test PASSED’ rc=0; musl: ‘Test PASSED’ rc=0. sysconf(_SC_TIMER_MAX)=-1 under both (glibc sysdeps/posix/sysconf.c:293-297, TIMER_MAX undefined on linux; musl src/conf/sysconf.c:66 =-1) -> loop runs 0 times. Mutant with timer_create((clockid_t)-12345,…) built with gcc and musl-clang: ‘Test PASSED’ rc=0 under both

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/definitions/sched_h/19-1-buildonly.c (openposix: conformance/definitions/sched_h/19-1-buildonly)

  • Category: WEAK (secondary: DOCS)

  • Claim under test: “inclusion of sched.h makes visible all symbols in time.h”.
  • Problem: POSIX only says inclusion “may make visible all symbols from the <time.h> header”, so the stated assertion is not a requirement.   • Suggested action: drop, or replace with a check of what is required (struct timespec, time_t, pid_t defined by <sched.h>).

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/aio_suspend/4-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/aio_suspend/4-1)

  • Category: WEAK (phase 1: FRAGILE) (secondary: WEAK)
  • Confidence: low
  • Claim under test: On timeout, aio_suspend() returns -1 (EAGAIN).
  • Problem: The test relies on a fixed workload (6x2 MB then 20 MB, O_SYNC) still being in flight when it checks received_selected before and after a 10 ns aio_suspend(). If the selected write has already completed (fast storage, tmpfs TMPDIR where O_SYNC is free), it reports FAIL, not UNRESOLVED, with no kernel/libc bug. 9-1 tests the same EAGAIN-on-timeout assertion and handles “I/O too fast” by retrying with larger buffers.
  • Evidence: aio_suspend/4-1.c (diff vs 1-1): early-completion check returns PTS_FAIL; aio_suspend/9-1.c retry loop in test_main.
  • Suggested action: Drop in favour of 9-1, or return UNRESOLVED/retry on early completion.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): REVISED via RUN,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT. Not reproduced in 64 runs: HPE btrfs 16 (5 under stress), HPE TMPDIR=tmpfs 10, VIRT 8 (5 stress), VIRT TMPDIR=tmpfs under ltpstress 30 -> all PASS. Early-completion window is lio_listio() return -> received_selected check (us) vs 6x2MB+20MB serial writes; tmpfs does not make it hit. Redundancy with 9-1 remains
  • Verification conclusion: The early-completion FAIL was not reproduced in 64 runs, including tmpfs under load. The selected 20 MB write is the 7th request in glibc’s serial per-fd queue, and received_selected is checked microseconds after lio_listio() returns, so the mechanism is unlikely in practice. What stands is the secondary point: the test duplicates aio_suspend/9-1 (which retries when I/O is too fast). Recategorise as WEAK, low: drop it in favour of 9-1, or turn early completion into UNRESOLVED.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): UNCHANGED via MUSL,RUN,REPEAT,STRESS. HPE glibc: PASS 5/5; musl: PASS 5/5, and 5/5 under ltpstress. musl runs one thread per request with no ordering for non-append regular files (aio.c:250), so the selected 20 MB write starts at once, but early completion still did not happen. Redundancy with 9-1 remains

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/fork/3-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/fork/3-1)

  • Category: WEAK (secondary: UNDEF)
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: the new process’ ID does not match any existing process or process-group ID.
  • Problem: the test forks, waits until the child has exited and been reaped, then checks kill(child,0) and kill(-child,0) return ESRCH. That verifies nothing about uniqueness at creation time, and after reaping POSIX allows the PID to be reused, so a concurrently started process on a busy system could take the PID and turn the test into a false FAIL. The meaningful check (child PID != any live PID/PGID while the child exists) is not done.
  • Evidence: fork/3-1.c:63-90; POSIX fork(): “The child process shall have a unique process ID. The child process ID also shall not match any active process group ID.” (applies to the live child).
  • Suggested action: perform the check while the child is alive (e.g. child checks getpid() != getppid()/getpgrp(), parent checks kill(-child,0)==ESRCH before reaping), or drop as low value.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/gmtime/1-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/gmtime/1-1)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium (phase 1: low)
  • Claim under test: “The names in the broken-down tm structure should correspond to its values.”
  • Problem: the test only range-checks each field of gmtime(time(NULL)); it never checks that the fields correspond to the time_t (e.g. by comparing with a known epoch value or with timegm/mktime arithmetic). tm_sec is required to be < 60 although POSIX <time.h> specifies tm_sec as [0,60] (leap second); tm_isdst is accepted as -1..1 although gmtime should give 0. Low verification value.
  • Evidence: gmtime/1-1.c:29 (tm_sec < 60), :95 (isdst -1..1); POSIX <time.h>: “int tm_sec Seconds [0,60]”.
  • Suggested action: test against fixed time_t values with known UTC broken-down results (e.g. 0 -> 1970-01-01 00:00:00 Thu, yday 0), allow tm_sec 60.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION. HPE as-is PASS. Mutation: after gmtime() set tm_year-=30, tm_wday=(wday+3)%7, tm_hour=(hour+5)%24 -> prints ‘year 1996’ for time(NULL) in 2026 and still ‘Test PASSED’ rc=0: only range checks, correspondence to the time_t never verified

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/killpg/4-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/killpg/4-1)

  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,READ,GIT. HPE: Test PASSED as-is. diff killpg/2-1.c 4-1.c: same killpg(getpgrp(), 0) call; 4-1 returns PTS_UNRESOLVED (not FAIL) when killpg fails, so it cannot report FAIL at all. Both date from the 2002 import

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/lio_listio/15-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/lio_listio/15-1)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium (phase 1: low)
  • Claim under test: the error statuses are the same as those from aio_read()/aio_write().
  • Problem: nothing is compared against aio_read()/aio_write(), and no error path is exercised. It only submits 4 writes and 6 reads at offset 0 and checks with “(err != 0) && (ret != BUF_SIZE)”. Reads may run before the writes and return 0 bytes, and the && hides that, so the check amounts to “no request reported an error”.
  • Evidence: lio_listio/15-1.c:106-109, :168.
  • Suggested action: submit the same failing request (for example a bad fd, or a read past EOF) through aio_read/aio_write and through lio_listio, then compare aio_error/aio_return; use || in the per-request check.
  • Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): CONFIRMED via RUN,MUTATION. HPE as-is PASS. Mutation: the 6 LIO_READ requests at aio_offset 1 MiB (past EOF, read 0 bytes) -> still ‘lio_listio/15-1.c PASSED’ rc=0; check ‘(err != 0) && (ret != BUF_SIZE)’ only catches err!=0, nothing compared with aio_read/aio_write

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/mq_open/speculative/2-2.c (runtest: openposix: conformance/interfaces/mq_open/speculative/2-2)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: A name without a leading “/” has implementation-defined behavior.
  • Problem: Both branches return PTS_PASS, so the test only prints which behavior it saw. It cannot fail and checks nothing. Linux behavior is documented (mq_overview(7): name must start with ‘/’; glibc returns EINVAL otherwise), so a real check is possible.
  • Evidence: 2-2.c:33-45.
  • Suggested action: Drop it, or on Linux assert EINVAL as documented in mq_open(3)/mq_overview(7).
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): REVISED via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS ‘does not appear to support’ (glibc sysdeps/unix/sysv/linux/mq_open.c:36-37 EINVAL if name[0]!=‘/’); musl: PASS ‘may support names that do not start with /’ (musl src/mq/mq_open.c:10 strips an optional ‘/’). Suggested ‘assert EINVAL on Linux’ would FAIL musl, which POSIX allows (impl-defined): keep informational or drop.
  • Verification conclusion: The two libcs really differ: glibc sysdeps/unix/sysv/linux/mq_open.c:36-37 returns EINVAL when name[0] != ‘/’, while musl src/mq/mq_open.c:10 strips an optional leading ‘/’ and passes the name to the kernel, which accepts it. The test is still WEAK because it can never fail. But the phase-1 suggestion to assert EINVAL on Linux is wrong: that would FAIL on musl, and POSIX makes this implementation-defined. Corrected action: drop the test, or keep it as informational only. Never assert EINVAL, because the “/” rule is a glibc convention, not a Linux kernel rule.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/mq_open/speculative/26-1.c (runtest: openposix: conformance/interfaces/mq_open/speculative/26-1)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: mq_open fails with EMFILE when too many descriptors are open.
  • Problem: The loop stops at min(_POSIX_OPEN_MAX, _POSIX_MQ_OPEN_MAX) = min(20, 8) = 8 queues. The extra open reuses the last name (an existing queue). On Linux, RLIMIT_NOFILE (1024) and queues_max (256) are never reached, so the call succeeds, the test prints “did not fail” and returns PASS. EMFILE is never exercised.
  • Evidence: 26-1.c:49-67 (loop bound and the success path falls through to PASS).
  • Suggested action: Lower RLIMIT_NOFILE with setrlimit() and fill it, then require EMFILE. Otherwise drop the test.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/mq_timedsend/16-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/mq_timedsend/16-1)

  • Category: WEAK (secondary: FRAGILE)
  • Confidence: medium
  • Claim under test: assertion 16: abs_timeout is measured against CLOCK_REALTIME when Timers are supported.
  • Problem: The code is the same as 5-3.c (child fills the queue, blocks, and the parent’s sleep is interrupted when the send times out). The only difference is that the deadline comes from clock_gettime(CLOCK_REALTIME) instead of time(). Nothing tells CLOCK_REALTIME apart from another clock: there is no clock step and no comparison against CLOCK_MONOTONIC. It also inherits the 1s nanosleep sync before SIGUSR1 (see 5-3) and never checks errno==ETIMEDOUT or the child’s exit status.
  • Evidence: 16-1.c:80-87 vs 5-3.c (same child loop); 16-1.c:113-116 (1s sleep, then kill SIGUSR1).
  • Suggested action: Merge into 5-3, or make it test the clock basis for real (e.g. check the timeout against CLOCK_REALTIME with sub-second precision and check ETIMEDOUT in the child via its exit status).

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/mq_unlink/2-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/mq_unlink/2-1)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: destruction is postponed while references remain open, and mq_open(O_CREAT) may fail meanwhile.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/mq_unlink/2-2.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/mq_unlink/2-2)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: high

  • Problem: Both branches of the final mq_open(O_CREAT) return PTS_PASS. The parent also never closes its own mqdes before the re-create, so “all references closed” never happens, and the scenario is the same as 2-1.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_attr_setschedparam/1-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_attr_setschedparam/1-1)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: pthread_attr_setschedparam sets the priority used for threads created with attr (SCHED_FIFO).
  • Problem: The test never calls pthread_attr_setinheritsched(PTHREAD_EXPLICIT_SCHED). With the default PTHREAD_INHERIT_SCHED, pthread_create ignores the policy and param stored in attr, so the new thread runs with the creator’s SCHED_OTHER/0 (and no privilege is needed). The only check is that the thread function ran, which is true whatever setschedparam stored. 1-3.c is the version that does verify this.
  • Evidence: 1-1.c: no setinheritsched call; the only check is if (thread_created == 0). pthread_attr_setinheritsched(3): “The default setting of the inherit-scheduler attribute in a newly initialized thread attributes object is PTHREAD_INHERIT_SCHED.”
  • Suggested action: Drop it (1-3 covers this properly), or add EXPLICIT_SCHED and verify via pthread_getschedparam in the thread.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_barrier_init/4-1.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_barrier_init/4-1)

  • Category: WEAK (secondary: DOCS)
  • Confidence: high
  • Claim under test: pthread_barrier_init() “may fail” with EBUSY when reinitializing a barrier that is in use.
  • Problem: POSIX.1-2024 has no EBUSY error for pthread_barrier_init(). Issue 7 removed it: reinitializing a barrier while a thread is blocked on it is undefined behaviour. The test therefore invokes UB, and it returns PTS_PASS on every path: EBUSY, any other return code, or blocking (the SIGALRM handler also prints PASS). It can only fail if the earlier barrier_wait did not block, which barrier_wait/1-1 already checks. The header quotes the removed “may fail” text.
  • Evidence: 4-1.c:9-14,61-66,116-128; POSIX pthread_barrier_destroy.html: “The results are undefined if pthread_barrier_init() is called when any thread is blocked on the barrier”; CHANGE HISTORY Issue 7: “The [EBUSY] error for a barrier that is in use or an already initialized barrier object is removed; this condition results in undefined behavior.”
  • Suggested action: drop the test (the outcome is UB and it always passes). Alternatively, turn it into an informational UNSUPPORTED/UNTESTED report.

testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_create/1-2.c (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_create/1-2)

  • Category: WEAK
  • Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
  • Claim under test: pthread_create() creates a new thread with the given attributes.
  • Problem: The only evidence of the new thread is that pthread_cancel(new_th) returns 0. glibc returns 0 for any valid handle, including one whose thread has already exited (ESRCH is not required), so this says nothing about the thread actually being created or running. The thread is never joined, and main returns while it sleeps. 1-1, 4-1 and 5-1 already cover creation with real checks.
  • Evidence: 1-2.c test_main, ret = pthread_cancel(new_th); if (ret) FAIL; PASS.
  • Suggested action: drop as redundant with 1-1/4-1/5-1, or join and check for PTHREAD_CANCELED.
  • Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): CONFIRMED via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS; musl: PASS. pthread_cancel returns 0 for an exited thread in both: glibc nptl/pthread_cancel.c:62-68; musl pthread_cancel.c:105 -> pthread_kill.c:13-14 returns 0 when t->tid==0. So ‘cancel returned 0’ proves nothing about the thread running, on either libc.
